Small Remarks on Big Matters.

[Będzin — town affairs: express trains and income-tax appeals; commentary.]
We hear nothing.
The newspapers reported that a conference on railway matters would take place in Sosnowiec, at which the question of the express ("courier") trains that do not stop in Będzin would also be dealt with. The conference — the press writes — in which representatives of the Railway Ministry, representatives of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce and railway directorates took part, has already taken place; but somehow we hear nothing at all about what became of the question, which is so important for the citizens of Będzin. We do not know at all whether the question was even touched upon, despite its having been on the agenda. We are told that a train from Katowice to Kielce has been added, whereas about this question we hear not a single word.
It is superfluous to show how far the town has been wronged by taking away from it the trains that run far off into the European centre. Every citizen, industrialist and merchant feels this well when he wants to travel. Does the Będzin railway station then have smaller revenues than other towns, where the couriers do stop? We know the opposite: Będzin yields considerably greater revenues, and yet it is somehow treated as a kind of stepchild. No account is taken of the fact that Będzin is a large commercial centre, has a starostwo [district office], a military command, military people. Apparently that is what they think of it. That it is a done thing and a finished business; it has gone onto the "long bench" [been shelved] — and that's that.
So, it seems[?], they think in the "high windows"; but we must nevertheless[?] not put up with it. We must do everything possible to correct the fault and not let ourselves be wronged to such a high degree. One must see to it that action is taken on the part of the merchant community, the municipal administration, industrialists, official and semi-official institutions, representatives of the authorities, etc. A unified action must be adopted, which should strive to carry through the adopted [?] law[?] for the whole town, without distinction between citizens.
But action must be taken right now, before the drawing-up of the new summer timetable ("Fahrplan"), which runs from 15 May. Now, therefore, is the opportune moment for the question to be resolved in our favour.
Characteristic is only this: the question was put on the agenda, and somehow we do not know what has happened with it; we hear nothing at all as to whether it was dealt with at all. Therefore one should not fool oneself, one should not think that someone is already "lobbying" [chłopotać] there for us, while it is very possible that the whole matter has been put off and is perhaps lying somewhere[?] there in the left corner — at the very time when the town goes about with the opinion that the question will be resolved in the town's favour, for the benefit of the local citizens.
So we must not let the question be postponed; every possible means must be applied so that it is dealt with and resolved at the present moment. If not, we shall lose another whole year, and then the matter [will be] even more outdated [verb missing as printed] and consequently even harder to resolve in our favour.

The system of the "sitters".
As we write these lines, sessions are taking place in Będzin that consider the appeals ("recourses") on the income tax. Well, how easy it is now to pay taxes, and on top of that from income — one need not tell anyone; we all know how sad the situation is, how terrible things look, so that one need not be a great genius to admit that incomes are minimal and that taxes must therefore be lower, small.
Yes, superficially one may hold the opinion just expressed, but in reality it is not so. One must think more deeply into the matter. Well, when the question was considered at a time when people were earning, one could declare that X can pay more and Y — less; nowadays, however, it comes down to saying that the whole community cannot pay — individuals, of course, do not come into consideration — and this is naturally not easy: one must show why and how so-and-so cannot pay. And here the question arises: were the representatives given the opportunity to acquaint themselves with the situation; are they capable of accomplishing this even with the best will? The Jewish representatives on the commission consist for the most part of artisans. One knows all too well that the artisans are a broken mass, an element that has become even more benumbed[?] because of unemployment; they have been impoverished and languish in want and hunger; one cannot imagine at all in what conditions the impoverished strata now find themselves. Well, them — we want to hope — the representatives will be able to defend, because the representatives know all too well the sufferings of their brothers [printed "triders"] to be unable to represent them properly — although there is a second question: whether anyone will reckon with them. Seemingly, then, the question is solved by the fact that the representation is made up of the proper elements.
But in doing so one has forgotten one more thing: that apart from artisans there is in town a sufficiently large contingent of non-artisans. There are, after all, people who are merchants, small traders and people without definite professions, who also figure as merchants. Who, then, is able to defend this large element of people? Are the merchants and artisans, then, also represented in the proper measure? Do they too have their representatives in sufficient number? Just as a merchant cannot defend the artisan, so exactly the artisan cannot defend the merchant. After all, it does not help merely to say a kind word. It is not a matter here of doing a favour to whomever it may be, which would achieve nothing anyway. It is a matter of defence from a professional standpoint: one must be expert in the trade, in the branch; know what percentage one earns, what percentage [? is paid] remains, and what percentage remains as lost debts. Just as a draper ("manufaktura" merchant) or a haberdashery merchant cannot be familiar with the carpenter's trade, so exactly the locksmith cannot know how much the grocery ("colonial goods") or fruit shop earns; and talking just into the blue serves no purpose, for it is not a matter of arousing feelings of pity in anyone at all.
It thus gives the impression that the commissions are composed out of habit: people have got used to them, so they call them; apparently it is more convenient that way, and before people it has an air about it, it makes a good impression. And later, when a wronged person comes into the office ("urząd") with complaints, he will be heard out quite calmly and answered: what can we tell you? We really do not know whether you may not have been wronged at some point, but that is not our business; your case was considered by the commission, in which you were represented, and it presumably knows what it is doing and how high to burden you. So it is not within our competence. Yes, quite often we hear such answers, and there the taxpayer is left standing helpless, speechless.
That is why, and for this reason, every stratum must have its own representation, its own delegation, its own representatives.
The professional institutions, the trade associations, must therefore reckon with this phenomenon. Commissions must not be put together merely pro forma, for afterwards they cause harm — indirectly, true, but harm they cause, and indeed colossal harm, which cannot be remedied afterwards.
At the given moment we do not know how the appeals were decided, whether the injustices were redressed and considered, whether the too-high income tax was reduced; we hold, however, that in such a way it is an impossible thing, because no one can speak to the point and effectively when he is not familiar with the branch, with the facts of the case, not versed in them; and therefore the representation cannot be competent in matters foreign to it.
Selekt.
The Sins of the Little Lamb

[Opinion — a fable on corruption and selective justice.] By Ch. Horowitz.
The fable is well known:
Once a plague came upon the animals, and a trembling fell upon them all, that any moment now they would be wiped out.
So they decided to investigate and find out on account of whose sin the epidemic had come. The lion, the king of the animals, called together a meeting of all his subjects and ordered each one to tell what sin he had ever committed, so that it would be known whose fault it was.
When the king commands, one must obey. So they set about confessing their sins, each in his own way.
The bear tells how many living creatures he has killed with his paws and devoured. But the king waves it away with his hand. That does not count as a sin. A bear was, after all, created for that. The wolf tells how many creatures he has snatched [?] with his sharp teeth and swallowed. One might have thought that this was a crime for which the world of animals had been punished. But here too the king ruled that this could not be the cause. The wolf's snatchings [are] absolutely natural and justified.
Out comes the fox with his bundle of sins and tells how with his cunning tricks he lured in various living creatures and killed them. But here too the king sees nothing at all out of the ordinary for which anyone should be punished — that is what he is a fox for, after all.
In this way the confessions of all the larger animals were heard, those that tear and bite, trample and snatch. Each one has thousands of lives on his conscience, but the conscience stays clean, because that is the way of the world.
Until the time came for the little lamb to tell something about her sins. And indeed she told that once she had seen a cart of hay driving past and she had felt like eating. Well, she could not withstand the temptation, crept up from behind and pulled a little hay out of the cart.
Before the little lamb even had time to finish her whole confession, all the great beasts [?] together with the king had already realised what sin had been committed. They understood that the little lamb was guilty of the epidemic, and it did not take long before she got her well-deserved punishment.
• • •
Now there is an epidemic of sins and crimes, dipped and smeared in filth and mud. The whole of social life is infected.
No wonder one searches for its causes. One searches everywhere, in all the larger and smaller towns. A continuous [?] investigation is under way concerning those guilty of bribery, swindling, theft, robbery, unethical conduct and — what not?
Things have gone so far that one must search. Those who hold power can no longer sit by indifferently. They must at least do a little searching.
Whom are they searching for, and whom will they punish?
There are the bears, the wolves and the foxes, who stand at the top and operate in grand style with heavy paws, sharp teeth and cunning tricks, and demand countless victims in every sphere of life. Are they being searched for? Will they be found out? Will they be punished? It does not look that way. There will be no reason at all to be surprised if these are not noticed at all and their sins are not looked at, which do not count as sins at all, because that, after all, is why they are bears, wolves and foxes.
The only difference is that people are not always in the same skin. Today's bear can fall tomorrow and be turned into a little lamb. Then, when the might is taken away from him, people set upon him and settle accounts with him. From time to time you can hear of fallen heroes who together with their power have lost their innocence and, poor things, have fallen in disgrace.
But at the time when the sun was shining and the power was great, it was absurd to expect that the same people would be prosecuted and punished for things which, among little people on a smaller scale, are a crime.
A fine example of this is the story of a young, naive lad who wanted to get a little money to continue his studies. He had heard so much about "swindles" of millions and tens of millions that he decided he would at least like 100 gulden for a good purpose, even if it were through a "swindle". You understand, of course, that the lad was caught and thrown into [—; apparently prison]. A little lamb wanted to snatch a little hay from the cart.
That is only one case out of thousands. Every day small employees are thrown out of public institutions for conduct that is considered improper or unethical, irregular or against the principles of the institution. If it can also be proved that such conduct is illegal, such a person will moreover be prosecuted.
Well, one does not search for honest [sic; probably "dishonest"] or illegal practice among lawyers and doctors. Whom do they search for and whom do they catch? It is the poor little devil who could not withstand the temptation and tried in a single case to do something not quite right, and did it so clumsily, without insuring himself with "protekcja" [connections], that he was bound to get caught. He did not understand that those who do it successfully are the big ones, who work on a large "scale" and have a whole machinery that runs as if greased and where everything is insured from inside and from outside.
And whom are they searching for? It is quite well understood that the bears with the wolves with the foxes are quite far from the first fire.
Everyone is searching for the sins of the weak little lamb.
— From "Der Yud".

The Rebellion of the Sated.

It is a rare case, but everything happens. A short time ago I happened to spend a few hours among sated people; or more precisely, not among half-sated ones, but among wholly, one-hundred-percent sated people.
Our conversation turned on social questions of a general character, and later we moved on to our local hodgepodge [?]. And what can one talk about regarding local affairs, if not the kehilla, merchants, artisans, philanthropic institutions and the like?
The sated were angry [?], the sated were embittered. They have, poor things, not a moment's rest: the doorbell keeps ringing, and there is simply nowhere to hide. People come from various strata and for various purposes... and all of them want to rob him of his little bit of satiety.
And indeed, the situation of the sated man today... is not to be envied: he is restless and nervous, he is not allowed to enjoy his satiety. The sated rebel, they protest, they complain about every "guest" who comes to them in the name of a public institution.
They are angry at the kehilla — why does it ask too often [?]; and when one does give the couple of złotys, one wants thereby to buy off one's satiety and be rid of all uninvited guests and communal workers.
"What do you think," a sated man argues to me, "is it such a great pleasure to sit at a nicely served table with tasty dishes, in the decorated, cosily warm room, and to hear every few minutes a ring at the door, so that your heart drops? And when the bell rings I already understand what it means. Here come the representatives of the hungry, disturbing me in my satiety, robbing me of my peace, embittering for me the taste of the tasty dishes, cooling the warmth of my room."
There you have the tragedy of a sated man...
And perhaps someone thinks this is exaggerated? No, God forbid. The sated rebel against the hungry; in the big-city streets it is frosty, in the frozen cellar-rooms and the holes under the attics children lie in their beds covered with rags, waiting, trembling, for a piece of bread and a couple of potatoes that their father — the carter or street porter — will bring them toward evening; and it is no better in many middle-class homes either. Yesterday's former rich men, and today there is nothing to get through the day with, and with outward clothes one only covers up the hunger that gives no rest, and the shame of having to turn to people who are still sated.
And the sated man rebels...
He is surrounded by an enormous mass of tens of thousands of people — hungry, barefoot, naked and without prospects; he is surrounded by the endless misery of thousands of children who have nothing to bite on when they get up from their sleep in the morning, by the bitterness of women-mothers who have nothing with which to still the hunger of their little ones.
The sated lock themselves behind seven locks and hate this hungry mass, which peers [?] at them from all the cracks and holes; but the sated man's unease is a needless one.
He is well protected on all sides: not only does the physical force of the guards, whose calling is to keep order, protect him, but he is also protected by the apathy, seriousness [?] and hopelessness of the hungry man.
And therefore it is natural that the sated man rebels, because in the hungry man every spark of hope has been extinguished.
True, the number of sated people in the Jewish street keeps shrinking. The great mass of hungry, hopeless people is growing — so the sated, whose camp keeps getting smaller, must indeed intensify their protest and strengthen their rebellion...
Jewish rich men and well-to-do people protest ever more often, ever more brazenly, against the hungry who surround them on all sides. But the Jewish "krans" [?] that guards their satiety cannot, however, shut the doors entirely, and even with the greatest caution the winds of the hungry street burst into the warm, bright studies.
And they... the hungry Jews without a livelihood, from whom not only the possibility of earning has been torn away, but from whom every hope and every prospect has been robbed, drag themselves around various institutions, knock at the doors of various public figures in whom satiety has not yet blinded the eyes and dulled the feelings of the heart... and try to wrest [?] from whoever has one a sigh, a word of sympathy.
But mostly the Jewish, livelihood-less and hungry mass is silent. With the dead silence of the Jewish artisans' workshops that have died out, of the ruined and destroyed businesses; it is silent like a helpless child that does not know what to do. Sometimes such a silent man from the mass also tries to open his heart. The two little eyes of his innocent little soul [i.e. his small child] drive him into the street, force him to knock at the doors of various "benefactors," and sometimes also to disturb the peace of the sated rich man.
But in the hungry Jewish man of the masses there is no trace of rebellion; he is rather ruled by the boundless apathy of a condemned man, of a man without a tomorrow.
And if the hungry man does find sympathy, somehow gets a little bit of support — it is from the half-sated, from the intellectual worker, the petty bourgeois, the working man, from all those who toil hard and bitterly to secure their minimum of existence.
The sated rebel against the Jewish kehillas and philanthropic institutions.
The sated rebel... because the hungry are ruled by despair and apathy.
A. Cincinnatus.
The Artist of Pain and Want

[Zagłębie — culture; art criticism.] (On the picture exhibition of the painter M. D. Gottlieb.)
The first impression — grey. A large number of small watercolours, kept in very pale colours, some of them as if veiled in mist, and perhaps an even larger number of grey pencil drawings — and everything merges with the grey, dirty background of the walls, not repainted for a very long time, of the premises of the "Merchants' Association" ("Sokhrim-Fareyn"), where the exhibition has found its refuge.
But already on looking at the first pictures and drawings one sees [?] that the "grey" is the artist's true style: the pain, the want, the dull despair of poverty, the frozen exhaustion, the faded rags in which his figures are wrapped — these have taken hold of the artist's eye and made him see everything grey, grey, grey...
Perhaps it is chance that right at the entrance, on the right-hand side, hangs a small head, "Cold". This very "coldness" symbolises the whole work of M. D. Gottlieb. He has carried over onto canvas and cardboard pieces of cold, frozen life, and he forces the viewer to remember that in Łódź there is a Bałuty, a Pfeffer Street, in Warsaw — a Smocza with a Niska, in Będzin — a "Buka-khine" [?] and the like.
Yet the opinion that the living colours of nature are foreign to the artist would be wrong. Proof — the miniature "The Little Trees". It is a true masterpiece. On such a small piece of cardboard to give such deep perspective and so much charm! One simply cannot tear oneself away from the picture. True, this little picture too is breathed upon by the artist's melancholy mood, but it is "warm"; a piece of quivering nature pulses in it. It is a great pity that the artist did not exhibit more such things.
It is very desirable that the widest possible circles visit the exhibition. The aesthetic pleasure and the benefit will certainly be much greater than from the foolish cinema pictures. And associations ought to organise outings of their members to the exhibition.
Yitzchak Peschson.
Heard and Seen

[Feuilleton — Będzin and Sosnowiec; crisis and hunger, education, a prayer-house, the burial society.] By Ben Amotz.
Hunger and... dance.
"I have a request to you," an acquaintance of mine says to me, "it is very hard for me to tell you and pour out before you my bitter situation. You know me, after all — always a man of means, I kept a respectable house, never refused any communal need. But for several months now I have been without work, I have already sold many belongings and—"
"Speak plainly — what do you want of me?"
"What I want of you," he says, "is that you intervene so they take my boy back into the cheder. For a whole week now he has been sitting at home, because I don't have the 30 groszy a week to give for the tuition... More than once a week my children go to bed hungry, there isn't even a piece of bread for them..."
At that moment I see from afar a second acquaintance of mine; he is in a great hurry, not alone but with his wife. They walk together, talking loudly, playfully, and—
A plan is born in my mind. He, the second acquaintance, is after all one of the communal activists, and a well-to-do man at that; so I will hand him the Book of Lamentations of this new-type "Bontshe Shvayg" [Bontshe the Silent, hero of I. L. Peretz's story], who would be a happy man if he had thirty groszy to pay his child's tuition.
"Oh, przepraszam bardzo [I beg your pardon], we have no time, we're in a hurry."
"Niech pan wybaczy [please forgive us, sir]," the little wife pleads, "we can't dawdle, bo tam już wszyscy są [everyone is already there]."
I become curious and ask: where are you going so dressed up on an ordinary Wednesday, where?
"Nie wiecie? [Don't you know?] You don't know że szykuje się bal purimowy [that a Purim ball is being prepared]?"
"Well! What's the great joy with Purim? We have Purim every year!"
"Eh, it can't be compared with what used to be; today there will be a Purim ball with a dance competition, we don't want to be any 'wiansek'[?] [unclear Polish word — probably 'left out' / 'wallflower'], and we are learning
— to dance..."
After parting from the "dancing" couple, I recalled a letter from Moscow in the year 1916. At that time — so the newspapers wrote — one part of the population was feeding on cats and another part was bathing in champagne...
It came back to my memory because of these encounters:
— Children go to bed hungry, and mothers of grown-up children are learning to dance...
— Hunger and dance...
High time.
Together with all the mothers and fathers I listened to the lecture given at the last "wywiadówka" [parents' meeting] at the Jewish gymnasium in Będzin.
The professor, speaking about the problem of modern education, established a "diagnosis": that a closer contact is needed between the parents and the teaching staff.
The plan for this contact consists of this: a "Koło Matek" [mothers' circle] is being[?] created, and this new "council" is to root out the undesirable — better said, harmful — "microbes" that corrupt the children's souls.
During the so-called discussions around the "diagnosis" a series of "modern customs" were brought forward, namely:
— "Children play with immoral cinema pictures, see dissolute revues, the children eat bananas and oranges for breakfast at a time when other children of the same class suffer hunger"...
It goes without saying that a yasher koach is due to the initiators, who have given thought to the matter and understand the importance of a permanent contact between the school and the parents. But, Mr. Professor! It is not the "Koło Matek" that will have the power, in this painful matter, to cure the "modern disease" — "it is not upon you to finish the work"; this is not a problem of [unclear word][?] or of organising "wycieczki" [excursions]; the notion of "common contact" we understand differently: the question is not solved within the four cubits of the school, but further on, outside the school...
And if that contact is realised, you will learn of very many things that are in need of radical changes.
And may I be permitted to say to you, gentlemen initiators: you have good intentions? Then let your deeds be fulfilled[?].
— Let a parents' meeting be called; we will finally get together and talk things through with you. The theme of our conversation will hopefully perhaps be as important as the talk about bananas and about strengthening the children's appetites.
— Do not call parents' meetings in the form of "wywiadówki". It is already
— high time...
An "error" in the calendar...
"We have a 'great sensation' for your paper."
"A great sensation? Please, tell."
In the large Radomsko shtibl in Będzin — the young men say — an "error" occurred last Sabbath after the Torah reading.
"For instance?"
The congregation "forgot" that they had only just read the Ten Commandments, and did not react to a vile deed of the kind that can happen on Simchat Torah, when the crowd is already well tipsy.
When the prayer leader, an elderly Hasid, began to say the "loud" Shmone Esre of Musaf, he received
— a galosh to the head...
And since the congregation, among whom there are God-fearing and upright Jews, did not react to this, it is proof that they "erred" and thought it was Simchat Torah.
— An "error" in the calendar..
The same Yente, only differently veiled..
For several weeks now the Będzin Chevra Kadisha has been on strike, and — stop!
The strike has stopped at a "dead point" and does not budge from its place; even the labour inspector, who has an interest in liquidating every strike, also stands at a distance and is exactly as indifferent to this strike as the heads of the kehilla of the holy community of Będzin.
But there is a time for everything; to everything comes its season. If the "salvation" has not come from within, it comes from outside.
The Będzin Chevra Kadisha now has a "consolation": the Będzin "fire" has jumped over to Sosnowiec too and "infected" [zarażył] the community (gmina) there, which has declared war on the local Chevra Kadisha. The difference is only this: the Będzin Chevra Kadisha demands its debt from the gmina, while the Sosnowiec gmina wants to be master over the moneys that flow in from burials.
— "It's the same Yente, only differently veiled"...

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Mishpatim)

[Oneg Shabbat — weekly Torah portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's sidra.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Mishpatim
Parasha
—o—
a) "Now these are the ordinances which thou shalt set before them" (21:1)
1.
"Which thou shalt set before them" — what you, Moses, will do before them: you, Moses, must be the first to fulfil the ordinances yourself, before you go and preach them to others... Arono shel Yosef.
2.
"Which thou shalt set before them" — the laws and ordinances you must know before the deeds; not act first and only afterwards come and ask whether you did it according to law and custom...
Rabbi Israel of Ruzhin.
—o—
b) "And his master shall bore his ear through" (ibid., 6)
"Said Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai: the ear that heard at Mount Sinai 'Thou shalt not steal', and went and stole — let it be bored." Mekhilta.
We make a past of all our commandments — "which heard at Mount Sinai": once we heard about it at Mount Sinai, but today we don't hear it, it doesn't concern us. Therefore — let it be bored.
At Mount Sinai it is said "ve-lo yasaf", which Onkelos renders "ve-lo pasak" (and it did not cease) — those commandments must ring in our ears forever; today too it thunders from Sinai: Thou shalt not steal.
Yalkut ha-Derush.
—o—
c) "And shall cause him to be thoroughly healed" (ibid., 19)
It is characteristic — Rabbi Eizel of Słonim used to say by way of a jest — that both doctors and the dead have one name in Hebrew: doctors — r-o-f-'-i-m, and the dead — r-f-'-i-m; it turns out that both, the dead and the doctors, are called alike...
—o—
d) "The cause of both parties shall come before God" (22:8)
The well-known sharp-witted giant [?] Rabbi Shmuel Zanvil Heller was received as rabbi in Przemyśl in place of the gaon and tzaddik Rabbi Yosef Asher. As for Rabbi Yosef Asher: if he sent for someone to come to judgment and the other did not want to come, the man was punished at once. He was a famous wonder-worker. People trembled before him.
Once, when Rabbi Zanvil sent for a litigant and the man would not come, the beadle said: "Alas for those who are lost." With the late tzaddik this would not have happened — the man would have been punished at once.
"Believe me," Rabbi Shmuel Zanvil answers him, "I too can punish, like Rabbi Yosef Asher; the only difference is that in those days the householders were God-fearing and wholehearted, and as he decreed, so they fulfilled. But today, a dissolute generation — even when I decree upon them that they should die, they don't obey..." Imrei Tzaddikim.
• • •
"The wicked are called dead even in their lifetime."
So why [?] are they not buried?
Because they are such wicked people that they don't let themselves be buried... the Rabbi of Lissa.
—o—
e) "According to the dowry of virgins" (ibid., 16)
The following incomprehensible words we find in the commentary of the Ba'alei ha-Tosafot:
"Ke-mohar amounts to two hundred, and this is one extra, and the reading has authority."
A correct answer to these incomprehensible words we shall gladly print.
—o—
f) "Thou shalt not be to him as a creditor" (ibid., 24)
1.
All the commandments against oppressing a fellow man were given to the Jews right upon their exodus from Egypt, from slavery, because the oppressed person is so saturated with his oppression that it enters his blood, and later he uses it against his fellow — that is how it is psychologically.
Apiryon.
2.
"Thou shalt not be to him as a noshe (creditor)" — noshe also means forgetting ("God hath made me forget"). When one lends a friend money and he has nothing to repay with, one forgets [?] the former friendship...
Siftei Da'at.
—o—
g) "And thou shalt take no bribe" (23:8)
Rabbi Yehoshua Falk, the Rabbi of Płock, used to say about rabbis who take bribes from young men in order to appoint them as ritual slaughterers:
"The rabbis behave like peasants. I once saw a peasant buying a scythe — he tests its edge on a coin. The rabbis too test the slaughterers' knives on a coin..."

Easing the Enforcement Pressure
[Poland — taxes.] The enormously heavy and harsh pressure of enforcement, in which the tax offices distinguish themselves, has provoked many protests and great bitterness among taxpayers.
The large enforcement costs have increased the tax pressure even further. Never before have tax distraints been so frequent a phenomenon as lately.
As we now learn from a reliable source, the Ministry of Finance has now issued a new circular, which arrived these days at the Treasury Chamber.
In the circular the ministry demands that, in view of the economic situation that has arisen, the enforcement pressure be eased.
As we learn, in connection with the circular the enforcement costs are to be reduced, and in general more caution is to be exercised in carrying out tax distraints.
Important Celebrities on the Polish Radio

The management of the Polish Radio [Polskie Radio] endeavours, as far as possible, to have the greatest artists — those who have already made a name for themselves in the world as phenomenal performers — appear before its microphone in the course of the winter season.
Beginning in autumn 1932, such musical talents appeared before the microphone of the Polish Radio as the famous Viennese singer Schumann [Elisabeth Schumann] and the pianists Backhaus [Wilhelm Backhaus] and Hoehn [Alfred Hoehn].
In November we heard one of the greatest composers of our generation — Sergei Prokofiev, who played at the great symphony concert in the Warsaw Philharmonic as well as in the studio of the Polish Radio.
Among the piano artists one must also mention Aleksander Uniński, the laureate of the International Chopin Competition, and the second laureate, the blind Imre Ungár.
From the group of singers the coloratura virtuoso M. Kurenko [Maria Kurenko] distinguished herself.
In December the world-famous masters Horowitz [Vladimir Horowitz] and Artur Rubinstein appeared. Aleksander Uniński also appeared once more, as did the famous German composer Paul Hindemith.
During the recent broadcast of Wagner's opera "Tristan and Isolde" from Dresden we heard the best German opera singers.
Mention must also be made of the broadcast from Geneva, from which we heard the piano-jazz artists Wiener and Doucet [Jean Wiener & Clément Doucet], who interpreted a series of dance hits in masterly fashion.
In the near future the appearances are scheduled of the violinist Váša Příhoda (26 April) and of the outstanding pianists: the Frenchman Robert Casadesus (24 February), Alfred Hoehn (16 March) and Nikolai Orlov (29 April).
In addition, international concerts are scheduled, namely: on 3 March from Geneva, with the participation of the best Swiss artists, and on 8 March from Berlin, from where we shall hear Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, for which the greatest soloists of Germany have been specially engaged.
The list of world celebrities enumerated above, who have already appeared and will yet appear before the microphone of the Polish Radio, proves that the programme management of our radio sees to it that its listeners have true artistic enjoyment and the opportunity to hear the greatest performers.
Although the number of radio listeners in Poland does not exceed 300,000 people, the radio listener already has, thanks to the efforts of the radio management, the opportunity to hear the greatest performers with a world name.
The Polish Radio, however, constantly strives to improve and broaden the scope of its programmes still further. For this task to be fully accomplished, the number of radio listeners must necessarily rise. Then the radio's income will grow, thanks to which it will become possible to engage artists with a world name for the radio concerts.
A Few Complaints of a Będzin Jewess in the Land of Israel (4)

[Feuilleton — Land of Israel; instalment 4, conclusion.] By J. Stawski, Tel Aviv.
In the „paper“ [the ruling] it said thus: since the court cannot establish who does throw [the rubbish] and who does not, they therefore make a compromise, that all the tenants („lokatorn“ [lokatorzy]) shall pay 25 piastres each and the landlord — 50 piastres!
In short, why should I drag it out for you[?], I had to pay the 25 piastres right there on the spot, otherwise they wanted to lock me up! Well, the landlord — when he had to lay out the half-pound from his fat purse, I thought he would die a strange death! He was so red and sweaty, as if he had come out, begging your pardon, of the bathhouse. That is how the „sendzia“ [sędzia — judge] flogged him with the half-pound!
Well, that I squabbled is no wonder, since I am a poor woman, and what kind of in-law am I to pay, when with the landlord the core is not clean!... That is the sort of Cossack[?] justice your „sendzhes“[?] [judges] have here — such justice on the landlord together with them!
Well, back we went with a hora[?], so that the streets boiled: the landlord in front and the 17 tenants behind, and we laid a few curses into him — may at least a tenth of them come true for him!
Well, I read out the whole „tokhekhe“ [the chapter of curses] at him... until he ran into a car and got away!
Such are the dealings I have here! What did I ever know about landlords? I had my own home, my own place, and was, as they say, a housewife like other people... I fancied the Land of Israel, so that my landlord — may they drag him out — should drag me around here through the courts...
Well, we'll be going. I still have, believe me, plenty[?] of work today!...
What else did I want to tell you? Yes! I have seen how the Yemenites walk about here! A curse on my head, when I catch sight of them, with that gait of theirs — everything goes dark before my eyes! What a black year is this, that they have no shame at all and crawl around in those long women's shirts! I imagine, if a couple of Będzin householders went out like that — why, truly, the whole town would run out to gape at the wonder[?]!...
Well, the Arab trousers please me about as much as my troubles.. But, be that as it may, at least they don't go naked!
Well, good day to you. It is high time, you hear, that the Messiah should come and make some sense of things in the Land of Israel!
She went off a few steps and turned back. Listen, she says with a little smile, I nearly forgot... You write something, the children say, for a Zagłębie paper — so I want to ask you not to write any stories about me, because back home there is a crowd that they call Yiddishists, and when they hear about the troubles I have in the Land of Israel — it will be, once again, Simchat Torah for them!
You think they really are, God forbid, such enemies of mine? — No! Their whole anger is only that I went to the Land of Israel. They say that Będzin is also quite a fine town for them, and there is no need to look for new lands, to break and stab yourself and make yourself into ash and ruin!
You think they are not right? But there is also a crowd that they call Hebraists, and they say exactly the opposite: that one must only go to the Land of Israel and one may by no means stay in Będzin!
So, as you hear, they can drive you mad: this one says — go, that one — don't go, and go figure whom to obey! Yes, and on top of that there is a business there with Yiddish and with the Holy Tongue, so don't even ask! The Yiddishists say that one must learn Yiddish, although, believe me, never in my life have I learned any Yiddish, and nevertheless — if only I knew the Holy Tongue as well as I know, thank God, Yiddish!..
Along come the Hebraists and say that one must learn the Holy Tongue. I don't side with „these“ or with „those“, but one has to tell the truth: a child must be able to say „ha-motzi“, say „modeh ani“, and when it grows older — it must know a portion of Chumash with Rashi, a bit of Gemara — as befits a Jew!
Well, we sinful women already have to read the „sidra“ in plain Ivri-Taytsh.. but a man won't go and read my Taytsh-Chumash, or say my tkhines, which are composed only for women!...
Then the Yiddishists come again and say, however, that the Holy Tongue is no language at all! Now that's a puzzle: if so — how then does God understand what we pray and what we say to Him?..
Along come the Hebraists and say that Yiddish is no language — a sign of it is that God gave the Torah in the Holy Tongue! The Yiddishists say that from the Torah there is indeed a sign that the people of Israel always spoke Yiddish, because had they understood what was written there — they would never have taken[?] such a „bargain“!..
In short, this one speaks — and this one is right; that one speaks — and, it seems, that one is right, and that's how it goes on for now, at table and on the benches! Well, I am a simple Jewish woman, maybe I don't understand their arguments all that clearly, but it's merry in the shtetl — people pull each other's „czuprynas“ [forelocks], just like me and my neighbour who speaks the Holy Tongue... Meanwhile I've remembered that I still have to do the washing today, and she has already hurried out with her „balyes“[?] [bundles of laundry] and will grab all the lines on me...
Well, good day to you, and remember, don't you expose me in the paper, because then, you hear, you'll have no shortage of troubles!
As you see, dear readers, I present her life to you and describe, nevertheless, her complaints... Perhaps it is indeed an injustice, but what can I do, it is my livelihood after all — should I take up[?] writing tefillin?!...
(The End)
On the Way to the Land of Israel. (Notes from a car journey from Będzin to Tel Aviv)

[Vienna — journey to the Land of Israel; travel notes; Nazis.] (Notes from a car journey from Będzin to Tel Aviv).
In the company of Nazis:
During our passage through Vienna we stayed a few days at the "Herberger" [Herberge — hostel], a kind of home for poor students. After the two nights we had slept there alone in the whole house, just the seven of us, the manager gave us the good news that tonight instructors of a certain party would arrive here, eighty persons in number.
At 7 in the evening they did indeed arrive. The manager prepared a bed for the night for each of them. To us, too, came 12 "guests"; they looked over the hall, greeted us and went away.
Two hours later they came again, this time in a bigger company: all 80 men came into the hall where we were, and some of them greeted us. They all sat down around a long table, probably wanting to hold some kind of consultation. Apparently they guessed that we were Jews, because soon afterwards one of them stood up and announced to the assembled that for certain reasons the consultation would not take place today.
We sat, each absorbed in his work: one was reading, another writing, etc. We kept ourselves at a certain distance from them. Now we already understood with whom we had the honour. Only one way out remained for us: not to provoke them, because we were fewer in number. We therefore resolved to be as friendly as possible, in order to avoid any conflict between us and them.
It just so happened that one of our comrades was sitting at the table finishing a large blue-and-white Star of David, painted on the cover of a big book with the inscription "Poland—Eretz Israel" in three languages, among them also German. The comrade was not frightened and went on with his work. For to break off the work would have meant capitulating to them, and that is exactly what we did not want — although we were afraid that because of the innocent "Star of David" the conflict would break out.
But exactly the opposite happened. After their consultation, which had not come about, they dispersed; only a small number remained.
Those who remained sat down around the table and began a conversation with us. We answered their questions politely, but with a certain reserve. To their question where we were going, we answered briefly that we were going to Palestine, where we would help build the Jewish land. When they heard from us that we were going to help build our own land, they were as if thunderstruck; the gentiles fell into rare admiration, expressing their delight at the Jewish achievements in the Land of Israel, and the upshot was that we spent time in their company until late at night.
Next morning they took friendly leave of us, wished us a happy journey and went away.
That same day we read in the newspapers the report under the headline:
"Hooligan attack by Hitlerite hooligans on the Jewish department store 'Herberger'."
The course of events was as follows: "At 10 in the morning stink bombs were thrown into the department store. Many customers were in the shop, doing their shopping for the Christian holidays. Someone cried out 'Fire!' — a terrible panic broke out, everyone pushed towards the exit, and many people were crushed and injured. The attackers could not be detained. We guessed who the attackers were. I went at once to Robert Stricker, with whom we often met, and Stricker passed on our suspicion to the police.
Two days later, in the provinces, according to the list that the management of the "Herberger" had issued, "swastika men" were arrested, eighty in number, who will soon stand trial.
With these very hooligans we had been in company a few days earlier, and they had wished us success on our journey to Palestine...
S. H.
Jews Have Nothing to Fear.

[Germany — the Jews in Hitler's Germany; the Leipzig Fair.] (From our Leipzig correspondent).
The Leipzig Fair Office is sending to all Jewish newspapers throughout the world the following statement:
The new German Reich cabinet has already declared itself clearly and plainly regarding the Jews in present-day Hitler-Germany. This statement of the government reads:
"In order to reassure foreign Jews concerning their brethren in Germany, we declare that the new German cabinet strives to bring calm and peace to all German citizens. We have no intention whatsoever of letting ourselves in for foolish experiments."
The Reich President, the Reich Chancellor and the whole government are obliged by their oath to protect all citizens of the country in general, and also every individual citizen of the country in particular, without any distinction of his religion or nation.
As regards the Leipzig Fair, which opens on the 5th of March, it is assured that calm and order will prevail throughout. In Germany people are preparing for the elections. On election day there is always the greatest order.
All the more so during the Fair in Leipzig, which is after all the vital nerve of the entire economic life of the whole country. Bound up with the Leipzig Fair are the honour of the whole of German industry and the future of German exports.
Throughout the country it is considered a matter of course that during the journey to the Leipzig Fair and the whole time of the Fair the greatest courtesy must prevail towards everyone, without any distinction of religion or nation.
It goes without saying that the people of Leipzig themselves see to it by all means that calm and order should prevail in the city, because the Leipzig Fair is after all the basis of the existence of the greater part of the inhabitants of Leipzig.
As proof in Leipzig's favour may serve the fact that, for example, right after the war, when in Belgium and in France almost everyone was agitating against Germany, Belgians and Frenchmen at the Leipzig Fair never at that time felt that they were "enemy aliens".
In Leipzig it has never yet happened that anyone complained that he was not received with the greatest respect because he was of another nation or religion.
It is worth mentioning that all year round, too, the best relations and the greatest mutual esteem prevail in Leipzig between Jews and non-Jews in cultural, economic and social life in Leipzig; in the book trade, in the fur trade, in the charitable institutions and the like the Jews play a very large role, and in Leipzig in recent years it has never happened that Jews should have any unpleasantness whatsoever.
Z. Haber.
Humour — In Soviet Russia

[Humour — anecdotes from Soviet Russia.]
The forge of Soviet humour never stops working, even in the very worst and gloomiest times. There is not always bread enough to eat one's fill, but the humour is not lost and pours itself out in characteristic stories and anecdotes, which are very witty.
•
A peasant is going to church. On the way he meets a Communist.
The Communist asks the peasant whom he is praying for now.
The peasant answers that he is praying for the Soviets.
"And whom did you pray for before?" asks the Communist.
Frightened, the peasant answers that before, he used to pray for the Tsar.
"Good," answers the Communist, "but do you know what became of the Tsar, what end he came to?"
"I know," answers the peasant, "and that is exactly why I pray for the Soviets..."
—
Rumour has it that a grandiose universal department store will soon be built in Moscow, with several dozen storeys, to be staffed by just one clerk. The clerk will stand all day long at the entrance to the building and repeat to every single person the words: There is nothing to buy...
—
A Soviet citizen wants to travel abroad. He submits a proper application to the G.P.U. He receives a summons to report to the G.P.U. The official asks him:
"What do you want to leave for? Don't you know the saying: everywhere is good where we are not?"
"Of course I know the saying," answers the citizen. "Everywhere is good where you are not — that is exactly why I want to leave..."
A King Who Fled His Throne in the Middle of the Night

[Historical serial — Henri de Valois, the king of Poland who fled; part 2.]
(Historical story) — by Al-Be.
2)
For readers who have not read the beginning of this interesting story, we give the summary:
In the year 1572 the Polish king Zygmunt the 2nd [Sigismund II Augustus] suddenly died. There was no one to be his heir, because he died childless. Around the throne an internal struggle flared up between the nobles and the Protestants, and there was a threat that civil war would break out in the country.
At last the parties came to an agreement to call a national assembly in Warsaw, and at that assembly a new Polish king was to be elected.
The French "empress" [so printed], the widow de Medici [Catherine de' Medici], seized the opportunity; she longed for her youngest son Henri [printed "Hegri"] to be elected king of Poland.
She was helped by the then French ambassador in Warsaw. By various means they succeeded, and on 11 May 1573 Henri was elected Polish king.
The new king was not pleased with the throne. He wanted to be free and to spend his time with his beloved, the Princess of Condé, but at his mother's command he took over the Polish throne.
When he had been king for barely 13 months, his brother Charles the 9th died in France, and Henri, the Polish king, became the lawful heir to the French throne.
And Henri, the Polish king, schemed how to leave Poland.
At last it happened: by night he fled from Kraków.
—
Henri fled from Poland on the 18th of June 1574. Accompanied by several friends he went out outside the town, ostensibly to take a walk in the evening hours. While walking he excused himself to his companions, asking them to wait for him, and went off by another road; and when he was already far from the town he leapt onto the horse that had been made ready beforehand and galloped at speed a whole night without stopping, until he reached the Austrian border.
The next day, when the Polish people learned that their king had fled, it made their blood boil. Could such an insult be done to Poland?
The people's anger reached its peak, and large groups formed which, arming themselves with sticks, sickles and other weapons, set out on the road to chase their king and bring him back to the throne at any price, by fair means or foul.
Their effort, however, was in vain.
The bands of Poles returned without a king, and once again friction and strife began over a new king.
Henri did not flee straight to France; he was in no hurry to take over the French throne, being sure that his mother, Catherine de Medici, would stand guard so that the throne would fall into no other hands but his.
Henri, the fugitive Polish king, after crossing the Austrian border, was sure he had nothing to fear. Here, in the Austrian realm, he was free and did whatever he pleased. He reckoned that he need not hurry to Paris. The French throne would wait for him, and indeed he lingered in Vienna, Venice and other cities and caroused for all he was worth.
It took two months for Henri to reach Paris. When he came home, bringing with him the diamonds taken from the Polish crown, he was received with a warm welcome and a great parade. His mother Catherine wanted to create a festive mood in the country in honour of the new French ruler.
On his arrival a whole staff of dressed-up ladies, rakes and also various animals from the zoological garden awaited him.. A disgusting scene it was.
And indeed it was not long before Henri the Third was anointed King of France.
In his time the French people too was torn to pieces; civil war raged in the country. The new king, who by nature was unfit to rule, did not concern himself at all with the interests of the country, made no attempt whatever to restore internal order and took scarcely any interest in affairs of state.
The whole apparatus of state, full power, was therefore in the hands of his mother and her favourites, who steered the helm of state, while he, the king, devoted himself to empty, foolish, childish amusements and was always surrounded by women.
The king had a particular craving to dress up as a woman and play all sorts of ugly pranks, or he would amuse himself with dogs, monkeys and donkeys like a little child. He was also a great coward and showed childish fears; above all he was afraid of thunder, and when it began to thunder he would hide in a cellar.
Many times feelings of piety came over him, and putting on a sackcloth of penitence he would join a religious procession barefoot; he would also disguise himself as a beggar and go from house to house collecting alms. On his beggar's rounds he was accompanied by his wife, the queen, and a whole retinue of men, women, dogs and cats.
Once a magnificent ball took place in the imperial palace. At this ball were the whole cabinet of ministers, courtiers and prominent guests, among whom was also the king's cousin, who coveted the French throne.
King Henri, who had a weakness for foolish pranks, came to the ball dressed as a woman.

The Kehilla Council Struck It Out, a Commission Was Elected, and the Little Shochtim Go On Slaughtering...

[Będzin — community.]
As our readers know, after the kehilla council struck the salaries (pensje) of the new “little shochtim” [ritual slaughterers] out of the new budget, a commission was elected whose task was to determine whether new shochtim are needed at all.
To this day the commission has not dealt with the shochtim question, and meanwhile the new little shochtim go on slaughtering, receiving 50 zł. a week each from the gmina [the Jewish community].
As we are told, the shochtim question does not depend on the commission but on the well-known “strong” shochet, who has the main say in the slaughterhouse, and “what he wants is what must happen”...
Conference of Merchants and Small Traders on the District Physician's Ordinance

[Będzin — commerce.]
Some time ago the district physician (lekarz powiatowy) ordered merchants and shopkeepers that shops selling articles of basic necessity may not be together with living quarters.
The Small Traders' Association then intervened with the starosta [district head], and it was obtained that the decree be held back until the 15th of March this year.
Because the matter is becoming topical, on the initiative of the board of the local Small Traders' Association a conference of all merchant organisations in Zagłębie was called.
In the conference, which took place on Sunday in the premises of the Small Traders' Association, representatives of the merchants' associations of Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Czeladź and of the Chamber of Commerce took part.
After a lengthy discussion it was decided to work out a proper memorandum about the decree. The memorandum will be sent to the starosta, the voivode and other competent bodies, so that the ordinance, which falls upon the merchants and shopkeepers as a harsh decree, be withdrawn.
A Plan to Lower the Prices at the Municipal Bathhouse.

[Będzin — municipality.]
The head of the economic department at the local magistrat [town hall] has presented to the commissioner [government-appointed mayor] a plan to lower the prices at the municipal bathhouse.
According to the plan the charge for a bathtub will amount to 80 gr., the steam bath (“shvits”) — 30 gr.
The discount prices in force until now, which were valid only on Wednesdays, are to be abolished.
A Horrible, Cruel Deed by a Drunkard.

[Będzin — crime.]
Last Sunday a horrible incident occurred in Ksawera [a district of Będzin], in which 30-year-old Kubiczek fell victim.
The incident unfolded as follows.
In the evening a group of drunken workers met in Ksawera, and a sharp exchange of words began among them.
At a certain moment Kubiczek's companion, a worker, ran up to him and cut Kubiczek's throat with a razor.
Because of the heavy loss of blood Kubiczek fell dead on the spot.
The Chief Cantor of the Białystok Synagogue Leads the Prayers This Sabbath in the “German” Shul.

[Będzin — cantorial music.]
The music lovers of Będzin have an important guest this Sabbath. The chief cantor of the synagogue in Białystok, Mr. Yosef Baniubka [?], will lead the prayers this Sabbath, Shabbat Mevarchim, in the “Daytsher” [“German”] shul.
Mr. Baniubka is a pupil of the famous Białystok cantor Mr. German of blessed memory. He possesses great musical gifts and arouses delight with his strong voice and beautiful nusach [traditional prayer chant].
Inspection (Lustracja) at the Gmina.

[Będzin — community.]
On Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday the vice-starosta, Mr. Mandyszewski, carried out a lustracja [official inspection] of the activity of the gmina [Jewish community] in the year 1932.
During the inspection Mr. Mandyszewski listened to the cries of the kehilla officials, who come into the gmina day after day for their salaries (pensje).

[Będzin — community life.]
On Sunday a brawl took place between Avraham Mandelbaum and Gutensztajn in the Radomsk [Radomsko Hasidim's] shtibl. The brawl broke out over taking revenge on young Gutensztajn, who on the Sabbath had dealt a blow to the baal musaf [leader of the Musaf prayer], Mr. Shlomo Mandelbaum.
Visit of Rabbi Engel's Son-in-Law to the Talmud Torah.

[Będzin — education.]
This week the well-known Torah scholar Morgenstern of Kraków, a son-in-law of the famous prodigy (ilui) Rabbi Yosef Engel of blessed memory, stayed in our town; he visited the Talmud Torah and examined the pupils of all classes.
Mr. Morgenstern expressed his satisfaction with the studies at the Talmud Torah.

Festive academy of 'Gordonia'

On Monday a large performance took place in the hall of the 'Nowości' cinema in connection with the 11th yahrzeit (anniversary of death) of the late leader of 'Gordonia', Aharon David Gordon.

The academy opened with the Polish and the Jewish anthems. Then Mr. Yehuda Epula-Lewicz [?] gave the opening address, speaking about Gordon's significance for youth in general and for 'Gordonia' in particular. Next the floor was given to the emissary of the Keren Hayesod directorate in Poland, Mr. Jakub Gożałka [?], who in his hour-long, substantial lecture explained the important and incomparable work of A. D. Gordon, dwelling only on the 3 words engraved on Gordon's tombstone: adam, oved, teva (man, labour, nature). The lecture was listened to attentively. The first part ended with a march-past (défilade) to the sounds of the orchestra.

The 2nd part, performed solely by the members themselves, as well as the 3rd part, showed the talent and ability of the Będzin 'Gordonia'.

Festive academy in honour of the 'Keren Hayesod' campaign in Będzin

On Sunday evening a festive academy took place in the 'Capitol' cinema with the participation of Deputy Yitzhak Grünbaum, dedicated to the 'Keren Hayesod' campaign in Będzin.

After the 'Hakoach' orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems, the academy was opened and chaired by Mr. Marek Szajn, who greeted the distinguished guest Mr. Grünbaum in simple words and stressed that the 'Keren Hayesod' is no longer a philanthropic institution, but an institution that yields profits and helps to build the national home in the Land of Israel.

On behalf of the Zionist Organisation Mr. Wygodzki gave a greeting, appealing for support of the 'Keren Hayesod' campaign at the present moment.

After the written greeting from the Revisionist Organisation in Będzin, Mr. Grünbaum was given the floor for his lecture on the subject 'The situation in Eretz Israel'.

With a series of interesting figures the speaker described the great achievements of the 'Keren Hayesod' and appealed to every Jew to contribute to the 'Keren Hayesod', in order to put an end to the thousand-year wandering in exile and to help build the Jewish national home in the Land of Israel.

The two-hour lecture was listened to attentively and the distinguished guest was showered with loud ovations.

Finally the orchestra once more played 'Hatikvah', and with that the academy was closed.
'Mother's Day' at Folk School 8 in Będzin

On Sunday a celebration called 'Mother's Day' took place at Folk School no. 8 in Będzin.

A large number of mothers took part in the celebration. After a rich programme of Yiddish folk songs, performed by the pupils under the direction of Mr. Aharon Barenblat, the mothers present made contributions for the free kitchen that operates at the school.

The song 'A Mother's Heart', performed by the mandolin orchestra under the direction of Leon Barenblat, won great applause.

Sosnowiec: Conflict between the community board and the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha

A 'Chesed shel Emet' society has been founded.

As our readers know, the deputy starosta Mr. Mandyszewski, while inspecting the activity of the community (gmina), ordered that all money from the community's revenues must be paid into the community treasury.

On the basis of this order the community board passed a resolution to take away the hitherto 'autonomy' of the Chevra Kadisha, so as to have proper control over the money coming in from the burial plots.

The resolution provoked opposition among the gabbaim of the above-mentioned society, who argued that the money for the plots, from those interested in buying a place in the cemetery, must remain, as until now, with the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha.

On this ground a sharp conflict arose, which led to the community board deciding at its Sunday meeting to found a 'Chesed shel Emet' society. In addition the community engaged 4 employees as burial attendants (mitasskim) and fixed for each a pension of 1,200 zł a year.

The Wł. Medem Children's Sanatorium in Miedzeszyn.
The 20th century has been called the century of the child. And indeed, what has been created in the last few decades is often to be admired. In this respect first place has been taken by Austria.
In Poland too this idea has lately awakened. But how far behind we still lag compared with Europe...
And on the Jewish street, where bitter want reigns, the crowding of the dwellings, unemployment, poverty and the mortality of the children, is it not terrible?
You walk through the Jewish streets of Warsaw, Łódź or some other town and you look at the children, who live through weeks[?] without seeing a scrap of sun, and you begin to understand why the percentage of tuberculosis patients among the Jews is especially high.
And it is out of this boundless want and terrible poverty that the Medem Sanatorium has grown.
Dozens of domestic and foreign newspapers and serious journals have already written about this sanatorium; men of science from Germany, America, France, Switzerland etc. have been delighted with it.
During the 8 years of its existence the Medem Sanatorium has passed more than 4000 children through its bright walls[;] 115[?] children in winter and 160 children in summer stay there permanently. They form there a true children's state, which is run by the children themselves.
Great medical care (2 doctors, 1 dentist, 4 nurses) with all the most necessary facilities, extraordinary understanding and true, sincere love for the child, the impressive cleanliness of the institution: these are only a few of the attributes of the Medem Sanatorium.
The official state institutions too, the greatest Polish authorities in the field, speak of the sanatorium with enthusiasm. The only Jewish children's sanatorium in Poland, which has earned a great world name, and it remains for us to wish it that it may be able to get out of the great financial difficulties in which it now finds itself, and that it may grow and develop ever more and ever better.

On Sunday, at an entertainment in the folk school in Modrzejów, a tragic accident occurred.
When one of the guests, a certain Cipek[?], put on his coat, a revolver fell out of the pocket; it went off and mortally wounded the cloakroom attendant.

Echo of the blood libel in Zawiercie.
In connection with the blood libel spread against Mr Liberman in Zawiercie, the local Endeks called a meeting at which the question of ritual murders was raised. The Endeks came out with "tongue", hurling all kinds of filth at the Jews. At the meeting, however, was the landowner, the apostate Mr Holenderski, who strongly opposed the attacks. The apostate assured the hooligans that the Jews have never taken blood for matzot, since he too was once a Jew.
Ben Ir [a native of the town].

Communiqués sent in.

The "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Będzin.
The Keren Hayesod campaign is in full swing in Poland. The visit of the great guest Mr Yitzhak Grünbaum left a strong impression on the town; the traces of his convincing explanations about the supremely decisive moment of hastening the building of Eretz Israel can be felt in the Keren Hayesod work, and despite the depressing situation of the Jewish middle class one must note with satisfaction the fact that precisely among the poorer strata the activists are received cordially, and with true self-sacrifice they sign their pledges to the Keren Hayesod for quite satisfactory sums. In general one notices among all donors a very serious attitude, and they know how to appreciate properly the great importance which the Keren Hayesod has today.
As an exception to the successful work so far we have only to record the conduct of the well-known local magnate and brewery owner Mr S. Rozenblum, who received the delegation in a very tactless manner and refused to sign even the most minimal declaration for the building of Eretz Israel. We wish to believe that this case will remain the only one in Będzin.
The Keren Hayesod Committee.

The 2-day general strike is to begin today in the coal mines of Upper Silesia and Zagłębie

As we have already written, in connection with the industrialists' decision to cut wages by 15 percent, a congress of workers' delegates was held in Katowice, which adopted a resolution to proclaim a 2-day protest strike in all coal mines in Upper Silesia and the Zagłębie districts.
The protest strike begins today, Friday, at 6 in the morning and will last until Saturday at 12 at night.
During this time all work in the mines will be stopped.
The workers' unions have distributed appeals in which the working class is called to fight for its rights.
The workers' union „Polska Praca“ is against the strike and calls on its members not to show solidarity with the strikers.
*
Tomorrow, Saturday, a conference with the participation of the coal industrialists will take place at the Ministry of Social Welfare in Warsaw.
Today they begin issuing vouchers for food products from the Będzin municipality / Dąbrowa cattle „ran off“ to Będzin

Today, Friday, at the distribution bureau „on the Wałes“ in Będzin, the issuing of vouchers to poor Jewish families who receive food products from the Będzin municipality will begin.
The vouchers were supposed to be given out only on Saturday, but thanks to the efforts of the guardian (opiekun) Mr A. D. Balimański[?], the vouchers will be given out from today.
Each member of the family receives 2 kilos of rye flour.

Dąbrowa cattle „ran off“ to Będzin.
The community (gmina) has a loss of 200 zł.
On Wednesday afternoon the Dąbrowa shochtim (ritual slaughterers) were late in coming to the slaughterhouse. The butchers, thinking that the shochtim were on strike, drove the cattle, 30 head in number, to Będzin for slaughter.
Through this mistake the Dąbrowa gmina has suffered a loss of two hundred zł.
As we are informed, the kehilla board together with the rabbinate will apply to the Będzin kehilla board to return the 200 zł. which the gmina took from the Dąbrowa butchers.

The kehilla board in Dąbrowa has already completed the tax (etat) lists of the supplementary budget for urgent aid to the poor Jewish population.

„If You Bring Shochtim at 25 Zł. a Week, We Will Bring Rabbis at 50 Zł. a Week“

[Dąbrowa — Kehilla.] This is how the Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] parnassim (community board members) threaten the local rabbi.
As we have already written, the starosta, after the inspection (lustracja) of the Dąbrowa kehilla, ordered that the monies coming into the gmina (Jewish community) be divided among the officials on a proportional basis.
The further part of the order says that, because the income from shechita (ritual slaughter) fell considerably last year in comparison with the year 1931, the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) are to take an oath by handshake (tki'as kaf) before the Dąbrowa rabbi that no illegal slaughter is carried on by them or by their families...
On the basis of the order concerning the proportional payment of the salaries, the president of the kehilla, Mr. Neufeld, called all the kehilla officials to a meeting, at which the starosta's order was handed over to them.
Also present at the meeting were the parnassim Kleinman and Nussbaum, who declared that the shochtim must receive their salaries as hitherto, so that „the question of kashrut will be properly safeguarded by the shochtim“.
The rabbi, who does not receive his proper salary from the gmina, was against this opinion and declared that the gmina should carry out the order of the starostwo (district office).
„If the shochtim — says the rabbi — go on strike, I will bring here shochtim who will be content with a salary of 25 zł a week“.
To this parnas Nussbaum answered: „If you bring shochtim at 25 zł. a week, we will bring rabbis who will demand no more than 50 zł. a week“...
As we are informed, the shochtim have resolved not to agree to any compromise whatsoever, and it is to be expected that we stand on the eve of a struggle in the communal life of Dąbrowa.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
A Bloody Family Tragedy.
In Zabrze a man shot his wife dead and seriously wounded her father.
The couple had quarrelled two weeks ago, and she had left with her child for her parents.
On Saturday night the man went there, to the flat of his wife's parents, with the aim of taking back the child. When he asked where the child was, he was answered that the child was asleep.
At a certain moment he pulled out a revolver and began shooting. Hit by the bullets, the wife's father fell into a pool of blood.
When the woman saw this, she went into another room and hid under a wardrobe. But the enraged man ran after her and with several shots laid her dead on the spot.
The murderer has been arrested.

A Two-Day Protest Strike against the Wage Reductions.
On Sunday the congress of all the mine delegates took place in Katowice. More than 600 delegates came, belonging to all tendencies. After the speeches of Deputy Stańczyk and of representatives of other parties it was decided to proclaim a two-day protest strike against the wage reductions.

A Letter to the Editor.
[Zagłębie — letter to the editor; labour and unions.]
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
In connection with the note in the previous issue of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ concerning the non-employment of Jewish workers in my bakery, I have the honour to clarify the real truth about the accusation hurled against me.
In my bakery, which has existed for some 40 years already, Jewish workers have always been employed, and now too I am ready to do so, on condition that the union, which supposedly fights for „holy ideas“, will recommend qualified workers to me, and not such as do not know the baker's trade and have only the intention „to realise Bundist socialism in my bakery and to bend the ‚Jewish bourgeoisie‘ down to the ground“... And it is precisely for these reasons that the whole conflict arose, which is being falsely spread by the gentlemen, and I am branded as an „enemy of the Jewish worker“.
By the way, it is worth drawing the public's attention to the fact that the gentlemen shouters do not take the wrong done to the Jewish workers so much to heart; their anger is also because the non-Jewish workers in my bakery are not members of their union..
Finally I wish to remark that I pass over the street gossip to the order of the day.
Respectfully, Józef Kac.
