What Is Heard Regarding a Passover Campaign?

[Sosnowiec — Welfare and philanthropy.] The newly founded "Beit Lechem" and the other philanthropic institutions — to whom should the mission be entrusted?
In Sosnowiec people began to look around, and they saw that the general situation was getting worse from day to day, that one could not go on standing like this with folded hands, helpless; that one must enter into the situation of the impoverished and the oppressed and must not let him fall into the bottomless depths — and for that purpose a "Beit Lechem" ("House of Bread") was created, whose task is supposed to be to help the one who has fallen, to share the feelings of the one who has become impoverished, not to let him lose his balance, not to let him remain in despair.
It goes without saying that institutions of this type are a necessity today, and one can only welcome it when such an undertaking comes into being. All this would have been fine, however, if we had had something to record to the credit of the said institution, if we had seen that they relieve the need, help to ease the hard situation of the hungry and the frozen. The institution surely ought to have done something in the course of the hard winter months — so why has it achieved nothing at all in its field? Why did it give neither bread, nor potatoes, nor coal to the one who needed provisions and still needs them? As soon as the institution was founded it must surely have had its aim, its purpose, its tasks — so why does it not fulfil them, why does it not carry them out? After all, one does not need to create an institution merely so that it gets registered and Jewish Sosnowiec is enriched[?] by one more philanthropic establishment on paper only. Better that something which brings no benefit should not be created at all, because that which brings no benefit not only fails to ease the hard situation, but actually harms the cause and disturbs the activity of other institutions. The work of a "Beit Lechem" must be carried out intensively above all in the winter months, precisely when it is hardest for the poor man to get by, hardest to exist.
We nevertheless want to believe that the administrators of the said institution do bear the responsibility on their shoulders, so that they must keep well in mind for what purpose they created the institution and what they intended by it; and from precisely this standpoint the public has the right to demand of the founders that the institution should not merely exist on paper, but should be properly put into practice and should perform real deeds.
If the initiators have until now taken their responsible work lightly, they must not continue to do so from now on. If in the hardest winter months they did not hand out any coal and potatoes, then from today on they must set about the useful work that will help relieve the need of the hungry.
We must render an account to ourselves of the hard situation in which we live, and we must remember that before Passover arrives — a festival which since olden times has been very hard to bring into the Jewish home, let alone in the present bitter time, when one no longer has the strength to think and to earn even a dry piece of bread — it ought therefore to be the task of the "Beit Lechem" to begin already now to take up the matter and to carry out a broad relief campaign in honour of Passover, so that it should help relieve the need and bring Passover into the home in a dignified and modest manner.
It is a rule that Sosnowiec does not respond warmly to relief campaigns; the citizens of Sosnowiec are always harried and busy, and to support such campaigns they will never have time for you; therefore the "Beit Lechem" must already now begin to make the necessary preparations, so that the campaign can be properly carried out.
One must not forget that at the present moment one cannot undertake a Passover campaign merely to discharge an obligation, merely to do what has to be done for appearances' sake; it must be taken into account that nowadays one will have to give the oppressed as much as possible, because the fallen will not be able to buy anything, and what they do not receive they will not have. Moreover, one must not forget one more thing: however many recipients one may reckon with, one will still be mistaken in the count, because one cannot at all imagine whom else one will have to count among the recipients. It is possible that many of those from whom one would want to take will themselves have to be given to — so colossally has the number of recipients risen and the number of givers fallen.
Therefore there is indeed a duty to begin already now to take up the matter, to treat it broadly and from all sides, and not to approach it haphazardly at the last minute, because the present Passover campaign must be conducted with deliberation and forethought and must bring the proper benefit to the broad strata of the impoverished Jewish population.
It would be more systematic and rational that the Passover campaign here should not be fragmented, that not everyone should "make Sabbath for himself", that no separate little shops should be set up, but that there should be one centre, one distribution point, which would provide for the impoverished masses without distinguishing to which camp and sphere the hungry person belongs, because it is self-evident that all the hungry must be provided with food.
So a kind of union must come into being in this field, in order to enlarge and multiply the necessary Passover relief campaign. It would therefore be desirable that the philanthropic institutions which are entertaining the idea of organising Passover campaigns should come together for a consultation and confer on the matter: to whom can this important mission be entrusted, which this year must turn out in a very dignified manner. It goes without saying that the mission must be taken over by safe hands in which Jewish Sosnowiec has confidence; otherwise the great and holy ideal is turned into a little shop in which nobody has any confidence, and then, God forbid, the necessary campaign could be ruined — which would be an unheard-of scandal, because in that case people would go hungry in the literal sense of the word.
Yes, one must set about the necessary work, and one must explain to the Jewish citizens what it is all about, so that those who have the means to help others should do so wholeheartedly and not try to get off cheaply[?] and hunt for "bargains".
—
And therefore we say: first of all the mission must be entrusted to responsible people in whom there will be confidence, and only then will it be necessary, without any excuse, to "work on" the stubborn rich men of Sosnowiec, so that they become accustomed to giving such contributions as befit their dignity; for precisely the rich men of Sosnowiec — be it said without disparagement — always[?] try to get off cheaply[?] when it comes to necessary charity, while the most expensive and the most luxurious plays no role for them [i.e. they spare nothing on luxuries].
But this is not only about the rich Jews. Everyone will have to care for their impoverished sisters and brothers, who find themselves in a state of tremendous impoverishment to which people had not been accustomed until now; and therefore the necessary preparations should be made already now, in order to carry out the Passover campaign in a proper manner and bring renown and honour to Jewish Sosnowiec.
Dr. Papuri.
The New “Pozhondkes” (Arrangements)

[Feuilleton.] It was a few days ago. I took a “droshky” [cab, Pol. dorożka] to ride to a certain place outside the town.
The driver was an elderly Jew with a long beard and a pair of large, clever eyes. His whole physiognomy somehow did not rhyme with his simple trade. And I began to suspect that the fellow was a refined Jew, for in the old days you would come across such curiosities. In some other places carters were well versed in the “small print” [“drobne osiyes”, the fine print of the commentaries]...
In any case I became curious to take his pulse, to strike up a conversation with him and see whether my guess was right.
But he was very busy whipping his scrawny, lean, undersized little horse. With the force of the whip he tried to explain to it and convince it that on a weekday one may, according to the law, take “large strides”...
The four-legged creature listened to him as one listens to a tomcat and dragged itself along slowly. He honoured it with a couple of original Będzin curses, sighed deeply and turned his face to me.
— You are surely in a hurry, — the carter said to me in an apologetic tone.
— No, I have enough time — I answered — leave your poor horse alone, let it go as it goes; what can you expect from such a small, starved creature!
My words touched a wound. His face clouded over and he cried out in annoyance:
— A small, weak little horse he is to you, but[?] you don’t know that he costs me a lot of money. A whole fifty złoty I paid for him, may he drop dead! A demon in his rotten bones!
I shrugged my shoulders and expressed great admiration. And precisely this, it seems, gave him a bit of satisfaction, and he talked on quite mildly in these words:
“And do you have any idea what the whole harness cost me — a fortune! The droshky alone costs 200 zł. Besides that, the horse-collar with the other ‘she’ar yerakot’ [odds and ends]. And now the police have decreed that every cabman must have two little lamps on both sides of the droshky. Tiny trifles, you would think, but how great is their price! Small too is the droshky, but how burning-dear it is!
“Yes, my friend — the driver sighed, giving the ‘dear’ horse a couple of good lashes meanwhile — times change, and we — willing or unwilling — with them.
“There were times when I lived in a small shtetl ten miles from here. Twice a week I used to drive here. My wagon was as big and long as the Jewish exile. Over the wagon I stretched a linen canopy to protect the passengers from the rain; a big lantern, a real ‘pillar of fire’, hung in front to light my way. My horse was as big and tall as Og, King of Bashan. Every leap of his left a verst behind him; he truly worked wonders of ‘kfitsas ha-derekh’ [miraculous shortening of the way]. And you ask what he cost? — it is a shame to say — as you see me alive!
“And the journey, even in winter, was a delight. When it got a little colder there was a remedy for it — an inn. Every three versts you had an inn, and I with my several minyans of passengers would climb down from the big wagon and go into a big room, sit down like counts on big long benches beside a big long table. We would take a big glass, gut[?] a big, long, fat-bellied schmaltz herring, eat a big ‘double-eight’ wheat roll and wash it down with a big beer glass, and for the whole feast we paid a couple of copper ten-groszy coins.
“But today, my friend [misprinted ‘freygt’], there is a new ‘pozhondek’ [order, Pol. porządek]: a little horse, a little cart, a little whip, little lamps, everything small. You go into an ‘inn’ to refresh your heart, you get a tiny, half-watery glass of schnapps, a small piece of bread, but when it comes to the chapter of ‘Reb Yankev Meshalem’ [the paying], you must, begging your pardon, take out the purse and pay like a [shote — word unclear].
“That, my friend, is the new reduction system. Oh, how dear it is, how great its price!
“You look at me strangely; maybe you think I have had a drink too many. But I assure you that you are mistaken, I am as sober as you and I know what I am saying. And if you think that the cheapening system exists only in the things I have listed here, you are mistaken again.
“You have probably happened to be at a ‘bris’ [circumcision]. Then you have heard what they say there: ‘Ze ha-katan gadol yihye’ [this little one shall become great]. Well, I tell you that these words sound harsh today, false: once it was indeed true, but today the matter is just the opposite. The little circumcised soul is now, precisely now, big, because it has been sanctified with the holy sign. But from now on it becomes smaller and smaller. The bigger he grows, the smaller the little Jew in him becomes... So that it would be, lehavdl, better fitting to say: ‘Ze ha-gadol katan yihye’ [this big one shall become small].
“Once among Jews, when a father was privileged to see his little boy reach five years of age, he would wrap him in a big long tallis and carry him off in great parade to the heder. There he would grow in Jewish learning as if on yeast. From the little siddur he would quickly move on to the bigger book called ‘Khumesh’, and from the Khumesh he would soon rise to the great Gemara, and only then would he [go on] in a great yeshiva, where the scholar in him grew bigger and bigger.
“But today, my friend, it is a time of schools, of gymnasiums; there is no time for Jewish studies. Jewishness is taught on the tip of a knife, everything follows the reduction system. Instead of the big books one uses tiny method-booklets[?]. One barely reaches the Khumesh, and if one does reach the Khumesh, it is a ‘kitsur’ [abridgement], a shortened, clipped, reduced one. The great Gemara, however, most people are not privileged to reach at all.
“Yes, my friend, such a time has come now. Don’t look at the fact that I am a carter; I was brought up in those days when the enlargement system reigned, and I too, thank God, tasted the flavour of holy books; that is why my heart aches so over today’s small ‘pozhondkes’, which have also penetrated our synagogues and batei midrash.
“Once, when you entered a synagogue, you found Jews wrapped in big long tallisim with enormous big tefillin on their heads, praying with great devotion.
“And when you entered the beis midrash you found big tables around which camps of Jews sat on big long benches and studied from big books.
“Today, my friend, the big tallisim have vanished, the big tefillin, the big tables, the long benches with the big books. Tiny silk little tallises, crumbs of tefillin, small benches and tables, while books[?] — not even for a remedy.”
Such was the sermon the carter delivered. And when I sat down today to write my feuilleton and could not find any Zagłębie topic that would touch my heart, I remembered that sermon and decided to discharge my feuilleton duty with it.
By the way, it can, at a stretch, be applied to our town too...
Ploni u-Vokhen.

The Jewish Artisan Must Wake Up

[Economy — artisans; article.]
The general economic crisis, which now holds almost the whole world in its iron grip, has of course had a fatal effect on the crafts and on small industry as well. But when people speak lately of combating this crisis, they have in mind only commerce, manufacturing, agriculture and big industry. Nobody gives any thought to rescuing small industry and the crafts, which the general crisis has already brought to the brink of total ruin.
If we look more closely at the state of the crafts among the Jews in Poland, the question appears far sadder still, because we Jews, for our many sins, have no understanding whatsoever of craftsmanship. We simply refuse to understand that the Jewish artisan is, in contrast to our predominant mercantile element, the most productive part of Jewish society.
Part of the blame for the decline of the crafts is borne by the Jewish artisan himself, who has so far remained passive toward his own everyday questions of life and interests. The Jewish craftsman is to this very day a raw mass, ridden by a handful of individuals, a handful of craftsmen with "mercantile" leanings.
The Jewish artisan is still sunk in a deep lethargic sleep, and his so-called leaders and chiefs are not at all interested in dragging him out of this "hen-roost" [? — word unclear].
The Jewish artisan has now reached a parting of two ways: one leads to his eventual revival; the other — to certain and complete ruin. Such moments are always the most important in the life and further development of a class.
The artisan is not the only one going through such a crisis; but neither the merchant nor the small shopkeeper has to fight under such conditions as those that have fallen to the lot of the Jewish craftsman.
It must be said openly that no social stratum is so helpless, so blind and dependent in the struggle for its existence as the Jewish artisan, who has already become the symbol of neglect and helplessness because of his passivity in the very most burning everyday questions of life.
The Jewish artisan has become a lump of clay to be kneaded, into which every bungler and careerist thrusts his hands and makes of it whatever his heart desires; the Jewish craftsman is like a kind of golem, into which everyone wants, so to speak, to breathe a spirit of life.
And as if it were not enough that he has become like clay in the potter's hand, a lump of clay for such kneading experiments, the Jewish artisan still believes with perfect faith that the shape given to him by this or that of his "providers" is indeed the true face of a craftsman.
But no! By no means!
That is not, and must not be, the true face of the Jewish artisan; that is not how the craftsman should look, on whom the future of a people is built; that is not how the new generation of Jewish craftsmen should be brought up!
We have already pointed out that to a certain degree the Jewish artisan himself is to blame, because he has not yet tried to reflect on the causes of his material and spiritual decline; because he has not yet tried to understand that self-awareness and education are perhaps no less necessary than air for breathing and a livelihood for keeping body and soul together.
While being thoroughly productive for society, the artisan is utterly helpless for himself; and that is precisely why he has such meagre standing and such little importance in public life.
Perhaps such a naked truth will not please some of the artisans. But the great majority of Jewish craftsmen should take it in good part, because what has been said above is, after all, the naked and bitter truth, without which one cannot make the correct diagnosis of the morbid lethargy into which Jewish craftsmanship has sunk.
One can no longer deny the fact that at a time when the whole cultured world supports and fosters every initiative for and about popular education, we observe among Jewish craftsmen exactly the opposite phenomenon: not only is there absolutely no concern for the spiritual condition of the simple artisan, but among us blindness and ignorance among craftsmen are actually maintained and cultivated.
It is very sad, but at the same time also "sympathetic" [probably a misprint for "symptomatic"], that some artisan activists quite often boast of their scant education and sometimes even of their complete ignorance; it goes without saying that these are purely demagogic manoeuvres, meant to tickle the ambitions of the very simplest artisans (that is: if a simple artisan can be a real big shot), and with such, so to speak, "injections of ambition" our craftsmen are being "culturally" educated...
We neither wish nor are able to go here into exact details about this artificial cult of ignorance among our craftsmen; here we wish only to touch, in very general strokes, on the causes of this disease.
Just as in former Tsarist Russia, the Jewish craftsmen's organisation is now being suppressed as well. Meanwhile, new laws and decrees appear day after day, which demand of the artisan in general, and of the Jewish artisan in particular, first and foremost general and vocational education; but the Jewish artisan, unfortunately, cannot cope with all these innovations, because, having taken a moral lesson from his "elders", he has not yet understood how to appreciate the value of general and vocational education, believing indeed that an artisan should and must be a simple "amkha" [common man].
But not today, not tomorrow — such a state of affairs will nevertheless have to come to an end, because the guild law, which perhaps hits the Jewish craftsman most sharply, has already come into force in all its severity, and those who do not wish to go under completely will have to adapt to it, willy-nilly.
We are far from being 100-percent devotees of the guild law, but one virtue of it is beyond all doubt: its strict impetus to train the craftsman culturally, technically and professionally — the craftsman who, as we have pointed out above, is far from being the least productive factor in the general economic structure of a people.
And if the guild law, too, does not succeed in tearing the Jewish artisan in Poland out of his lethargic sleep of up to now — then his further fate is sealed...
Natan Rodiner.
Whom Are They Punishing?

[Taxes — article.]
It concerns the so-called "kary" [Polish: fines], the monetary penalties for overdue taxes, which the tax offices impose with a liberal hand on the taxpayer, who is downtrodden enough as it is.
There is constant talk of remitting overdue taxes; it is discussed in government circles and in the Sejm, and certain decrees in that direction have even already been issued. At the same time, however, the tax offices go further [?]: they punish the "sinful" taxpayer for the "sin" of not having the means to pay by imposing on him, on top of the basic tax, a special levy which they call a penalty ("kara"); for these monetary fines — of which, just as of the tax itself, they cannot collect a single grosz anyway — they distrain the last poor belongings, for which there are no buyers anyway. They merely fill up the storehouses and ruin the merchant's existence down to the ground.
But is it really in the interests of the state that its citizens be reduced to poverty by the tax offices and driven to ruin?
Whom, then, is one punishing here in the end? If the taxpayer is unable to pay the principal of the tax, he is already a punished man anyway; will the penal measure of carting off his belongings turn him into a solvent taxpayer and, in general, into a citizen of the country capable of existing?
Clearly: enough of the penal distraints on citizens whose "sin" consists in being unable to pay the tax! Enough! More consideration! With such measures one does the country only a bear's favour [a disservice], and in return a definite harm to the citizen, who is, after all, not to blame for the crisis.
A. Y.
A little letter to my Będzin friends before my departure for Palestine.

[Feuilleton — a farewell letter to Będzin.] Yoel Mastboym.
A little letter to my Będzin friends before my departure for Palestine.
Very soon now, my dear ones, I shall leave your black-diamond treasures and move over there, to the land of cedars. There I shall probably meet your Będzin Jews and Jewesses who have perhaps already forgotten their beloved little coal-wagons, sit in their orange groves, flirt with their orange orchards and live the good life — in the Tower of David instead of your Będzin "Wiusza" [?]. Yes, my outlook will change, and very soon indeed. I shall pass on greetings from you: how well off you are in the world; how the Jews of Manduszewer [?] Street are living in clover without head-worries, without paying taxes and without creditors, without interest-paying.
I am going to the Land of Israel, and there I shall tell of the good life the Będzin "dozors" [kehilla board members] lead among themselves, how there is never any quarrel between one dozor and another, and how loans at the free-loan fund are given out as soon as one asks for them.
When I come to the Land, I shall tell how the Będzin parties live well together, and how, as soon as one party organises some undertaking, the other, God forbid, does not boycott it.
And I shall tell what a great "revival" and what a "cultural life" you have.
Yes, many kind greetings I shall pass on; but the main thing is that I am truly glad that this summer, instead of coal-air, I shall rather stuff myself with oranges, dates and the air of the Land of Israel.
And so I already envy myself not a little for the fact that my journey will be in a railway carriage and on a ship, second class — upon my life, I envy myself.
Heard and Seen

[Column — scenes and gossip from Zagłębie.] By Ben Amotz.
"500 bastards"...
I saw this scene in the offices of the Będzin kehilla.
A young woman, a poor vagrant [shlepperke], weeps, shouts and begs that the gmina [kehilla] should help her so that her dead child may be brought to burial.
The matter aroused my interest. Can it be said that the gmina does not want to bring a Jewish child to a Jewish grave? — after all, the main activity of the Jewish kehillas, ours among them, is, so to speak, nothing other than
— to bury Jewish dead...
Later the matter becomes clear to me. The gmina does not have the legal means to do the "favour" of burying the child, because the child is not registered at all — a soul that belongs to no one.
— And the mother? — I ask
— Not registered either.
— Her parents? — Not either; even her great-grandparents — the official explains to me — do not figure in any registration books...
— Have the kehilla representatives ever given thought to this painful [?] question?
Instead of an answer to my question the gmina secretary points me to a bundle of papers: here — he tells me — lie
— "500 bastards"...
???...
At the time — he gives me to understand — when the gmina carried out an exact statistical survey of the Jewish population of Będzin, it turned out that there are "500 bastards".
Quite literally, 500 children who live, grow up and
— belong to no one...
— I have — says the secretary — collected rich material on this, prepared a report, only...
— Only what?
More than that he, the secretary, will not say a word to me on the matter; but I can guess that he means that the present dozors [kehilla board members] have no time to occupy themselves with such "trifles" as legalising
— "500 bastards"...
—o—
— "Is this the 'Głębia'?.."
With this question one of the world of the margins turns to us — she came to the newspaper of "Głębia" to tell of the "good deeds" of her "husband".
And she tells:
"My 'husband' left me with 4 children and went off with a housemaid 'tramping the country'. He, that 'husband' of mine, wanted — she says — the maid to live together with us in one home; he says that a beggar does not fulfil his duty with one wife — don't all beggars have several wives?..."
We take her "word", promising that we will "put her husband"
into the — "Głębia"...
Later I was again in "contact" with the "wandering poor" — with the band of beggars, which grows from day to day, and no one gives thought to the plague; on the contrary, new charity societies are created with the aim of providing for the gang that is "fighting" against the ban of Rabbeinu Gershom [on polygamy]...
Now the Passover holiday is approaching. Charity-knockers will roll up their sleeves, collect donations, distribute provisions to able-bodied beggars, and the kosher matzot will be baked
— by shiksas from Ksawera...
— "Good morning, Veks!" [?] Yes, the number is correct: 4 wives and 2 men —
— a "collective"...
I am glad that my donation [?] got me rid of them [?]; I reckoned that the wives too would demand of us:
— that their husbands be put into the "Głębia"...
—o—
"Jak bieda"...
A polemic between two party pillars.
A former and a present president — Michel and Madejski.
The first has at his disposal the "Kurier Zachodni", and the second — "Express Zagłębia".
The polemic, which began in the field of economic abilities, has gone beyond its bounds and passed over to
— personal abuse.
Each honours the other with unethical expressions and insults.
And into this Michel—Madejski round-dance [korovod] have been dragged
— the Jew and the Jewish question...
Among the 4 questions that Madejski asked his opponent Michel there is also the fourth question:
"Just tell me, little brother, what is your attitude to Jews in general and to Jewish questions in particular?"...
To this question Michel has not yet given any answer — "I still have time — he says — I will answer you." Incidentally, the whole matter lies for us in the left sidelock [i.e. we could not care less].
The only interesting thing is that we are always
— the little mirror...
When one party wants to blacken the face of the other party, it takes to its help
— the Jews, the unhappy people that lets itself be content when whoever it may be throws it
— a little bone...
And unhappily, when "our own" bite each other, we are always
— the little mirror...
—o—
A little letter from Zawiercie...
A few lines in all:
"The kierownik [head] of the 'Opieka Społeczna' [social welfare office] has turned to the Zawiercie rabbi asking him to rebuke the Jews for the informing they do on those who receive the relief payments"...
That is the content of the little letter from this genius [?] of a kierownik. He apparently thinks that only in Zawiercie are there such "żydki" [little Jews] who tell everything that goes on among Jews.
— You are mistaken, Mr Kierownik: this whole leprosy is present in plenty in every town and shtetl; thanks to the worms, all the "urzędy" [offices] are well informed — there they even know which Jew buys fish for the Sabbath...
That is what we would have liked to tell you, Mr Kierownik, on reading the
— little letter from Zawiercie...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Terumah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Terumah
The Portion
—o—
a) "Of every man whose heart maketh him willing" (Ex. 25:2)
1.
In pronunciation one cannot tell "yidvenu" (is willing) from "yiduvenu" (aches) apart. For there are such people whose "heart is faint within them" — their heart aches when they have to give a donation... Kli Yakar.
2.
"Greater is he who causes others to do than the doer, as it is said: And the work of righteousness shall be peace, and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever." Bava Batra, folio 9.
So that charitable deeds should bring about peace, so that at a charity drive people should not rebel — it is only good when the one who causes the giving is "greater than the doer": when the one who causes it, the charity canvasser, gives more than the doer [the donor]... That besides "whose heart maketh him willing" one should also practise "ye shall take my offering" — also take money... Binah le-Ittim.
—o—
b) "And this is the offering which ye shall take of them: gold, and silver, and brass"
1.
With the first offering, that of "whose heart maketh him willing" — of one who gives only "unto Me — for My name's sake", who gives only with the heart — it is not specified what he should give, since with the heart everyone presumably gives only zahav, gold... Whereas with the offering of "which ye shall take of them", of those from whom one already takes in actual fact — from them [it is] gold, silver and brass. Arono shel Yosef.
2.
"Which ye shall take OF THEM."
That the offering should be their own; it should not be stolen and gathered from other people's fortunes... Perah Levanon.
—o—
c) "Whose heart maketh him willing."
The Rabbi of Lissa [Leszno] once came to a rich man, a miser, to ask him for a donation for an important cause. The latter, hearing that the Gaon was coming to him in person, prepared a magnificent reception for him. But the rabbi will not taste anything and says that he forgoes the hospitality and the kind words — he only wants to see money from him...
The rich man, a learned scholar, retorts with a Gemara: "He who gives a perutah to a poor man is blessed with six blessings, and he who consoles him [with words] — with eleven." So it follows, surely, that the consolation, the kind words to the poor man, are worth more than the charity itself.
The rabbi answers him that this is an ignoramus's interpretation, for the true meaning is that kind words together with money are worth more than money alone; but kind words without money are worth nothing.
And meanwhile the rabbi settles it with him [?] with a sharp-witted saying:
— "He who says 'mine is yours and yours is mine' — is an am ha-arets [ignoramus]", because the money the rich man gives — he gives only God's money ("The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the Lord"); the commandment the rich man fulfils only by his friendly giving of the money to the poor man.
But he who says: "mine" (what belongs to me — friendliness when giving charity) — "is yours", this I do for You, God, with this I want to fulfil the commandment; but "yours" (what belongs to You, God — "the silver is mine and the gold is mine") — "is mine", this I want to keep for myself — "am ha-arets": he is an ignoramus, because he interprets the said Gemara in such an ignorant way as here [?]..
Toldot Yaakov.
—o—
d) "And they shall make an ark.. two cubits and a half.." (Ex. 25:10)
The ark of the Torah had — unlike the other vessels — measurements in halves, because Jews too must be added to the Torah: Torah without Jews is no completeness.
Siftei Kohen.
Remark: Yet this is the opposite idea to the Hirschian doctrine (German-Agudah [?]), that Jews were created only for the sake of the Torah and not the Torah for the sake of the Jews...

"Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself — this is a great principle of the Torah."
If Jews love one another, love each other, even those who are not pious — "this is a great principle of the Torah", then the Torah has a tikkun [repair]. Whereas if one excludes certain kinds of Jews from the community, there is also a division among the letters of the Torah, for as many Jewish souls there are, so many letters there are in the Torah, and he who excludes one soul from the community tears a letter out of the Torah.
Shem mi-Shmuel.

e) "And their faces one to another" (Ex. 25:20; printed "25:2")
1.
The symbol of the Ark of the Torah are the cherubim, whose faces are "one to another"; whereas those scholars who quarrel with each other do not deserve the name. Orah Hayyim.
2.
In the Ark there were two tablets: one with the commandments "between man and his fellow" and the other with the "commandments between man and God". The cherubim that stood over the tablets symbolised that "their faces one to another": both must harmonise, both must be observed at the same time and in equal measure. "For thou knowest not the reward of the commandments" — which is higher before God, those "between man and God" or those "between man and his fellow".
Ha-Torah ve-ha-Mitzvot.

An answer to the incomprehensible words in the commentary of the Tosafist: "kemohar — amounts to two hundred, and this is one too many, and there is authority to the reading." The word "kemohar" amounts [in gematria] to as much as "200 zuzim" plus one, i.e. one more, for the word kemohar with the vav (because "there is authority to the reading", and one does read it with the vav — "kemohar") amounts to 271, while "200 zuzim" amounts only to 270. That means one must pay more than the two hundred gulden, and it is a fixed sum. That the verse means "zuzim" — in the plural.

Laws every citizen must become acquainted with

[Law — "Laws every citizen must know"; followed by: new regulations on bus traffic; Będzin — donations to the singing and music society.]
Court costs in a civil lawsuit.
If the litigating parties conclude a settlement at the court proceedings, the court costs are divided equally between the two of them.
When [?] the parties consist of several persons, the court costs are divided according to the number of participants, unless their claims are not equal. In the latter case the court costs are divided according to the extent of participation.
On the other hand, if the participants in a lawsuit are jointly and severally (solidarily) liable for the claims put forward, the court costs too are awarded against them jointly and severally.
When court costs are awarded, the interested party must remember to ask the court for them before the verdict is pronounced. In case a certain party is not satisfied with the decision on the court costs, he can lodge a complaint against the decision, even though no appeal is lodged against the verdict itself.
The record of the court proceedings.
The parties in a civil lawsuit have the right to demand that the statements entered in the record at the court proceedings be read out; they likewise have the right to enter corrections and additions into the record.
Restoring a missed deadline.
In case a party is late in lodging an appeal or carrying out another procedural step, and the delay occurred through no fault or negligence of his own, he can apply to the court to which the late step should have been submitted, with a reasoned request within 7 days after the impediment ceased, that the missed deadline be restored to him.
The actual procedural application must be attached to this request at the same time.
There is no complaint against the court's decision on restoring a missed deadline.
Submitting a request to restore the deadline does not suspend the force of the contested court decision, unless the court itself suspends it upon a special application by the interested party. In this case too there is no complaint.
The costs of the action to restore a missed deadline — regardless of whether it was granted or rejected — must be borne by the party conducting that action.
Ing— [?]

New regulations on bus traffic.
In accordance with the international convention on bus transport concluded in Paris, which was also signed and ratified by Poland, a decree of the Minister of Communications has been issued that regulates the legal provisions of the bus-traffic system.
The said decree determines what technical equipment buses must have, how fast they may travel in various situations, what qualifications one must possess in order to be allowed to drive a bus, and under what circumstances one loses, or may lose, the right to drive a bus.
The decree comes into force on 15 March 1933.
Y. A.

Clear of Winter!...

Gentlemen, I can announce good tidings: thank God, I am already laughing at the "trisis" [sic; read "crisis"] together with the winter!...
Jews, I have made an invention that surpasses all your "Hoover [?] plans", "dzhvinkatses" [?], "radios" [?] and other such rubbish [?] — I have invented a means... of how to get through the winter with its frosts!...
Listen, Jews, to what I have invented:
Not long ago my wife says to me: Tsadok, what will be the end of it, now that the little shop [?] no longer gives anything "out of the book" [on credit], the butcher no longer chops "pisz na ścianie" ["write it on the wall", i.e. on tab], at the baker's the debt rises as if on yeast. There's nobody to grab an interest-free loan from, because all the "millionaires" suffer from "an empty pocket"; nobody pays rent, there isn't a crumb of wood or coal, and the winter is still here — Tsadok, what shall we do?
"Stop 'Tsadok'-ing me!" — I got angry [?] at my wife, but in my heart I thought: is she not right, my wife? What really will be the end? One must [?] after all [—] [—] [—] [—] — just go and think that the whole town is one big cemetery. Can you do much with the dead?...
But "I toiled and I found" [Talmudic saying], which in plain Yiddish means: when you put your head on the right side, you find. As I lay like that on my "crisis-style" straw sack (the mattresses are at the "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office]), thinking about how my wife "Tsadoks" me, a brilliant idea occurred to me — listen, Jews, what an idea:
I live in a house with 5 neighbours, paupers — the same sort of "magnates" as I am, all of them "flirting" with a smoked herring... and they all have wives and children, and all day long one dreams of a bagel — so why shouldn't we found a kind of beggars' collective? Gather all the beggars in one room, cook together, eat a "collective" krupnik [barley soup] together; instead of heating 5 stoves — heat one; instead of cooking in 5 kitchens — cook in one kitchen; instead of washing 5 pots — wash one pot. In a word — a collective life!
No sooner said than done. That very evening the "founding meeting" of the new collective took place in my corner.
I, as the initiator of the whole project, delivered a hot speech in my ice-cold room:
"My gentlemen beggars and lady beggaresses! A time has come when all the rich have become paupers; with everyone the wind blows through their pockets, and in the iron safes 'my' [sic; probably "mice"] dance the foxtrot. His Majesty, Poverty, sits everywhere at the head of the table; we are all in dire straits. Let us all live together with our wives and children and found a collective — all for one and one for all."
"Bravo, bravo!" everybody shouted. "Agreed, agreed!"
That same evening the new collective was founded under the name "Kabtsonu Yakhad" [Beggars Together].
"How is our collective doing?" — it was said [?] in all the drapery shops! Everywhere there is death, and in my "Kabtsonu Yakhad" it is lively!"...
On the very first day all my 5 neighbours with their wives and children packed up and moved into my flat. Each one brought a bit of wood, the pot, and we live "collectively".
One day Yente the market-woman [?] heats the stove, the second day — Pesl the draper's wife, the third day — the shoemaker's wife. One day Feige Leah the shoe-upper stitcher cooks the "collective krupnik", another day — Zelde the carpenter's wife, and so on.
Well, the days are days, one manages somehow. The worst, however, is the nights. The collective days can still be endured; the worst, though, is the collective nights...
One woman gets "labour pains" in the middle of the night — they wake up Chairman Tsadok and I have to run for the midwife.
A woman gets a "napad" [fit] — I, the chairman of the collective, have to run to the "Linat HaHolim" [sick-care society] and take her temperature...
A "członkini" [female member] of the collective falls ill with the flu — she calls me to rub her down with with [sic] French turpentine...
And are the men [?] any better? First of all they all have trouble with their stomachs. Every evening another one takes castor oil — and it's lively and merry...
We would have managed somehow, if not for the young folk: one has a son who is a Bundist, and the other has a daughter who is a Poale Zionist; the Bundist will on no account warm himself at one stove with the Poale Zionist girl, the Poale Zionist girl for her part will not sleep under one roof with the Bundist, and a third neighbour has a daughter who is a "Red" — she will on no account taste the "bourgeois krupnik"...
But who asks them? My "Kabtsonu Yakhad" develops from day to day; we eat collectively, and with sleeping too, thank God, we manage.
We buy everything "hurtowo" [wholesale]: powder we buy by the kilo, lip colour by the box, nappies we buy wholesale — and live it up.
And now — our revenge on the sequestrator [tax bailiff]? Oh, listen, we have our revenge on the sequestrator! He goes from door to door chasing yesterday's days, and if some madness takes him and he drops in on our "Kabtsonu Yakhad" — we whirl him into a little dance and treat him to our collective krupnik...
That, gentlemen, is how I invented an invention for overcoming the crisis.
I have my own "Kabtsonu Yakhad" and I laugh at the frosts!...
Now, gentlemen, you can found in your own house a second collective named "Ozer Dalim" [Helper of the Poor].
Y. A—K. [?]
Jewish Wealth and Jewish Poverty

If you want a vivid picture of our „good times“, it is enough to look into the advertisement section of the newspapers.
This section, in which Jewish trade and commerce, Jewish businesses and weddings [?] used to be reflected, is today [?], thank God, just as dead as livelihood is dead in the Jewish street.
This section now speaks more clearly and plainly about the grave crisis than the best and sharpest articles and feuilletons.
Two weeks ago, for instance, there was an advertisement in our paper that a secretary was wanted for a society.
Well, this small advertisement simply stirred up the town. For a whole week the door of the [newspaper's] administration did not close because of applicants for the position, although the entire salary came to barely a hundred „gulden“ [złoty] a month. Young men and young women who had had the good fortune to finish gymnasium „fought“ for the post — some even with matriculation certificates, some even with diplomas from commercial courses, some even with a good knowledge of several languages.
And fathers came to beg for protection [string-pulling], and out of the extinguished eyes — both of the young people who brought in the applications and of the older ones who sought the string-pulling — looked out the whole misery, the whole great, hopeless want of the Jewish street.
And now, not long ago, a small advertisement appeared that someone wishes to buy an iron safe.
How many iron safes, do you think, turned up in Zagłębie?
After all, not just anybody had an iron safe even in the good old days; such a thing was owned only by someone who had something to put into it.
But it turns out that our Zagłębie was, apparently, once a centre of rich men.
No fewer than several dozen iron safes answered the small advertisement!
In these iron safes there once lay Jewish fortunes, solid Jewish account books, red bill-of-exchange portfolios and thick bundles of banknotes.
Today all these safes stand empty and desolate — the fortunes have trickled away, the account books are now wrapping paper, the bills of exchange — protested, and the bundles of banknotes have been devoured by the inflations, the taxes, the carts [?]...
Several dozen Jewish iron safes answered the small advertisement — a vivid sign of the ruin of the Jewish wealth of former days.
Keren Hayesod and Keren Haneshama

About Keren Hayesod — who [?] has not written already? What has not already been said and printed?
Keren Hayesod is everything: a national home, foundations of Torah and faith, a working Yishuv, small-farmer settlement, a spiritual centre, industrialisation, and what not?
This is right and at the same time wrong.
Nomberg once said: you Zionists have such a brilliant object for propaganda, and you campaign so badly.
And there is a bit of truth in that.
We build well and campaign badly.
We build a home, a future, an eternity... and campaign — like retailers in a shop.
To each — according to his taste.
The Emek [Jezreel Valley] — for the pioneers. Orange groves of the Sharon — for the wealthy, yeshivas [?] — for the pious.
As long as you give money.
God forbid mixing things up and showing the rich man the „communist“ kvutza, and the proletariat the „big industry“ of Tel Aviv.
And where is the Land of Israel?
The one and only, luminous, indivisible Land of Israel?
The suffering, working, emerging, pure Land of Israel?
Why do we show it chopped to pieces, broken up, crumbled?
Does it really deserve such cruel propaganda?
No, Keren Hayesod is not foundations of faith, nor a crafts bank, nor kvutzot, nor electrification.
Keren Hayesod is something more
Keren Hayesod is coming-into-being, realisation, renewal.
Keren Hayesod is the charm and the birth-pangs of our fatherland.
The perfect and the flawed of creation. That which pleases you and that which does not please you.
Keren Hayesod is not a sample-book of facts and episodes, but the great scroll of our becoming, of our coming into existence.
Keren Hayesod is growth. The organic blossoming of a scattered, decayed nation. And therefore Keren Hayesod is not merely a financial fund but also a spiritual, soulful one.
This is the Keren Haneshama [the Fund of the Soul] of the Jewish people.
Nine Jews may perhaps not understand this today, but the tenth will understand it.
This is our tithe, the tithe of our deepest, holiest feelings.
• • •
But we are obliged to explain it also to the nine who do not pay the tithe of the soul.
They ask us: how come, and once again how come: at such a time? In such a cruel hour of crisis, lack of livelihood, hunger, bankruptcies — a campaign is held for the „Keren Hayesod“?
And we answer those who sincerely want to understand us:
That is precisely why — we are building the Land of Israel.
A safe refuge — against a bankrupt life, against a two-thousand-year-old crisis, against an eternal spiritual hunger.
Now is the time!
Descent — is for the sake of ascent.
Through crises and stagnations the soul is uplifted.
Satiety demoralises, stifles the divine spark, covers up the image of God.
As the verse says: „But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked.“
Precisely in hard hours of existence the eye grows sharper to see the great vision, the sense of hearing grows more delicate to hear the footsteps of the herald...
Now!
Now, in the grey twilight hour of our economic ruin, the holy words may perhaps sound more understandable, warmer, more motherly: a home of our own.
A. Lewinson.
March.

[Literary feuilleton — seasonal impressions.] By Kehat Kliger.
(Moods.)

Winter is wrestling in the last minutes of its life. It has already breathed out its cold breath onto the ice-bound [?] windowpanes and lies like one in his death-throes on the broad streets of the town.
The snow is already muddy and trampled in places, black, and its natural sheen, with a pallid colour upon it — it weeps and pours with big, full tears from the roofs, from the trees and branches, melts away so quickly — it has already resigned its pride, its power, which earlier, only a few weeks ago, was so mighty, so stubborn, unwilling to budge wherever it had found its place, its bed.
The street has already freed itself bit by bit from the cold, frozen burden — so much sun has spread into every corner, the snow melts so helplessly and yieldingly, it falls in pieces, in strips, in heaps, and melts away into little rivulets of water that vanish, have vanished [?] and are no more...
The days are already longer. The sky frees itself from its [?] constant, black and gloomy sheets of cloud and shows itself clean in all the fullness of its blueness.
Winter, stubborn unto life and death, has lost its bitter struggle with summer; it has fallen, fainted on the threshold of time without strength, no longer able to get back on its feet...
The winds have caught up the last sound of its lament [?] and carried it far, far away from us — a little wind chases along whistling and gives a mischievous whistle over the air —
March!
The month that comes and announces tidings, those golden tidings, for every living creature, for everything that breathes and lives, for everything that has a living spirit — the time of expansive life, of freedom, of gladness, draws near to us with great, rapid strides — the time of awakening, of rousing.
The sun warms so mildly, so revivingly good, and strews an abundance of pure gold on the cold, still-frozen earth, and strokes, strokes with such motherly tenderness, promising bright, sunny days.
Here and there a bird is already flying — emissaries from a warm and free land somewhere — they caw into the clarified, clear and fresh air so cheekily and roguishly — the bluish horizontal space fills with lively movement, with motion, with fluttering joy, with song-like sound and echo.
Already faces of people appear in the street, in that street — who sat the whole time in their homes, shut off from the street, not even glancing at a stroll — laughter is carried along, loud and broad, carefree and free. Children romp and fill the whole surroundings with their young, childish little voices, merry shouts — the tumult and the noise grow ever livelier and livelier.
A surging [?], foaming joy has seized the low, hunched, bowed-to-the-ground old little houses of the poor quarters of want.
The souls — worn out and tormented — in these little rooms have suddenly received so much hope in their hearts, deadened by the hard winter. A broadened, boundless [?] will to live has taken hold of them — for these people live only with summer; the sun, the warmth are their deliverer, their redeemer!...
— — — — — — —
Outside it blows and whistles [?] with stronger and weaker March winds; the air grows cleaner and cleaner.
Listen —
It is the pleasant breath of spring! —
A King Who Fled the Throne in the Middle of the Night (A Historical Tale) (3)

[Serialized historical tale — Poland and France, King Henri de Valois; installment 3.]
By El—Be.

For readers who did not read the beginning of this interesting story, we give a summary:
In the year 1572 the Polish king Zygmunt the 2nd died suddenly. There was no one to be his heir, because he died childless. Around the throne an internal struggle flared up between the nobles [the "poritzim"] and the Protestants, and there was a threat that a civil war would break out in the country.
At last the parties came to an agreement to call a national assembly in Warsaw, and at that assembly a new Polish king was to be elected.
The French queen [?], the widow de' Medici, took advantage of the opportunity; she was eager for her youngest son Henri to be elected King of Poland.
She was helped by the French ambassador in Warsaw at the time. By various means they succeeded, and on 11 May 1573 Henri was elected Polish king.
The new king was not pleased with the throne; he wanted to be free and to spend his time with his beloved, the Princess of Condé [printed "Kondeai"], but at his mother's command he took over the Polish throne.
When he had been king barely 13 months, his brother Charles [Karl] the 9th died in France, and Henri, the Polish king, became the lawful heir to the French throne.
And Henri, the Polish king, deliberated how to leave Poland.
At last it happened: at night he fled from Kraków.
The flight of the Polish king in the year 1574 provoked popular anger. He was searched for, but without success.
The king fled to France, where he was crowned king. But he did not conduct himself in the right way: he occupied himself with follies, played with dogs and cats, and moreover he had a craving to disguise himself as a woman. Once it happened that he came to a royal ball dressed as a woman.
———
All these foolish antics repelled the French people's sympathy from the king. This was exploited by Henri's cousin, who strongly coveted the French throne and on that account sought to increase his popularity among the people. Above all he sought sympathy among the pious Catholics, because Paris was ruled at that time by the so-called Commune. This was a municipal organization led by a committee of 16 persons, and this committee was inclined [?] toward the Duke of Guise, Henri's cousin. The Parliament, on the other hand, was for the king, i.e. for Henri.
Around the throne a sharp struggle flared up between the two bodies, between Parliament and Committee, which led to the municipal committee falling upon the Parliament and putting forty deputies in prison.
Henri's mother Catherine de' Medici knew how to master the situation that had arisen; she steered and combined matters so that she could keep hold of power. There was not a single crime of which she was not accused. In every conspiracy she had a hand. All the parties declared loyalty to her and afterwards betrayed her.
The queen did one more thing which at that time caused a storm in the Catholic world. She herself was an ardent Catholic fanatic, a niece of the Pope, the organizer of the St. Bartholomew massacre — yet she went and married off her daughter to the leader of the Protestant princes, Henri of Navarre (later Henri the 4th, the successor of Henri the 3rd). She took this step because she had political calculations in it.
Some time later the mother of Henri the 4th died suddenly, and he accused his mother-in-law of having poisoned his mother.
She also intrigued with the Duke of Guise, the one who coveted the French throne. Earlier she had been his enemy, afterwards — his friend. She became so friendly with him that she became his secret partner in the conspiracy against her own son, Henri the Third...
When Henri the 3rd ascended the throne, his first task was to put to death the Protestant leader Montgomery, who had been taken prisoner during the civil war between the Catholics and Huguenots.
The king's hatred of the Protestant leader was very strong. In political circles this hatred was explained by the fact that Montgomery, during a fencing match with Henri's father, had wounded him unintentionally, and of those wounds Henri the Second died.
The Protestants used every means of influence with the king so that their leader would remain alive. But nothing helped, and the Protestant leader was beheaded. The tragic death caused great agitation among the Protestants.
Henri had another brother — the Duke of Alençon. Henri cast suspicion on him that he was intriguing to overthrow him and take over the throne.
"In order to avoid the suspicion" [sic] Henri worked out a plan to murder his brother, the duke. But the plan did not succeed: the duke fled in time, and in revenge he joined the Huguenots, who were waging war against the Catholics.

Będzin: A Jewish Child Lay 3 Days Before It Came to Jewish Burial

[Będzin — community.] A child of 1½ years died in the home of Mrs. Cyla Gutman; it had not been registered, because the mother and her whole family did not appear at all in the registration books of the civil registry office.
The gmina [Jewish community] intervened in the matter with the starosta, who, after an understanding with the kierownik [head] of the civil registry office of the Będzin magistrate, ordered that the proper certificate be drawn up on the basis of witnesses' testimony.
Settling the formalities meanwhile took 3 days.
The Magistrate Moves to New Premises

[Będzin — municipality.] As we are informed, on Tuesday a final agreement was reached with Mr. Zmigród, under which the magistrate [town hall] moves into Zmigród's house, where the Realschule used to be.
Christian Small Traders Do Not Want to Go Together with the Jewish Ones...

[Sosnowiec — economy.] In the previous issue of our paper we reported on the conference at the local small traders' association concerning the doctor's [health officer's] decree for shopkeepers, that shops may not be joined to living quarters.
At the conference, in which representatives of all Jewish and non-Jewish small traders' associations in Zagłębie took part, a resolution was adopted to intervene jointly at the starostwo [district office] so that the decree, which is to take effect on the 15th of this month, be withdrawn.
This week the Christian small traders' association in Sosnowiec officially announced through its secretary that the Christian small traders withdraw from further conferences on the above-mentioned matter and in general do not want to go together with the Jewish small traders...

What Should We Do with the Jews — Perhaps Slaughter Them?
So Asks a Group of Listeners at the “Świetlica”

[Będzin — antisemitism.] A few weeks ago the magistrate opened in the premises of the “Piast” the so-called “świetlica” [day-room], a shelter for the unemployed.
Last Sabbath a professor [teacher] of the Polish gymnasium gave a lecture in these premises.
The lecturer — as we are told — allowed himself in a base manner to pour out all his [?] wrath and said that “the majority of Jews are communists, Jews make counterfeit money, and in general, for every misfortune, may it not come, the Jews are to blame.”
The lecturer's “objective arguments” threw part of the listeners off balance, and they put the question to the lecturer: “Are Christians not communists? Do Christians not spread counterfeit money? And above all, tell us, Mr. Professor, what should we do with the Jews — perhaps slaughter them?”...
The interjections led to a scandal, because of which the lecture was broken off.
It is to be hoped that the magistrate, as the landlord, will introduce proper control, so that such “lectures” no longer take place in the “świetlica”.
From Craftsmen's Life

[Będzin — craftsmen.] A meeting took place in the premises of the Craftsmen's Association, at which the present board gave a report on its activity up to now.
After the report, which was heard with satisfaction, the chairman Mr. Goldsztajn made the following statement:
“Since a Polish weekly has appeared in our town which wanted to be supported by craftsmen, but after the first issue we established that it is a rag, we declare that we need speak no more about that paper.”
— In the course of the week meetings of the tailors' sections took place, which discussed a number of current questions concerning the tailors' guild [cech].
Prices at the Municipal Bathhouse Reduced

[Będzin — municipality.] From Wednesday on, the prices at the municipal bathhouse have been reduced: a bathtub costs 80 gr.; the sweat bath on the first floor — 60 gr.; at the back [?] — 30 gr.
The reduced prices that were valid only on Wednesdays have been abolished.
Convenient Bus Connection to Upper Silesia
[Będzin — transport.] The buses that leave every hour from Browarna Street for Siemianowice are timed to connect with onward transport to the Upper Silesian towns and villages.
Exhibition of Paintings by the Artist M. D. Gotlib

[Będzin — art.] Because of the great interest that the Łódź painter M. D. Gotlib aroused with his exhibition of paintings in town, the exhibition is being extended by another 3 days — Friday, Saturday, Sunday — in the premises of the Merchants' Association, 3 Maja [Street] 4.

General meeting of merchants.

Next Sunday the annual general meeting of the members of the local "Merchants' Association" will take place in its own premises. Besides current business, the meeting will hear a report on the new law on courts of arbitration, and the required number of judges will be elected.
Two-day strike of the young shochtim.

On Monday the young shochtim (ritual slaughterers) went on strike, because they are not paid for their work at the slaughterhouse.
The "strike" lasted until Wednesday afternoon. When the chairman, Mr. Liwer, wrote them a friendly[?] letter, the young shochtim went back to work.
The premises tax for 1933.

Last Tuesday the deadline for paying the first instalment expired, and those who did not pay it on time will be charged interest.
After the close of the tax year the Magistrate will draw up lists of the bad payers, which will be handed over to the fiscal authority for collection by distraint.
A lecture.

The Society for Local Knowledge (Landkentenish) is holding a lecture this Saturday night, after the Sabbath, by Mr. Bromberg, director of the Medem Sanatorium in Miedzeszyn, on the topic: "The life of the children in the sanatorium".
A General Halutz founded in Ząbkowice.

On the initiative of a group of Right Poale Zion members, the founding meeting of the "General Halutz" (HeHalutz HaKlali) in Ząbkowice took place on Saturday.
Mr. Reuven Laudan opened the meeting and proposed Mr. Yaakov Goldsilber as chairman of the meeting. After Messrs. Laudan and Goldsilber had spoken about the Halutz, a committee was elected consisting of: Reuven Laudan, Yaakov Goldsilber, Yisrael Yitzchak Biderman and D. Klin.
R. L—n.
The dispute between the kehilla board and the Chevra Kadisha — settled.

As readers know, a sharp dispute broke out between the kehilla board and the Chevra Kadisha (burial society). The dispute consisted in the board having adopted a resolution that all the income of the Chevra Kadisha, especially from burial plots, must be paid into the community treasury.
Because of the negative stance of the Chevra Kadisha, a "Chesed shel Emes" was founded at the community, which performs the functions of the Chevra Kadisha.
This week a meeting of both sides took place, and they reached an agreement to settle the dispute in such a way that of all income from plots that the community will have from the cemetery, the Chevra Kadisha will receive 15 percent.
The shochtim must receive their salaries at the community office.

The starosta has sent the board the following order:
Since the latest inspection of the community shows that the community's collector at the slaughterhouse pays out the shochtim's salary there, it is hereby ordered that the shochtim must receive their salaries only at the community office.
A burglary at a cigarette shop. The thieves are already in prison.

On Piłsudski Street 2 burglaries were carried out. The first burglary was committed at Dymant's butcher's shop, and from there the wall of Nussbaum's cigarette shop was broken through, from which tobacco and cigarettes worth 1,757 zł were taken.
The police, who undertook an energetic operation, arrested the thieves and put them in prison.
On Debt Settlements

[Poland — economy and legislation.]
The government has drafted a new law on the settlement of debts when one falls into payment difficulties. The present law on "court supervision" [nadzór sądowy] is being abolished.
Merchants and manufacturers who fall into payment difficulties will be able to apply to the court with a request to be allowed to carry out a settlement of their debts. As soon as such a request is submitted, the execution of all kinds of seizures [zajęcia] and enforcement proceedings will be halted; they will no longer be valid until the settlement negotiations are concluded. To obtain permission to negotiate a settlement with the creditors, one will have to submit a list of the state of one's assets and of all [?] debts ["kunrishe" — unclear word].
To settle the debts at 70 percent, the consent of a simple majority of the creditors taking part in the meeting will be required. To settle at less than 70 percent down to 40 percent, the consent of a larger number of creditors will be required.
The law does not provide for any settlement below 40 percent.
Crafty Swindler Dupes 40 Unemployed

[Sosnowiec [?] — crime.]
He cheats them out of 200 zł. and tells them to wait at the border.
A few days ago a young man appeared at the Piotrków [?] market and, presenting himself as the "manager" of a German firm, began recruiting seasonal workers for Germany.
Naturally there was no shortage of takers, and the so-called manager signed up 40 candidates.
After the registration he told them to come the next morning, bag and baggage ["vak [?] un pak"], to the train. At the appointed minute all the candidates turned up; the "manager" told them to buy train tickets to Częstochowa and from there to Herby, near the German border. The "manager" himself travelled as far as Herby at the candidates' expense. In Herby he declared that the German border gendarme demanded 5 zł. from every smuggled worker. He did indeed collect 5 zł. apiece, 200 zł. altogether, and told the crowd to wait.
Having waited like this a whole night, the workers only then understood that they were the victims of a crafty swindler, and with no choice they went home on foot.
The police are now searching for the crafty swindler.

Theatre, Music and Cinema Notes

Second Concert
of the Choir of the Jewish Song and Music Society in Będzin
Tuesday's concert was truly a genuine "artistic feast" — unusual for our circumstances — in the best, most distinguished style.
The short interval between the folk choir's first concert and today — three months in all — is certainly too little. People who work hard all day and devote only 3–4 hours a week to the culture of song cannot allow themselves to perform such difficult works as Haydn's oratorio. And yet we see that the choir is developing, and Prof. Baruchka, who fully masters the vocal material of the choristers, managed to draw a brilliant concert out of voices not yet polished.
One can only regret that the Jewish Song Society, which must first of all care for the development and spread of the Jewish folk song, does not try to enrich and popularise its repertoire with the newest pearls from the treasury of Jewish folk music. Alongside the great oratorio works, much more room in the repertoire must absolutely be given to pure Jewish music, from which one can draw full treasures.
The evening began with Gelbart's "Ver hot es" and "Shmidn yungen" in a not very free tone. But then came "Benkshaft" (Longing) in the successful arrangement by Fiwiszis [?], where Prof. Baruchka succeeded in bringing out of the choir such a lyrical sadness that it riveted all the listeners.
Also successful was Fiwiszis's second song, "Vaserlekh shtilinke" (Quiet little waters), where the choir displayed great maturity, especially in the closing chords of the song. The main thing we had been waiting for, though, was the Spring fragment of Haydn's oratorio, which, incidentally, has never yet been performed in Będzin. But despite the [difficulties?] of performing the oratorio without an orchestra, and although one noticed the loose connection between the separate parts — surely a result of the hasty preparation for the concert — the choir nevertheless stood at the proper height and triumphantly performed the splendid song of spring's arrival.
The strongest attraction, however, was Peretz's "Meyn nisht" (Don't think), already familiar to us, which the choir sang with harmonic wholeness, full of fire and expression, so that the audience was carried away, rewarding the choir and Mr. Baruchka with stormy, long-lasting ovations and compelling them to sing the number again as an encore.
The young accompanist Miss S. Epstein — discreet and careful where she had only to accompany, very good in "Meyn nisht", where she also had to play on her own, and with high technique in the oratorio, where the piano must replace the whole orchestra — truly deserves to be mentioned with praise.
Mr. L. Rechnitz was excellent in his two violin numbers; Mr. L. Rechnitz possesses a fine technique and a very tender tone.
A few words about the solo appearances: the male quartet performed Zelman's "Ikh shtey baym vald" (I stand by the forest) with taste, and the 2 folk songs sung by Mr. Danziger would surely have come out better had they been accompanied by the whole choir. In general it would have been better if the Jewish folk songs that are written for solo singing were sung by individual soloists with a choral illustration.
Altogether the concert was a great achievement, and we wish the society further successes.
A. Lin.

As we have already written, an action has been organised at the „Sz. Fürstenberg“ gymnasium [the Jewish secondary school in Będzin named after Szymon Fürstenberg] for the feeding of a large number of children of needy parents who study at the gymnasium.

Pieces of glass fly during a funeral.

On Wednesday during the day, during the funeral of Moshe Grünwald, who died so suddenly, [the procession] passed by Zmigród's[?] leather shop on Kołłątaja Street, and two younger brothers of the deceased, in an act of revenge, smashed the shop windows.
A cry of woe to the rich Jews of Będzin!

The festival of Passover is approaching. Thousands of families who only a year ago figured on the lists of donors are today, unfortunately, among the recipients. The silent suffering, grief and want of these people are indescribable, but only I, unfortunately, can gauge the great economic ruin among the Jewish population of Będzin.
I therefore appeal to the well-to-do part of the Będzin kehilla: do not make light of this matter that cries out to heaven — these are things that stand at the summit of the world. Come to the meetings about the Passover campaign; if not, your conscience will not remain clean if the hundreds of Jewish families go hungry on Passover.
Respectfully, Mendel Rozenzaft.

90 thousand workers took part in the demonstrative strike in the Polish coal districts

[Poland — miners' strike.]
On Friday the 6th [as printed], in the morning, the 2-day general strike of the mine workers began in all three Polish coal districts (the Dąbrowa, Upper Silesian and Kraków districts). The strike broke out as a protest against the industrialists' wish to reduce wages.
On the first day about 50 thousand workers struck in Upper Silesia; altogether up to 90 thousand workers struck in all three districts.
In the Dąbrowa district 18 of the 22 pits were idle; only 1 pit worked, where 600 workers are employed.
A series of meetings took place. In general both days passed quietly.
From Monday on, work is proceeding normally at all pits.
Almost a blood libel in Wolbrom

[Wolbrom — a blood libel averted.]
At dawn on Sabbath the dead body of an old woman lay in front of the house of Mr. Janowski. After an investigation it became clear that the woman was the 65-year-old Regina Raszkiewicz, a peasant woman from a nearby village, who had hanged herself.
The dark elements wanted to exploit this; they wanted to plant the dead body on a Jew. Luckily the gate of Janowski's house was locked, and the devilish plan was not carried out.
Shot his wife dead and wounded his mother-in-law

[Błędów — a family tragedy.]
In the village of Błędów, Będzin county, the following family tragedy took place:
Several years ago the 29-year-old Słota married a girl from the same village. The couple lived well, but suddenly domestic peace was shattered and the young wife went off to her mother.
This week the husband went to his mother-in-law's flat to persuade his wife to come back with him to their home.
When she rejected the proposal, the husband shot at her and killed her.
The mother-in-law was also wounded by the revolver shots.

Trial of a merchant who set fire to the goods the bailiff wanted to seize.
Before the court stood the merchant Heinrich Szuba of Świętochłowice, who was accused that when the bailiff (sekwestrator) of the Urząd Skarbowy (tax office) wanted to carry out an act of distraint in his shop, Szuba poured methylated spirit over a burning stove, as a result of which a fire broke out in the shop.
Before the court Szuba defended himself, saying that he had done it in a highly agitated state, because a few minutes before the bailiff came into his shop he had sent 400 zł. to pay towards his debt of 1000 zł., and when the bailiff rejected his request not to take the goods, he lost his patience and committed the deed.
The court took into account the circumstances of the incident and sentenced Szuba to only one week's arrest, which is to take effect only two years later.
