Small Remarks on Big Matters

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — community, welfare and civil registration; opinion column.]

On an outpatient clinic in Sosnowiec.

The Sosnowiec "Linat HaHolim" [society for nursing the sick] has undertaken to carry out a welcome and responsible mission. The institution is setting up an outpatient clinic alongside it, where the poor strata of the population will receive medical help and medicines — that is, those who cannot pay the doctor for the visit and the pharmacist for the prescription. The mission is unquestionably a welcome one, because until now no one has fulfilled this duty towards the poor strata; and it is a responsible one, because once it takes upon itself to perform this good deed, it cannot be done "standing on one foot", i.e. it must not fail to function steadily and regularly. As soon as the clinic is opened, it must fulfil its obligation properly and give the necessary help; the founders must take this well to heart, for otherwise not only will they bring no benefit but quite the reverse — in that case the poor are actually wronged, because then a useful help, an essential support, is taken away from them.

And therefore we are of the opinion that the "Ligat HaHolim" [sic, for "Linat HaHolim"] should consider this properly and see to it beforehand that there will be money to cover the budget. They must first of all popularise the idea among the local citizens, so that these will have understanding for the matter, and then they will naturally support it.

It may be that the initiators have reckoned on a minimum for the budget, but one must not forget that the broad strata of Jewish Sosnowiec have been impoverished, and the clinic will no doubt have plenty of work, plenty of useful activity — this must be reckoned with, and for this reason one must approach this useful undertaking with deliberation and with a certain calculation. One must therefore remember one thing: as soon as the clinic is opened, it must, without any excuse and without any pretext, remain open and carry on useful activity for the benefit of the needy, poor and hungry.

It therefore only remains for us to point out to the "Linat HaHolim" that they should approach this clinic with a certain calculation, with a proper plan which will enable the institution to function and its activity to be continued normally.

And therefore we think that all this must be foreseen in good time, so that the institution will afterwards be able to be run on its normal course according to a plan reckoned out beforehand. It is understood that for this one needs the help of the town and the support of the better-situated citizens, and therefore everything should be done according to a plan reckoned out beforehand, and then the town will without any doubt have the proper benefit, with which Jewish Sosnowiec will certainly remain satisfied.

We therefore wish the initiators success in their useful work, which must expand widely and make possible proper help for the poor and helpless Jewish masses.

A conference on the "mamzerim" [illegitimate children] question.

A small and perhaps unnoticed note slipped through the columns of our newspaper last week. A note of only a few lines in all, so that many perhaps did not read it at all, and those who did read it surely did not dwell on it and most certainly did not consider it — for whom among the tormented and overworked people with heavy heads and great worries can it interest that a child lay in Będzin for 3 days before it could be brought to a Jewish grave. It seems that today the head cannot bear to stop and consider such "small matters"; the head is heavy as if filled with lead, so that one does not know what to worry about first — whether about the scrap of livelihood, which for our many sins has become a rare phenomenon, or about how one might be able [misprinted] to pay an overdue tax. And therefore one cannot wonder that the public takes no interest in such matters, in problems which at another time would certainly have received much attention, and one would certainly have striven to have them solved, in whatever way.

A child died which had not been registered in any registration books, so that it belonged to no people and no religion, and nobody knew where to bury it. More interesting, however, is the fact that both the mother of the deceased child and the mother's mother, as well as the whole family, have to this day not been registered anywhere.

This fact is confirmed by our gmina [the Jewish community], our local Jewish parliament, and what is more interesting — that there are in Będzin no more and no fewer than 500 such unregistered people; incidentally, it is established that to this day not all newborn children are being registered.

The statistics show us that in Będzin a total of 300 children are registered in the course of a year, whereas by all probability the number of births is certainly considerably larger.

We will grant the community that nowadays there are other, more important worries, but nevertheless one must give it a thought: can it and may it remain like this? Can a people so degrade itself, and no one take an interest in such a problem? May we remain so indifferent, so apathetic to this question? After all, we have communal workers, kehilla leaders, public representative bodies with handsome budgets — and really, can we in such a case leave this to God's counsel? May we remain cold to such a matter, which brings disgrace and shame upon the Jewish community? Can it be permitted that people today should reproach us that we live like gypsies, like wild creatures, or as somewhere beyond the Mountains of Darkness or in Honolulu?

Do we even give ourselves an account of what disgrace we suffer from such apathetic indifference? And what is interesting is that in matters of Jewish public budgets we are, God forbid, not behind all other peoples: we have kehillot and leaders and chancelleries and officials and rabbinates and religious leaders, so that everything costs money, and the Jewish population pays for everything separately — but as for there being order and conducting ourselves like decent people, there is no one to take care of it.

If this is to be called a consolation, one can only console oneself with the fact that Będzin is no exception in this case; in all other Jewish communities the order is no better. But what comes of this consolation? True, a trouble shared by many is half a consolation, but because of that one must not allow this system to go on being run like this. True, the Jewish press in Poland has already devoted several articles to the matter, but nothing substantial that would finally solve the question has, unfortunately, been done at all. Let us therefore not rely on others in this case. We must not remain indifferent to this question, which degrades us in the eyes of the European peoples. With us the "mamzerim" question must be solved once and for all, and measures must be taken so that the stain is removed from our neck.

Let Zagłębie in this case act on its own; let the kehilla leaders of Zagłębie come together to consider the matter, in what way it can be solved. Let a conference be called, at which the question will be dealt with from every side, and then a remedy will certainly be found for the affliction, which has long needed to be healed.

How We Will Look

[Essay — the times and the judgment of generations.] By Leo König [Leo Koenig].
1.
I wonder what people will think about us and our time in a hundred, two hundred years. Now it often seems to us that the distant generations to come will envy us for our privilege of living in such a wonderful, interesting time. Just as, for example, in the last pre-war years we used to envy the generations that lived through and "went through" the great French Revolution, the Napoleonic era. In those last pre-war years it seemed to us that our lives were so boring — diplomats played at secret diplomacy, artists and aesthetes many times created new artistic movements and "isms" simply out of boredom — and so we often returned with envy to the happy generations that stormed the Bastille, to the generations that had the privilege of living in eras of Sturm und Drang.
It seems [?] to us now, therefore, that in a hundred, two hundred years (when people and nations will already have solved all their social problems and will be living in a boring peace) they will envy us in the same way.
There they are, people will say pointing at us — those were the happy storm-birds: they fought and suffered; they (that is, we) knew what life was, not like us, who yawn and are bored in prosperity and peace.
(For indeed, is not our time far more interesting, greater and more historic than the era of the great French Revolution.)
Perhaps one day people really will point to our generations as to giant and tragic people, and will say: on their shoulders worlds and social problems broke; they, with their "superhuman" eyes, saw an old world go down and a new world rise.
In their (that is, in our) time a new man was born, a man with a new psychology, with a new soul with mighty wings of steel. They (do you recognize yourselves?) lived through the great birth-pangs of the Messiah; they were the historic, universal "generation of the wilderness".
And the luckier among them, the more active, themselves lived through within themselves the death of an old world and the rising of a new world, of a new man.
They were their own graves [sic; probably "gravediggers"] and their own midwives; revolutions and counter-revolutions they had by the tens; Napoleons — by the dozen. That was a heroic time, a generation of heroes, of giants.
That was a time in which it was worth living.
And people will envy us.
So perhaps people will think about us and our time in a hundred, two hundred years. That is how we often imagine it. Our self-love — every generation, like every individual, has a collective egoism; a collective self-love dictates to us this very notion, the picture that future generations will paint of our time, of our era.
And we have a bit of a right to imagine it so, because, as said, we ourselves in the quiet and normal years [looked] with the same envy and idealizing eyes upon the great historical eras of the past.
2.
I wonder what people will think about us and our time in a hundred, two hundred years: and perhaps they will not think of us at all, but will simply laugh at us and at our great era.
Perhaps in a few hundred years they will look down on us as on comical primitive creatures who got entangled and could not crawl out of the trap they themselves had devised and set up.
How could people even live in such a foolish, wild time? — so perhaps they will think about our time in a few hundred years — what pitiful, comical, primitive people they (that is, we) were.
They invented machines upon machines (or perhaps they will call them "little machines" — mashinkes) and got themselves caught in them.
They did not know what to do with their great harvests, and they died of hunger. Out of small everyday things their "wise men" made enormous tangled "problems" that they were unable to solve [printed "lezn", read; evidently meant "leyzn", solve].
Simple questions of bread and food, and that everyone should live equally and work equally, they turned into holy and great ideals.
And they used to tear at each other and slaughter each other, worse than the wildest creatures.
What primitive people and what a primitive time (ours) it was.
They did not even know where a simple cold comes from. They did not believe in their doctors, and their doctors did not believe in themselves. Nevertheless the primitive people (do you recognize yourselves?) drank colored [?] little waters that the doctors, like sorcerers of old, told them to take.
A strange primitive time with primitive people; they did not believe in politics and let themselves be led by the nose; they made themselves various little dictators and — pardon the expression — let themselves be whipped by them.
And when it rained they went about like wet hens; and their clothing was wilder, less comfortable and less healthy than the clothes of the wildest and most backward tribes.
And these comical, pitiful and primitive creatures, who did not know how to eat, destroying their own true gods, still had the impudence to think of themselves as heroes, as tragic personalities, and of their primitive time as a great historical era. And they did not even grasp how much more comical than tragic they were.

The Jewish Craftsman Must Wake Up *)

[Craftsmen — economy; article.]
2.
In the previous article we already pointed out that the guild law [prawo cechowe], for all its shortcomings, may nevertheless have the merit that it will perhaps, in the end, help to wake the craftsman from his hitherto lethargic state, forcing him by compulsion to unclench his hands, open his eyes and look around to see where he stands in the world.
We stressed at once that we are far from being hundred-percent devotees of the guild law, which under present circumstances and in its present form is truly a harsh decree for the Jewish craftsman, who even with the best will cannot immediately adapt himself to all its demands. Not for nothing was the initiator, and perhaps also the author, of the guild law none other than St. Grabski [Stanisław Grabski].
But the first, if indirect, yet important effect of the guild law we have already felt: it has, namely, opened our eyes to the present lamentable condition of the impoverished and backward Jewish craftsman.
In fact we observe in Poland today two kinds of Jewish craftsmen: one kind, the richer and more powerful, is perhaps still able to adapt itself, at least purely outwardly, to the formal requirements of the guild law; the second, the far poorer and weaker one, feels altogether helpless and crushed face to face with the harsh guild decree, if only because, owing to his heavy worries about a livelihood, he has no time at all to think about all those "gifts" with which the guild law has "favoured" us.
Thus the guild law has already now divided the Jewish craftsmen themselves into privileged ones and almost rightless ones. To what extent the former are really privileged — we do not yet know; on the other hand, we already know that the latter are simply hounded and persecuted by those very institutions and authorities which are precisely called upon to protect and strengthen the craftsmen's estate.
And if certain naive craftsmen, Christian and Jewish alike, believe that putting difficulties in the way of new craftsmen setting themselves up with an independent workshop may help to increase the work and the profits in the already existing "privileged" craft workshops — they too are making a great mistake, to say nothing of the fact that, because of the artificial suppression of free competition in the crafts, every better craftsman will in time be forced to turn into a bungler [partacz], since the one who has the say in the field of the crafts is made by the guild law to be not the artist-craftsman but the merely privileged one; the state and the economic life of the country will gain very little from it at best.
The state is, after all, called upon to support and foster every initiative in the field of improving the crafts, whether it comes from private persons or from whole institutions; but on no account may the government create privileged sections of merely diploma-holding craftsmen, who are to prosper at the expense of their poorer brother craftsmen, who are in fact victims of the severe economic crisis. Not to mention that because of this the whole level of the crafts and of small industry in the country may sink low.
In general, now is not the time to introduce such innovations as the guild law; for if it is actually carried out in all its strictness, it may have a fatal effect on the condition of the crafts in Poland.
On the other hand, one cannot entirely deny the partly positive sides of the guild law either, namely first of all its strict requirement of proper vocational training, practical preparation and general education of the craftsman. Were we given the possibility of beginning, from precisely this side, to adapt gradually to the guild law, we would perhaps really be on the way to turning the guild decree into a blessing.
For this, however, one should first of all have prepared the remedy before the blow, by opening a widely branched network of supplementary vocational courses specially adapted to Jewish craftsmen, and also elementary vocational schools throughout the country. And only later should the guild law have been introduced (and that, too, in a milder form), when the ground for it would already have been better prepared.
But here they did the opposite: first the guild law was introduced, and in all its harshness to boot; and as for opening the proper supplementary vocational courses and elementary vocational schools for craftsmen, nobody has even begun to think about it yet. True, a few such schools already existed before — but not for Jewish craftsmen.
In this way the guild law may contribute to Jewish craftsmen being gradually pushed out of their positions [placówki], and their places being taken by others, non-Jews, who have every possibility of adapting themselves better to the law.
Against this danger of the guild law the craftsmen must defend themselves with all their strength.
Natan Rudner

Rents Must Be Reduced

[Housing — rent; opinion.]
The campaign of the tenants' associations to reduce rents, which has now been under way for a year, rests on the following premise: the incomes of the town's inhabitants have fallen by roughly 50 percent. Reductions, [cuts in] pensions and working days have become a daily occurrence, unemployment keeps growing, and the prices of all goods and raw materials keep falling.
In connection with the latest decree of the Finance Minister, under which the interest rate on building loans was reduced, the members of the housing cooperatives obtained a rent reduction reaching as much as 35 percent.
The tenants living in the houses of "ZUPU" in Katowice, too, put forward the demand that their rent be reduced by 40 percent. When the management of "ZUPU" refused to go along with this, the tenants paid only 60 percent of the rent for January, regardless of the fact that "ZUPU" had refused to agree to it. The management of "ZUPU" sued the tenants, and the case was heard by the District Court in Katowice. The court dismissed the management's suit.
In Warsaw and in a number of other towns tenants' strikes are breaking out. The strikers put forward the demand that rents be reduced by 40 to 50 percent, and as long as their demand is not met they pay no rent at all. It is worth noting that besides these striking tenants there are also a great many tenants who are not paying any rent at present; in particular the tenants who occupy large flats are not paying. This is the best proof that the impoverishment of the population is so great that the present level of rents far exceeds the population's ability to pay. That concerns the old houses. As for the new houses, there is no need even to speak: there the rent is so very much too high that by far the greater part of the tenants in these houses are unable to pay any rent at all. This explains why the campaign to lower rents is growing steadily sharper and is spreading with tremendous speed across the country. This often leads to misunderstandings and conflicts between tenants and house-owners, which bring unpleasant results and dangerous consequences to both sides.
Everything has become cheaper, and earnings keep falling. And the Sejm must immediately issue a decree reducing rents in line with the fall in the prices of goods and with the reduced incomes.
We wish to state here with complete categoricalness that the tenant should and must pay rent. The landlord has invested his capital in the house; he must pay all kinds of taxes on the house. It is therefore the tenant's duty to pay rent. But on the other hand the house-owners must not oppose the tenants' demand to lower rents. What do they gain from rents remaining at the same level as hitherto, if the tenants will not pay any rent at all? For the house-owner himself it is better to receive rent, even if it be less, than to have a large debt on paper and be left with empty pockets. Because the tenants will not pay at all. Besides, the house-owners' resistance to the tenants' campaign will hardly help. Life is stronger than everyone, even than the house-owners.
Life will force the house-owners to adapt to the present situation. Such an enormous gap between the prices of all articles, between earnings, and the rent cannot and must not continue. Even when there are certain house-owners who are ready to comply with the tenants' demand and lower the rent, the government stands in the way, as it does not want to reduce taxes in proportion to the reduced rent. This causes house-owners who acknowledge the justice [of the demand] of the tenants nevertheless not to agree to a rent reduction. This state of affairs must come to an end! The problem of lowering rents concerns all the tenants in the country. The problem must be solved as quickly as possible in the spirit of the tenants' demand; otherwise a flood of evictions threatens the country. Refusing to meet the tenants' demand will only lead to the municipal councils being forced to put up barracks for hundreds of thousands of homeless. Therefore rents must be reduced! That is the commandment of the hour.
A. Berman.
Poor Hitler, You're in Trouble!...

[Satire — Germany, Hitler; antisemitism in Poland.] (A letter from the "Green Ribbon" to the "Brown Shirt".) [The green ribbon was the badge of the antisemitic Polish nationalist (Endek) students, "zielona wstążka"; the brown shirt — the Nazis.]
"Kochany Adolfie" [Polish: "Dear Adolf"]!
First of all, in the name of all the green-ribboned "shubrakes"[?] [scoundrels? — from Polish] and cudgel-heroes, I wish to congratulate you on your office as Chancellor of Germany.
Yes, przyjacielu [my friend], one thing I don't understand: Adolf was a clever one [Hebrew "shepikeach haya"] — such a brave fellow, I only wish I could hold out as long with my "green ribbon" as you with your "brown shirt"... how does such foolishness suit you — what good is the chancellor's chair to you. Firstly, it is not for your house-painter's head ["malarska"], and secondly, what a face you will have in a tailcoat — the brown shirt with the "shubrane"[?] "gshibe"[?] suited you so well, "do twarzy" [Polish: became your face], what a face you will have in a tailcoat with a top hat — you will look like a Purim-player...
Did you take a look in the mirror, how you look in a top hat with the white collar[?]? You surely burst with laughter — you must have looked like a pig in a tallis katan or a Cossack in a shtreimel! I am sure that in your "brown shirt" you felt much "wygodniej" [Polish: more comfortable] than now in the tailcoat with the top hat...
But all this is nothing. We now live in a time when "kapusta" [cabbage] has become an "intelligent dish", and to be a "head" one needs no head... the main thing is the fist ["kulak"], and since you have all these virtues, you are [the "right man in the right place"...
In one thing, you see, kochanie Adolfie, I do not envy you: what will you do now with the antisemitic hobby-horse? What will you do now with your "rubber truncheon" ["gumowa pałka"]? As long as you went around with the ladder and the brush[?] you could allow yourself such "fun" as to put holes in the heads of a few hundred "żydowskie" [Polish: Jewish] students. As long as you went about in the "brown shirt" and lived together with your comrades in the "Brown House", you could freely and openly take a "stroll" over the "żydowskie" heads and break the windowpanes of Jewish shops, you could allow yourself to chatter[?] and mouth off ["piskeven"] about everything under the sun, but now, kochany Adolfie, as chancellor you must after all keep up "façon" [decorum]... How will you, in a tailcoat and a top hat, set about splitting Jewish heads and breaking the windowpanes of Jewish shops? Parliament is, after all, no beer-tavern, where you can mouth off in your "shubrane"[?] language — what will you do now, poor thing, I sympathise with you, kochany Adolfie..
But since we "green ribbons" and the "brown shirts" are after all somewhat "related", since we both trade in one "article", I, as a "członek" [member] of "Bratnia Pomoc" [the students' mutual-aid association, an Endek stronghold], have decided to help you out of your difficult situation — I will give you, kochany Adolfie, a lesson in how such a simple "chai vekayam" [Hebrew: "living and existing" — a nobody] as you [printed "ווי די"], how one of "ours", a "yat" [a fellow], must run the state and hold the "hołota" [rabble] "za mordę" [Polish: by the snout]...
Listen with your head, kochany Adolfie, to my lesson:
First of all you must grow a longer moustache; your [printed "דייגע"] "wąsiki" [little moustache] suit a waiter or a hairdresser.
Once you are sitting firmly "in the chair", take a broom and start sweeping out.. the undesirable elements — everywhere "eigene" [our own people] must sit...
For Minister of Education you can appoint a "gegrivet"[?] cobbler or a waiter — as long as he is a sworn "członek" of the "Brown House".
For Minister of Finance you must appoint a "blatn yat" [an underworld fellow] who knows how to swindle a few marks out of the "yoldn" [suckers].
For Minister of Health you must appoint a "kowal" [blacksmith], who must know how to "skoshcheshen"[?] and should know how to "make himself healthy" [i.e. line his pockets]...
The Minister of Trade must be a strong personality, who will have the strength... to tear trade out of the "żydowskie" hands..
The Minister of Posts must be a man of "far-sighted vision", who will see... what goes on in the American offices...
For Minister of Railways you should appoint a professional cab-driver ["zawodowy dorożkarz"], and he must know that "if you grease, you ride"...
The Minister of Justice must be a "Fachmann" [expert], who is well acquainted... with the prison ["turma"] guard...
Now, kochany Adolfie, you should take on the smaller fry; everywhere your "brown-shirted spirit" must rule...
And when you feel "firm in the joints" ["fest in di fuges"], you should take on the newspaper people, and the newspaper that will not say "amen" after you — you should tell it the story of the Silent One ["Shvayger"]...
Now, kochany Adolfie, I want to teach you how to "nabierać" [Polish: dupe] the masses: before every election you should send out your agitators from house to house and promise the voters: cheap flats, electric light in the side-alleys, bridegrooms for brides, dowries for "pszedzienna"[?] [perhaps: old-maid] girls, "pożyczki" [loans] for craftsmen, exemption from taxes, fighting the crisis, building houses, stopping evictions, employing the jobless and "po kupie"[?] — you know the rest!...
With parliament too you need not trouble yourself much: if the honourable deputies are good and pious — if they do what daddy and mummy tell them — they will be well off; if not, if they open their "gęba" [big mouth], don't fret too much — take them by the collars [printed "קעלנער", waiters] and "odjazd" [Polish: off you go]...
You need not be a "naczelnik" [sole ruler], and you should not close parliament altogether — it does not look good abroad; you may some day need a "pożyczka" [loan], and then they will start asking you questions: why this, why that; therefore one must keep parliament "for show" ["oyf puts"] — the "shmandakes"[?], that is the deputies, should sit in the tavern and drink a "bańka" [jug] of Bavarian beer, and you should heed them like last year's snow. If they say night — you say day; if they say "hoydes" — you say "boydes"; you must show that your name is Adolf, and when you give the command "eyes right" they must stand "na baczność" [Polish: at attention]...
That is my lesson; if you keep to my programme you will be well off and live long, and if not, you will suffer a grim, bitter defeat...
Poor Adolf!
For what troubles did you need this? What good did the tailcoat with the top hat do you; would it not have been healthier for you to have grown old in joy in your "brown shirt"; what good did a parliament do you — wasn't it much more "wygodniej" [comfortable] in the "Brown House"...
Poor Hitler, you're in trouble, poor thing...
Y. A. K.

Radio and Weather — the influence of weather on radio

[Radio — science and technology.] The influence of weather on radio
This year's winter is not the worst as far as radio listening is concerned. Noises and other interference have lately not been especially strong, so that the radio waves come through quite tolerably.
In the daytime one can hear a whole series of foreign radio stations on the long waves, such as Kalundborg, Zeesen, "Radio-Paris", Oslo and many Soviet radio stations. In the evening many dozens of radio stations can be heard excellently on the medium radio waves.
But one does not always hear all these radio stations well. Quite often it lasts for several days that the reception of radio music or speech is poor. In order to find the causes of this phenomenon, not yet fully explained, scientists have for a long time been carrying out much research in this field. This research is conducted simultaneously at various points of the earth, often under very difficult atmospheric conditions.
The very first results of this research have proved that good radio reception depends on the difference between the atmospheric conditions on the ground and at a height of 3000 metres. It has turned out that in places where low atmospheric pressure prevails radio is heard well, whereas in places surrounded by high atmospheric pressure radio is heard considerably worse. Thus one can already today say precisely whether radio reception will be good or bad in the evening.
Probably all radio stations will soon, following the example of the meteorological bulletins, begin to inform their listeners every evening about the prospects of good or bad radio reception.
Also interesting is the research the scientists have carried out on radio interference. It has turned out that every time strong gusting winds have blown and large masses of cold air are carried from one place to another, one immediately hears in the earphone or the loudspeaker a characteristic short crackle, "just like on a frying pan." It is precisely this sudden shifting of cold or hot air masses that has a decisive influence on radio reception.
Statistics have shown that in ninety per cent of cases the cold air masses have a favourable influence on the radio waves. This indeed explains the fact that the radio stations located to the north-east and east are heard better than those located in other directions, where warmer air masses are found.
The "Gunpowder Purim" in Vilna

[Jewish history — Vilna, R. Avraham Danzig, author of "Chayei Adam"; for Purim.]
Moshe Fajnkind.

An episode from the life of the "Chayei Adam".

In Vilna lived and worked the gaon R. Avraham Danzig, the author of "Chayei Adam" and of other books of religious law.
He came from Germany; his father, R. Yechiel, had come to Vilna from Danzig and set up a business there.
Besides being a great scholar, R. Avraham Danzig was also a great merchant. Year in, year out he used to travel to the great fairs in Leipzig and Königsberg to buy goods and bring them to Vilna to sell. His shop was on Glass Street (Glezer Gas).
Since he was known in the world as a great gaon, the rabbinate of the largest Jewish communities was offered to the "Chayei Adam", but on no account did he want to become a rabbi, not even in his own Vilna, where he was highly esteemed and honoured. He simply did not want to live on the community's money.
On the night of 15 Kislev 5564 (1804) a great explosion of a gunpowder store took place in Vilna on Glass Street; it levelled all the houses on that street to the ground, and some 31 people perished there in the terrible fire.
Among these houses was also the house in which the "Chayei Adam" lived, and remarkably he and his entire household escaped alive from the terrible catastrophe.
This miracle caused great astonishment in the town, and the public interpreted it in various ways.
But the "Chayei Adam" was now badly impoverished: all his fortune and the shop's goods had gone up in smoke.
He no longer had anything to trade with and had to resolve to become a dayan (rabbinical judge) in Vilna — the town absolutely demanded it of him.
The day on which his household was saved from certain death, however, the "Chayei Adam" designated for his descendants as a day of fasting and prayer, and in the evening a festive meal was to be held, to which only scholars and poor people were to be invited. For a long time the relatives celebrated this day of remembrance, which the public crowned with the name "Gunpowder Purim" ("Pulver-Purim")..
* * *
After the catastrophe the "Chayei Adam" made a vow that as soon as he had married off his children he would settle in Jerusalem.
But in the meantime the "Chayei Adam" passed away on 4 Tishrei 5581 (1821) at the age of 72 (born 5508) and was buried in the old historic cemetery in Snipishok (Šnipiškės), where the Vilna Gaon and other Vilna gaonim also found their eternal rest.
In the course of time the "Gunpowder Purim" was forgotten in Vilna, but the relatives in America still celebrate it today.
A King Who Fled His Throne in the Middle of the Night (4)

[Serialized historical tale — France and Poland, Henri III (Henryk Walezy); installment 4.]
(Historical story)
By El—Be.

A short time after the Duke of Alençon, Henri's third brother, had fled, it came to a clash between the Huguenots and the Catholics. The Catholic army stood under the command of the Duke of Guise, who during the clash won a victory over the Huguenots. In the battle the Duke of Guise received severe wounds in the ear and on the face. For this the Catholics honoured him even more, and he became in their eyes a true hero and a saint.
The Duke of Alençon, however, did not give up his warlike mood, and with a reinforced Huguenot army he marched on Paris.
His mother, Catherine de Médicis, instead of meeting him with an army, decided to find another way to meet him. The mother, knowing the character of her third son, engaged a large number of the most beautiful and alluring women, with whom she went off to visit him.
The plan worked out unusually well for her. Her flattering little speeches and the roguish glances of the females had an effect on the Duke, and he concluded a peace agreement with his mother.
In gratitude for the peace concluded, the mother tripled his estates, and he left the Huguenots.
Henri of Navarre, the son-in-law of Catherine de Médicis, who had also been with the Huguenot army, also made peace with his mother-in-law.
Henri of Navarre had been held prisoner by order of his brother-in-law after the St. Bartholomew's massacre, but he had escaped from captivity. All these sins Catherine forgave him, provided he would withdraw from the Huguenot army.
The Catholics, on learning of the concessions that had been granted to the Huguenot leaders, became terribly incensed. They regarded it as treason on the part of the king.
The Jesuits exploited the favourable moment, and thanks to their agitation Catholic leagues were created — in order to maintain the supremacy of Catholicism and at the same time to keep up the persecution of Protestantism.
At the head of the fraternity stood Henri of Guise. His own aim was something else entirely: he wanted to exploit the campaign against King Henri for himself, so that when Henri III was deposed from the throne, he would be the heir.
This plan was approved in Rome, and also the Jesuit [sic] Philip II of Spain promised to support it with money and with men.
In December 1576[?] the national assembly took place in Blois. All the deputies (except one) were supporters of Henri of Guise.
Henri III, seeing that his power was hanging by a thread, made a diplomatic trick: he declared that he was in full agreement with the Catholic League and promised that he was ready to place himself at the head of the League in order to suppress the Protestant heresies.
The diplomatic gesture, however, did not find favour with the Catholic League, which had no trust in his words, and the League put a demand to him:
"The 36 elected deputies of the Estates-General shall form a council which shall help the king to rule the kingdom."
The proposal was rejected by Henri, because if such a council were created he would after all cease to be ruler.
In the country a civil war broke out between the Catholics and the Protestants which lasted a full 3 years. At last both sides grew tired, and for the seventh time a peace was concluded.
In 1581 a revolution of the Flemings against Philip II broke out in Spain [sic]. Henri's brother, the Duke of Alençon, who was again looking for a way to rise to greatness, formed an army with which he marched to Spain to help the Flemish revolutionaries.
The army under the Duke's command won victories over the Spaniards, and the Flemings crowned their redeemer as their hero, proclaimed him their Duke of Brabant and titled him Count of Flanders.
Of this honour the Duke of Alençon relieved himself: he was, after all, a son of Catherine de Médicis — he cooked up a mess with the Flemings themselves; he busied himself with intrigues that led to the Amsterdam[?] bloodbath, and the incensed citizens drove him out of the country.
Out of great heartache and shame the Duke of Alençon died in the year 1584.

On the Cymbal [Yiddish idiom "to take someone on the cymbal" — to mock him].
(Like a leading article [pun: "leyd-artikl" — Leitartikel / "leyd" = suffering]).
All year long we must look on and keep silent about the injustices that cry out to heaven, that are perpetrated in our world; we must be indifferent and keep quiet while our golems, good-for-nothings ["drerd-ligers"], shmendriks and boors[?] run wild, going about with the phrase "whose honour?" — and against you it is "to destroy and to slay". We grind our teeth, we clench our fists, but we can do nothing at all. So it goes a whole round year, until dear Purim comes, when one can pull something out into the open...
So we have indeed taken our "grogger" in hand and we will rattle along the whole front... Everyone we will take on the cymbal — it is Purim after all, so everyone must be taken — on the cymbal.
Dear Reb Haman.

[Humour — Purim; satirical poem.] Dear, beloved Reb Haman!
Well, a demon take your father;
See how your rascals ["yatn"] grow
Just like mushrooms after rain.

You're quite an important merchant, I'd say,
With such fine dealings:
Your sons were hanged,
And still you left behind a seed...

You have no shame at all
In that fine mug of yours;
A little bastard — and not just one —
You left us as an inheritance...

You ask: what harm can it do?
You may indeed take pride and joy,
For they are — just to spite us —
Ten times worse than their father...

You wanted to strangle us
According to law and according to justice;
Why, you're a big fool ["yold"],
There's none like you anywhere...

See, your clique does better than you,
It behaves — my good brother —
Quietly, nicely and without a fuss:
They strangle us — in silence...

And they boast of your name
And they keep your words:
See, they throw us out of our places
And they empty out the shops...
Vayehi...

[Humour — Purim.] "Vayehi" ["And it came to pass"] — the Megillah begins with a "vayehi", and we know that wherever "vayehi" is written, there it smells of trouble [after the Talmudic saying: "wherever 'vayehi' is said, it denotes woe"].
And since troubles are certainly not lacking today, we too must begin our "grogger" Megillah with the luckless "vayehi", for the Haman of the Megillah would be ashamed before the Hamans of our time...
A "vayehi" in the factories, a "vayehi" in the businesses, a "vayehi" among the house-owners, a "vayehi" among the tenants ["lokatorn"], a "vayehi" among the craftsmen, a "vayehi" among the workers.
A "vayehi" in the town councils ["magistrates"], a "vayehi" in the institutions, a "vayehi" in the schools, a "vayehi" in the universities, a "vayehi" in the banks, a "vayehi" in the newspapers, a "vayehi" among the writers, a "vayehi" among the young men, a "vayehi" among the girls, a "vayehi" among the fathers, a "vayehi" among the grandfathers.

The Modern Megillah.

Translated, with new commentaries, by Lejb Sztabiński.
"When the heart of the king was merry with wine": when Ahasuerus was good and "full", he ordered his own wife brought, so that she should show everyone her beauty.
Boasting of one's own wife can only happen when one is "full"; had Ahasuerus been "lacking", he would surely have ordered a strange wife brought...
"And Mordecai walked every day": today Mordecai too goes every day out of one business and into another. Now he goes to write appeals, now he runs to the relief committee, and now he goes to hand back his trade licence...
"And he made a release to the provinces": while Haman was still alive Ahasuerus granted the country a release [from taxes], and after they had hanged him the Megillah says: "And the king Ahasuerus laid a tribute upon the land" — he imposed a tax on the land.
Poor Haman! You had little sense; you should have handed Ahasuerus a project to lay a big tax on the Jews — he would have been rid of them anyway...
"And he arrayed Mordecai": once Haman dressed Mordecai, today he strips him...
"[And it was] written to reverse the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha": it turns out that Esther asked to annul Haman's decree that Jewish merchants must keep commercial books...
"For Mordecai was great in the king's house": once Mordecai grew greater every day, today Mordecai grows smaller from day to day.
"And these days of Purim shall not pass": because in every generation there will be Hamans who will want — will want to destroy the Jews.

What Is the Difference?
— What is the difference between a baker and a landlord?
— The first throws in [into the oven] and the second throws out.
— What is the difference between an aeroplane and a merchant?
— The first goes up and the second goes down!
— What is the difference between a steam bath and the tax office (Urząd Skarbowy)?
— Into a steam bath you go in naked, and out of the tax office you come out naked...
— What is the difference between a deputy and a widow?
— A deputy looks forward to the first [of the month — payday] and a widow looks forward to the second [husband]...
Knapo.
If Only It Weren't Saturday Afternoon.

The worries of a Sosnowiec bachelor-bridegroom.
Yosl the matchmaker comes to a young man to propose a match.
— I have a lucky match for you, an ideal young lady.
— Who is she?
— Miss Salcze [?] Dalmafsówna.
— But she limps, doesn't she?
— That's only an accident, a misfortune, poor thing — the tram ran her over; that can happen after the wedding too.
— But she's as ugly as the night!
— What do you care? By day you sit in the shop, at lunch you read the newspaper, so you won't see your wife anyway. After lunch you go back to the shop, at supper you read the newspaper again, and at night it's dark anyway... Remember, a dowry of 2 thousand dollars doesn't come walking along these days...
— You're right, but what will I do on Saturday afternoon, when I don't go to the shop?...
A Letter from a Tenant to His Landlord.

Esteemed Landlord!
Firstly I can inform you that, thank God, I am doing very well. Against the eviction order that you obtained against me I have already even lodged an appeal. I have heard it said that lately you suffer, pardon me, from "opfirung" [diarrhoea; literally "carrying-off"] — you keep carrying out evictions... I would ask you to put hot compresses on your heart, so that you should not have a cold heart...
As for money, I can tell you that when I have it, I'll hand it over to you, for I know that you are a Jew who is a "kabbalist" — you like to receive... and, by the way, also a great philanthropist — you like to give
— evictions..
I would ask a favour of you!
When you go to throw out a tenant, don't hire the bailiff (komornik) for it, but one of your own — namely my own wife; she throws, I tell you, better than all the bailiffs. And if you don't want to believe that she can throw, then come up, if you please, to my flat when my wife wants to go to Zakopane, or wants a new coat for Passover — you'll see how she throws... rolling pins, bowls, pots... all the bailiffs can go hide before her throwing...
— I have heard it said that the rent is going down... into the landlord's pocket... Is it true?..
Respectfully,
Your tenant X

— Whence is it deduced that Haman had 10 sons?
— Had he had 10 daughters, he would have hanged himself..
— Whence is it deduced that today's girls are prettier than Queen Esther?
— Queen Esther was "green" [sallow], and today's Esthers have all the colours...
— What is the difference between Queen Vashti and a woman of today?
— Queen Vashti was ashamed to go naked, and a woman of today is ashamed to go dressed.
Ahasuerus Was a Faithful Husband.
Ahasuerus really was the true faithful husband to his wife — may it be said of all men; for example:
1) Being at the ball among his ministers, he ordered his own wife to be brought so that all the men should see her beauty. Men of today, being at a ball, thank God that their wife is not beside them...
2) Ahasuerus prided himself that his wife was the most beautiful. Men of today say that the other fellow's wife is the most beautiful and their own is the ugliest.

On what foundations can the Sosnowiec Merchants' Association be reopened?
In Sosnowiec a meeting took place of the former members of the Merchants' Association at Piłsudskiego 12, which dealt with the question of reopening the Merchants' Association.
After a long and passionate discussion it was resolved:
1) To exempt the members from the monthly payment.
2) Every evening each member shall enjoy free of charge at the buffet a sweet glass of tea with a biscuit. (On Friday nights a glass of beer with beans.)
3) Every Saturday night a melave-malke shall be arranged at the association.
4) The members shall receive from the municipality tickets for a free mikveh and steam bath.
5) The members who play cards — the association shall give them money "to stake".
6) When a member has to marry off a daughter, the association shall give him a dowry and also money for the wedding expenses.
7) The association shall buy back for the members their protested bills of exchange.
From the "Bridge Association"
Because of the great success the "bridge" courses are having — so much so that it is already hard to find in Będzin an "intelligent" woman who does not play "bridge" — the women's circle has decided to found other useful courses for women.
From a conversation that the "Greger" [Gragger] had with the management of the "bridge" game we learn that first on the plan is the opening of courses for women-matrons and for women pilots (to fly an aeroplane).
The news about the pilots' courses has aroused discontent among the men. Every one of them is afraid that as soon as his wife flies a little over the street, she will rise up and fly away...
Popular hygiene through "TOZ".
The new board of the Zagłębie branch of "TOZ" [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jews] has decided to conduct a special activity in the field of school hygiene.
In this connection we have received from "TOZ" the following appeal to Jewish parents:
"Jewish parents, if they want to have healthy children, must leave the damp flats and the dark, wet cellar-dwellings. Every Jewish family must have at least 5 rooms with a kitchen and a bathroom. The walls must be painted in oil paint. The sun must be in all the windows the whole day; the linen must be changed twice a day; every woman must have two maids, one for cooking and one for cleaning.
Every child must sleep in a separate bed; care must also be taken that the food served to the children turns out tasty; every day the dishes must be served according to the newest cookbooks."

From the General Meeting of the "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim-Fareyn).
After a break of two years, a general members' meeting of the Merchants' Association took place on Sunday. At 5 o'clock the meeting was supposed to begin with whatever number of members [were present]. But the clock already showed 6 and... the hall was still almost empty... Even part of the board did not come to the meeting.
Quietly, monotonously, the greater half of the agenda was "disposed of". Possibly the Polish-speaking, both by the chairman and by the presenters of reports, caused none of those present to ask for the floor in the discussion; and the proof: when the chairman announced that "he is breaking the tradition" and that Jews would be able to speak in Yiddish, only then did "the common folk" get some tongue...
* * *
The president of the Association, Mr. Rubinlicht, opens the meeting and hands the chair to Mr. Yekl Sandower[?]; Messrs. Ch. W. Steinhart and Lipa Openheim are invited to the presidium.
The reports on the activity during the years 1931 and 1932 are delivered by Mr. Rubinlicht. He points first of all to the terrible apathy and indifference among the merchants. It may be, says Mr. R., that the crisis affects the merchants so heavily that they have already lost their lively interest in the institution which is always ready to defend their interests; but the result ought to be the opposite: the greater the crisis, the more the members should seek protection with the Association.
In the further part of the report Mr. Rubinlicht points to the wide-ranging activity of the Merchants' Association in all fields; in particular the Association was active in the field of tax matters, when a series of memoranda was sent concerning the annulment of tax arrears, etc.
The Merchants' Association has its representatives in: the Chamber of Commerce, the Commercial Court, the Labour Court, the District Court, the Assessment Commission, etc.
At the Merchants' Association there exists a legal-advice department. During the reporting period 219 consultations were given.
During this time the secretariat sent out 655 letters and 25 memoranda, bought 300 trade licences (patents), and issued 228 certificates concerning postal matters and 80 certificates concerning tax questions.
The balance sheet is presented by the secretary, Mr. L. Rechtman. The budget in the year 1932 — 5828 zł.
After the adoption of this year's budget in the sum of 5,460 zł., the most important item on the agenda is dealt with: the regulations (regulamin) of the arbitration court according to the new law.
Mr. Rubinlicht explains the importance of the arbitration courts, and after a short discussion the following judges are appointed:
L. Rubinlicht, J. Goldfeld, M. Lewin, B. Rembiszewski, S. J. Rynski, P. L. Buchwajc, S. Liwer, S. Fridler, K. Kapłowicz, P. Unger, A. Ptasznik, A. Gitler, A. Szwarcbaum, M. Krakowski, J. Jungster, M. Gold[?], Ch. W. Steinhart, M. Tenenbaum, A. Lidzbarski, M. Gertner, H. Unger, M. Grundman, J. M. Kurland, M. Dąb, H. Kaniński, J. Najmark, S. Krakowski, J. Regirer and Marek Szajn.
Because those assembled declare that the judges are only from the "upper ten thousand", it is resolved that at the next general meeting the board will present new candidates, and also six persons will be struck from the number, because according to the regulations there should be only 24 judges.
Under free motions it is resolved: 1) on the motion of Mr. S. Fridler, that the Merchants' Association should begin a campaign against harmful competition; 2) on that of Mr. Sznajman, that parcel post should not be delivered on the Sabbath; 3) on that of Mr. Leszman — that instead of monthly tickets on the railway, weekly tickets should be introduced; and 4) on that of Mr. Majtlis — that the Association should organise lectures on merchants' questions.
On the "front" of the composition of the board and representatives — no changes...
Homeowners Must Pay for Water. A Decree of the Finance Minister.

[Będzin — municipality.] On Wednesday the local Magistrat [town council] received the decree concerning the rights of the water-supply bodies.
According to the decree, payment for water to the Magistrat is to be made not by the tenants, as has been the case until now, but by the homeowners.
We consulted on this question with the kierownik [head] of the Magistrat's main office, who gave us the following explanation:
In contrast to the decree, under which the homeowners must pay for water, the tenants' protection law already states that in houses which had water in 1914 the tenants are exempt from paying for water, because the costs of water were already included in the amount of the rent; whereas in houses that had no water, the tenants are obliged to pay for the use of water.
The new decree also provides that if a tenant does not pay for water, the matter can be settled only through the court; through the Magistrat or through the tax office [urząd skarbowy] the tenants will not be called upon to pay.
The proposal that homeowners should pay for water was introduced by alderman Mr. G. Rechnic at the plenum of the local commissarial council.
The Meetings on the Forthcoming Passover Campaign — Did Not Take Place.

[Będzin — community.] The kehilla administration, in connection with this year's Passover campaign, called 2 meetings, to which a large number of householders and communal workers were invited.

At the Police Commissariat the Shochtim's Strike Was Liquidated.

[Będzin — community; ritual slaughter.] At the local slaughterhouse shochtim's strikes have lately been breaking out every Monday and Thursday.
Not a single week passes without a strike: when the old shochtim slaughter, the new ones strike, and vice versa.
Last Monday the old shochtim went on strike because the gmina [Jewish community] does not pay them their pensions.
The veterinary doctor of the slaughterhouse turned to the police commissariat about the strike, asking that the strike be liquidated, arguing that the strike was causing damage to the Magistrat [town council].
On the strength of this intervention the shochtim were summoned to the commissariat, where they were prevailed upon to break off the strike.

[Będzin — society.] On Zawale [?] Street a tna'im [betrothal-contract] ceremony was to take place these days between a Będzin girl and a young man from Żarki.
When everything had already been prepared and the guests had gathered for the celebration, a telegram suddenly arrived from Żarki saying that the bridegroom should come home at once.

Linen Collection for the „Linas ha-Cholim“ Society in Będzin

[Będzin — charity.] On Sunday the administration of the Będzin „Linas ha-Cholim“ held a meeting, at which the special commission on the economic situation of the society delivered a report.
The report shows that both in the maternity home and in the „Moshav Zekenim“ [old-age home] the stock of linen has diminished enormously; many linen articles are no longer available at all.
It was therefore decided to carry out a linen collection among the Jewish population of Będzin in general and among the manufactured-textile merchants in particular.
It is to be hoped that the linen campaign will be properly supported and bring the desired success.
Sosnowiec. The Government Must Not Allow the „Klimontów“ Coal Mine to Be Flooded.

[Sosnowiec — economy; mining.] The „Sosnowiec Company“ [Towarzystwo Sosnowieckie] has decided that, owing to the bad economic situation in coal production, the „Klimontów“ mine, which belongs to the above-mentioned company, is to be flooded, and that „Mortimer“ too is to be idle for a longer time.
In this connection several conferences took place this week with the participation of several Sanacja deputies, who decided that a special delegation should intervene with the government so that „Klimontów“ should not be flooded, since 2,000 workers are threatened with losing their bread.
Tried to lead a 10-year-old girl astray.

[Sosnowiec — Crime.] On Rudna Street an unknown person approached a 10-year-old girl and promised the child one złoty if she would carry the letter there, to Bem Street.
The child gladly took on the "business" and went with the person to the address indicated.
When the person entered a house on Bem Street, after going in he locked the entrance door. He told the little girl to wait on the first floor, and he went up to the second floor, where he listened in on a conversation from a certain [?] apartment.
The scene was seen by a maidservant of the house, who raised the alarm, whereupon the mysterious person ran away.
This is already the second case in which under-age girls are being led astray.

Anti-Jewish Excesses in Milówka, Rajcza and Ujsoły

[Poland — anti-Jewish riots; Żywiec district.]
Hundreds of górale [highlanders] attack Jewish shops. — The mob throws stones at the police. — 7 wounded, 1 killed, 83 arrested. — Calm has been restored.
On Tuesday evening a mob of hundreds of górale and town residents, armed with axes, shovels and poles[?], attacked the Jewish shops in Rajcza, Milówka and Ujsoły. A detachment of 5 policemen, with the help of officers staying at the Rajcza sanatorium, put down the disturbances. The mob also pelted the police with stones, to which the police replied with gunfire, and several people were wounded. One of the wounded died on the way to the hospital.
21 Jewish shops were demolished.
Those guilty of the excesses, 83 men in number, have been arrested.
The chief ringleaders are Endek [National Democrat] gangs.
Thanks to the energetic intervention of the authorities, calm has been restored to order.

"The Jews Are upon Thee, Poland!" — The Endek "Kurjer Zachodni" Trembles at the New "Danger"

Hitlerism, which is now celebrating orgies in Germany, is for our home-grown Hitlerites — Endeks, as they are called in the vernacular — a stick with two ends. On the one hand they are pleased with the tremendous growth of the Hitlerites — no small matter: their like-minded comrades multiply from day to day, their government grows stronger, and a holy war has been declared on... Freemasonry and the Jews. But on the other hand, that very policy of extermination forces many German Jews to flee to Poland, and this second end of the Hitlerite stick has stuck like a bone in the throat of our Endecja [National Democrats].
Almost all Endek newspapers are sounding the alarm about the new danger, a kind of "The Jews are upon thee, Poland".
The Endek "Kurjer Zachodni" too weeps crocodile tears and draws the government's attention, asking it not to permit the immigration of German Jews to Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.
It seems the Endecja is not destined to have full joy. From Hitlerism one could have had pleasure, but great is the heartache lest a few German Jews come into Poland.
The "Kurjer Zachodni" has a double grief: the German Jews — writes the paper — who come to Zagłębie are paupers, and from them the Endek organ cannot hope to get any advertisements...
Bloody Drama in Częstochowa — Industrialist Shoots His Partner Dead and Commits Suicide

On Monday in daytime a bloody drama played out in the gateway of the house at Waszyngtona 20.
Eng. Józef Szklarczyk, a native of Zagłębie, who has been living for several months in Częstochowa, seriously wounded his former partner Kabalański, a knife manufacturer in Radomsko.
When Kabalański lay seriously wounded on the ground, Szklarczyk fired at him 3 more times and shot him dead.
Then Szklarczyk shot himself. He was taken to hospital in serious condition.

Meeting of the Zionist Organization in Dąbrowa

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the Dąbrowa Zionists took place in their own premises. Before a fairly large number of those present, Mr. Dawid Kożuch opened the meeting, and Mr. Eliezer Tenenbaum was elected chairman; he invited Messrs. H. Rozencwajg, Kożuch, M. Rozenblum, Krawiński and Najer to the presidium.
Mr. Tenenbaum reported on the activity of the board since the last general meeting, namely: shekels, Keren Hayesod, National Council, in which the material results were satisfactory.

Elected to the new board were: Tenenbaum, Lenczner, Krawiński, Lejtner, Rozenblum, Liberman, Kajzer, Bukowski and Kożuch.
The Olkusz Starost Conducts an Investigation in the Pilica Community

We are written to from Pilica:

The Passover Campaign and the Matzah Question

[Będzin — The Passover relief campaign and the matzah question; opinion article.]
(The "great concern" of Będzin's rich men. — The fat morsel from the Passover kashrut certificates)
A week ago Friday our Sosnowiec correspondent complained that with them[?] in Sosnowiec everything has come to a standstill. Jewish life is cold and frozen. He proves this by the fact that his community workers are apathetic toward the coming Passover campaign, and he concludes that in Będzin it is quite different. With us — he says — such matters are treated with due attention and awareness. Sosnowiec thus envies Będzin, which has more understanding and sense of obligation toward social problems. And what is true must indeed be admitted. Będzin really has more interest in social-philanthropic matters than its sister town.
And yet... and yet, what is this to such warmth, such concern, such support[?]. Well, that Jewish life is now hard and bitter and dark is no secret to anyone any more; we all know it, we all feel it, the grave situation oppresses every one of us, it presses unbearably, there is no more strength to breathe, people are at a loss, the masses stagnate and their strength gives out one by one. Everyone knows this is not written just like that, to remind us that things are bad; everybody feels it, and the Jewish middle class and the artisan are simply living through something unnatural, incomprehensible. When one begins to take stock of the prevailing situation, one loses one's balance and cannot grasp where the strength comes from to hold out so long, to live so long on sheer miracles.
So people torment themselves all year, so they barely drag themselves along on their feet. People go hungry of whom everyone thinks that they are well off, that they are to be envied. In reality, though, there stretches a long chain of troubles and worries, torments and afflictions, beyond endurance.
But however bad and bitter it is all year, it becomes considerably worse and more dangerous during the Jewish festival days. Above all when it concerns the hardest Jewish festival — Passover, when one must prepare to live for 8 whole days, at a time when today one cannot really prepare even for a single day. Besides, one must not forget that everyone has to partake of Passover foods. Hence the kosher-certified products become dearer. Everyone feels it somehow a kind of mitzvah to lay a hand on the Passover products, and with every touch the prices are screwed up.
But let us say the prices will not be screwed up this year — will the Jewish public be able to reach Passover? Will the broad strata of the Jewish population be able to provide food for all 8 days of Passover? Does anyone at least think of providing for those who go hungry all year? Do those who still have, somehow, the means to get through the day with dignity think of their brothers and sisters who have become so terribly impoverished that they must be provided for in a dignified way over the 8 days of Passover?
Sosnowiec envies Jewish Będzin that we relate warmly to philanthropic matters; and it is characteristic that the "warmth" reaches such a degree that the kehilla board has already twice convened meetings at which it was to be considered how to approach this year's Passover campaign — and characteristic it is that both meetings did not take place, because nobody came: all the rich preferred to warm themselves at home rather than carry their "warmth" over to the meetings. That is how it looks in Będzin, in the town where there is understanding and where people feel for the suffering and the hungry.
We know the hearts of Będzin, we know they will not bear people going hungry, and the Passover campaign will certainly be carried out — but all this will happen at the last minute, and then it is done in a rush. So in that case both the givers and the receivers suffer. Then it costs much more, and what is done is done without a system, without proper calculation — and that must not be allowed. After all, it is now high time to organise the relief campaign energetically, so that it must be arranged in such a way that both the products and the money coming in bring the greatest possible benefit. This year it must not be done merely pro forma, just so that it can be said that a campaign is being run. Nor would it be desirable for everyone to "make Shabbat for himself" separately. There is a Beit Lechem, which already has some practice and routine in this field; the artisans will surely do something for their fellows; the gmina [municipality] too wants to run such a campaign — in this case it would definitely be wiser to merge all these institutions into one large Passover campaign. That would save much money, time and manpower, in which we are so poor, and then a certain order could be introduced: the giver would need to give only once; he would then know that nobody would come to him again to collect for this purpose, and he could therefore allow himself to give more — whereas as soon as everyone makes Shabbat for himself, he gives as little as possible, because he does not know who else will come to collect for this purpose. It will also be a good thing for the givers, because one institution will not rely on another, and they will know that a family belonging to the impoverished [yordim] must be provided with the necessary products.
It would therefore be very, very desirable for the campaign to be concentrated in one place; that way it will bring the greatest benefit to the hungry.
It would also be only fair to consider a matter not directly related to this question. We mean the baking of the matzot. First of all, one must not let oneself be fleeced; not everyone should exploit the "poor man's matzah" and tear off as big a slice of it as possible. Then one must see to it that Jewish hands, too, earn from the work — from the rolling, kneading and making of the matzot. After all we have enough unemployed; let them earn from their work for Passover, and at least[?] there will be no need to give them [alms]. On this question one must absolutely stop and see to it that it is solved not as in every year.
People start baking late, and then even Christian helpers are lacking, at a time when Jews are not taken into account — and among us the camp of beggars grows. This lawlessness must not be allowed to continue like this. Here we cry that people have nothing to do; they would take on[?] any work whatever — and when it comes to baking matzot for Jews, which must be kosher even for the most scrupulous of the scrupulous, one cannot get Jewish helpers. Isn't that ridiculous? Isn't it a slap in the face? Must we let ourselves be humiliated like this because our idlers and good-for-nothings want it so? This system, rooted long enough, must no longer be tolerated, above all when poverty and destitution whistle[?] over the broad Jewish masses.
The Passover campaign and the matzah question must therefore be solved as quickly as possible, in a dignified and rational way.
R. Les.
Work! Work! Work!

[Zagłębie — halutzim; labour.]

Healthy, tall young men from the halutz kibbutzim in Zagłębie pour out their bitter hearts at the editorial office.

Other Jews, on the other hand, have „pity“ on the halutzim and do not want to give them this or that work, because it is too hard or too dirty.
Do write, the young men ask, that no „leniency“ should be shown us; we can bear the hardest work and at the same time also the most highly skilled. For What Period Must One Pay Turnover Tax?

[Taxes — industrial tax; legal advice.]
The industrial tax in the form of patents (licence certificates) is levied for a whole or a half year; so even if the enterprise is opened on the first of December, a patent must be bought for half a year.
It is quite different with the industrial tax in the form of turnover tax. This tax one is obliged to pay only for the time during which the given enterprise was actually active.
Thus, if the enterprise was opened on 3 December, one must pay industrial tax in the form of turnover tax for 1 month only.
Since the enterprise was not active for 5 months during the given tax year, one pays turnover tax only for 7 months.
One must remember, however, that the tax authority regards as new only an enterprise which really did not exist before, but not one which was previously run under another firm or by another person.
Jews of Zagłębie Who Are Going to the Land of Israel

[Zagłębie — emigration to Eretz Israel; the Palestine Office in Warsaw; sketch.]
The first pictures with which I shall begin my road to Eretz Israel in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ will be pictures of the people I meet at the Palestine Office; there, in the gullet [?] of what are called the Jewish Dardanelles, I encounter the joys and sorrows of the Jewish people, for there I meet all sorts of „bankers“, workers, [?] ladies and ordinary people who hang about the Palestine Office.
Several times already I have been observing the stream of people bursting into and running out of Mariańska 10. Let us, then, describe the life there.
I arrived in the morning, when the rooms were flooded with a host of pale-coloured, red and green little hats of girls who come looking for certificates. I am not exaggerating: lately the certificates, especially for the girls, have become a kind of cult, a kind of sanctification, just as once there was the rich American uncle whom people fussed over because he was the angel of dollars. Here a group [?] of three young ladies came up to me; each young lady carries her papers, and according to the papers they are from the „three neighbouring towns“: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa. Three friends they are; all of them have already given up their acquaintances, friends, fathers, and they are looking for... a certificate. Now the young lady from Będzin comes up to me, a girl of about 28; she holds out her hand to me with a very sweet, warm smile:
— Don't you recognise me? — she asks. — Don't you remember that we met at my sister's? You even lunched with us. I do not recognise the young lady, but she smiles more deeply and talks at me so that I should recognise her:
— Why, we gave a banquet for you, we even took you to the train.
— Yes, I recognise you — I say just so, to be rid of her — and how can I be of service to you?
— Dear friend — that one addresses me amiably — I have a request to you, I have something to ask of you; you are, after all, a good and kind man, perhaps you will help me with a trifle, I mean, that you should get me a certificate.
— No more than that? — I ask ironically.
— Is it really hard for you? — she says. — No, you can, you can do anything, you only have to want to.
— Am I then the master of the certificates?
— Yes, if you want to, you can.
— Unfortunately I cannot.
— Then I ask this: since you have influence with the director of the Palestine Office, see to it that the journey should cost less.
— That too I cannot do.
Then the two remaining young ladies proposed a trifle to me.
— Listen to me — says the young lady from Sosnowiec, a tall, slender girl with thin painted little lips and a blonde [lock?] like an Englishwoman's — I know that writers take women with them, secretaries, who note down their thoughts; I want to go with you, I want to be your secretary. I do not lack money; on the contrary, I will even keep you — only, the main thing, take me on your passport, I will go with you wherever you wish.
The girl from Dąbrowa was jealous, and she interrupted:
— If only the gentleman would take me along, I would go with him across the world; he would have in me a sole friend, a dear friend, only what...
The girls began to shower all kinds of compliments, but it did not help; I refused them my help.
From one side a trimmed little beard came up to me with a broad „sholem aleykhem“; he introduced himself to me as a pedlar from Katowice. For many good years he had worked with his wares among his customers, but when the business went bust he came to look for a certificate; that, however, he does not get, so he comes to demand a certificate of me. And the Jew did not come alone: he brought with him a sister, a tall Jewess with long earrings and painted lips like an Egyptian queen. The woman, a person of about 46, planted herself before me like an oak and began to describe to me her great earnings of former times; today, however, she is ready — provided she becomes a halutza — to take off her fine shoes and put on wooden clogs. But I stood and looked at the people who had surrounded me like an army, and looking at the women I thought to myself: have not the words of the prophet already been fulfilled — „And seven women shall take hold of one man“? One may say this has come true in our present time, there at the doors of the Palestine Office. Women, especially dowryless ones, do not merely travel — they run, they tear themselves by force into the world of palms and cedars. It is truly a joy, this striving to get here; but let us be frank: it is a tragedy of hundreds of Jewish girls who have come running to save themselves from the dowry,
