Can the Homeowners Reduce the Rent?

(A few words from a homeowner on the housing question and the building movement.)
We give space to these remarks, wishing to acquaint our readers objectively with the situation of the house-owners.
(Editor's note.)
Lately the tenants' associations have been working very hard to have the government compel the homeowners to reduce rents. I would therefore like to have a little talk with the tenants.
Let us first see how far it is right, under our present order, to compel the homeowner to take as much rent as the tenant wants to give, i.e. that the homeowner should take the price the tenant wants, or the price the tenant can give. Imagine, dear tenant, that someone comes in to you and says he demands that you hand him the piece of goods for this or that price. "What do you mean, you demand? — you will answer — what are you, some kind of master over my goods?"
The customer will answer: first, because the goods cost you little, and second, because I can no longer pay more and I must have the goods, because I go about naked...
You will answer: "In the first place, how do you know that it cost me little? And in the second place, even if it did cost me little, that is my good fortune; and as for your not being able to pay more and going about naked — am I a charity institution, then?"
That is surely how you would answer the customer. And if the customer were insolent on top of that, you would surely take him by the collar and throw him out.
Why don't you now ask yourselves, dear tenants, whether it is right, under our present, non-Bolshevik order, to demand this of the homeowner? But if you like the Bolshevik order and want to follow that system, then do as in Russia: apply the system to all merchants and manufacturers — why only to the homeowner?
Now I will answer the tenants' complaints. The first complaint is that everything has become cheaper and rent has not.
You are mistaken, dear tenants: rent has also become cheaper, and not by a little, but by a full 42 per cent. Many tenants know this too, but they pretend not to know it: the złoty with which one pays now is worth 42 per cent less than it was worth in 1924, when the tenants' law came out. Then the dollar was 5 złoty and 18 groszy. For 5.18 zł. one could get a dollar, and today one must give 8.92 for a dollar — that means the złoty has fallen by 42 per cent, and rent has become cheaper by that much. Had the złoty not lost value, a tenant who has to pay 100 złoty a month would have had to give 19 dollars and 30 cents, and now he gives 11 dollars and 22 cents. When the tenants' law was made, it was calculated that one would now pay with the złoty at 5.18, not at 8.92.
Besides, all articles except rent were free; everyone could charge as much as he wanted. And therefore, when the złoty fell and times were not bad, all articles went up, but rent was limited by the tenants' law — one could not charge as much as one wanted. Hence there is now nothing to come down from.
Now let us look at the "fortunes" the homeowners make, that they are so decried and so envied.
A house that cost 100 thousand roubles or 50 thousand dollars before the war is now worth 40 per cent — that is, 20 thousand dollars. If the homeowner owed 60 per cent on the house before the war, as was mostly the case, and even if he paid nothing for those 60 per cent (which was not the case), the homeowner has still gained nothing on the pre-war debts, for by as much as the debts amounted to, the house is now cheaper (there were usually exceptions, who owed more than 60 per cent and who owed less than 60 per cent).
That means the 20 thousand dollars the house is now worth are the homeowner's property, on which he has a right to interest. It is the same when someone now buys the same house and pays 20 thousand dollars for it. A house that cost 100 thousand roubles or 50 thousand dollars before the war brought in 10 thousand roubles in rent before the war. Now it brings in 26,600 zł. Deducted from this: government tax 18 per cent, magistrate [municipality] — 7 per cent, together 25 per cent. Caretakers, gendarmes [?], removal money [?], some decent repairs — all this costs at least 20 per cent. Together 45 per cent. "There are homeowners who owe more on their houses than they are worth, and of those I will not speak; but 50 per cent of the value of the house is owed by 80 per cent of homeowners; that means that on the house that costs 20 thousand dollars, or barely 200 thousand zł., he owes 100 thousand zł. If we reckon the present cheap mortgage interest, it comes to 6 per cent with amortization. Altogether 51 per cent is deducted. What remains to the homeowner from rent for the 10 thousand dollars he has standing in the house and for his work as supervisor of his house is 13,034 zł., or 231.42 zł. a week.
If one adds to this that there are also tenants who do not pay, there seems to be nothing at all to envy the homeowners for. They are, it seems, not at all so fortunate that one may be ironic about them, calling them at every opportunity "the unfortunate homeowners".
I would also like to describe what the houses, and above all the whole housing question, would look like if the tenants succeeded in forcing the homeowners into a 30 per cent reduction of rent. I will only say that if the tenants' demand to take 30 per cent off the old houses is unjustified, the demand to take 40 per cent off the new houses is simply a crime against the workers, the craftsmen and against the tenants themselves — one may even say against the whole world, because there are still people who have stashed away a little money "in the sack". I myself know several such people who wanted to build houses. Workers and craftsmen would have had work, one would have taken in money for bricks, for iron. The trades would have revived and hundreds of people would have had a livelihood. And the main thing — dwellings would have been added! But they took fright at the fine agitation of the tenants to have 40 per cent of rent taken off them and to have them brought under the tenants' law, and they stuck the money back "into the sack".
Y. B.
The Jewish Artisan Must Wake Up

[Article — Jewish artisans in Poland; series, part 3.]

3.

In the previous articles we have already pointed out the causes of the decline of the Jewish artisan in Poland. The guild law, as well as in general the harsh policy of eradication towards the Jewish craftsman — on the one hand, and the so-called "providers" of the craftsmen, as well as the blindness and neglect of the mass of craftsmen itself — on the other hand, have contributed not a little to the present catastrophic situation of Jewish crafts in Poland.

The apathy of the Jewish artisan has already gone so far that the overwhelming majority of them ("rov minyan ve-rov binyan") think that this is how it must and should remain, and that it simply cannot be otherwise.

We stress, however, that even now, when the situation of the Jewish craftsman is almost hopeless, when the artisan is literally standing on the edge of the abyss — one must not sit with folded hands and await with resignation the supposedly unavoidable death throes. One must oppose with all one's strength the harsh verdict that has fallen upon the fate of Jewish craftsmanship.

With a strong and energetic campaign, and above all with a firm and purposeful will, a great deal can still be done for the Jewish artisan; but radical means are required to cure the Jewish craftsman of his disease of neglect and to pull him out of his fatal "hiner-plet" [?].

First of all, care must be taken of the general and vocational education of the Jewish artisan. There must be created (perhaps at the kehillas, because the craftsmen's organisations are not capable of it) professional trade schools, which should at least properly train the young Jewish craftsman, who will still have a hard time struggling with all the new strict industrial requirements and who, willy-nilly, will have to adapt himself to the harsh guild law.

At the same time care must also be taken of the older generation of craftsmen, for whom specially adapted vocational supplementary courses and special relaxations of the guild law are required.

But at the same time we must demand that the above-mentioned schools be granted equal rights with the state schools; one must fight for the government to maintain the Jewish trade schools on the same basis on which it maintains its Polish craftsmen's schools. Here one need not beg for favours; here one must demand the right that is due to the Jewish artisan as a citizen with equal rights. One must storm and move heaven and earth so that of the roughly 40 million zł. which the government allocates every year for the vocational training of artisans, the Jewish craftsmen should benefit in equal measure with the non-Jewish ones; so that from the special levy on the patents [trade licences] for maintaining vocational supplementary schools the Jewish schools should receive their proper share (not as until now, when they do not get a single grosz of it); and finally one must demand of the government that it itself create and maintain such schools for Jewish artisans.

Our sincere and conscious craftsmen's activists must once and for all shake themselves free of those who are ready to sell, for a seat ("benkl"), the bloody interests of the craftsmen's community. At the magistrates [municipal councils] and the kehillas they must, at every opportunity, describe the want that prevails among the Jewish artisans. It is not a matter of this or that individual; here the whole of Jewish craftsmanship in Poland is at stake, slipping out of Jewish hands and thereby declassing the most productive part of Jewish society.

Within the craftsmen's associations special discussion evenings and various educational lectures must be organised, which should make clear to the Jewish artisan the whole seriousness of the present moment.

The Jewish craftsmen's activists must once and for all put an end to the lazy "politics", when what is at stake is already the to be or not to be of Jewish craftsmanship in Poland.

The craftsmen's activists must now think very hard about the situation of the Jewish artisan, so that later the responsibility for the ruin of thousands and tens of thousands of Jewish livelihoods should not fall upon their conscience.

The Jewish artisan must with his own strength shake off the congealed chains of his lethargy, as long as it is not yet too late.

Nathan Rudner.

[Zagłębie — Purim; feuilleton.]
(A stroll through the Purim entertainments)
By S. Libaszon.

...If I had the chance, I would visit the grave of Haman the Wicked and express to him my warm thanks for the "good idea" that arose in his head — to destroy and to kill... I believe that the "miracle" of extermination has a far greater significance for us Jews than the miracle of Haman's downfall. On the contrary, tell me: were it not for Purim, how could we, even once a year, forget all our worries, troubles and headaches? How would we have the possibility of not brooding over the fate of the German Jews at the present moment?... That is why we all say again and again that "all the festivals will be abolished, only the day of Purim will remain"... And the more the troubles grow, the "harder" Purim is celebrated — Jews are a stiff-necked people...
...Polish Jews flee from Germany, boycott terror against the Jewish department stores and shops, new tax projects, want, hunger and
— Purim entertainments...
And I among them "abolished" the old and new Hamans, and on the night of the fourteenth I visited the so-called Purim balls in Zagłębie and, together with everyone,
— "drowned my troubles in drink"...
My first visit I had a fancy to make at the Będzin gymnasium. For months people had been talking about the great preparations for the ball. The exaggerations could arouse even in such an ordinary flesh-and-blood mortal as me a craving to enter the palace of the "upper ten thousand"...
Most of all I wanted to see the "white bears" which — as people said — had been brought from the Eastern lands... Unfortunately I did not manage it, and, dressed up in "vinegar and honey", I had to leave the "House of Lords", because they demanded of me the
— "invitation" [zaproszenie]...
Neither my pedigree letters nor the merit of my forefathers helped, nor even a few identity cards of the "seventh power" [the press].
— "Bez zaproszeń wstęp wzbroniony" [No entry without invitation]... and having no choice I was forced to "wander" after midnight to Sosnowiec...
And I did not regret it.
In Sosnowiec I was quite a sought-after guest. Already at the railway station I was surrounded by elegantly dressed-up couples, and each one of them begged:
— "Come to us, with us you'll have a good time, with us"...
At that moment I thought they must surely be touts, and that they did not recognise me and took me for a Ślązak [a Silesian]; later, however, it became clear to me that the couples were all of "one garment", only the lining was different...
— Mrs. "WIZO" with her daughter "Re-WIZO"... are conducting a "competition" between themselves like the stones of our father Jacob. A Purim ball at "WIZO" and at "Re-WIZO", and each one cries
— Upon me shall he lay his head...
My senses began to work hard:
— Where does one go first? Where shall I drink the first cup and where shall I say the blessing over the eating of matzah?...
And after lengthy deliberation I decided to make the start with the young "WIZO", called "Re-WIZO", since I must after all help build the Jewish state... That, after all, is the be-all and end-all for "Re-WIZO"...
On entering the hall I first of all sought out my friends, the Revisionist activists, and with them carried out a "revision" of the hall. After a long search we established that at this "national" ball
— "there is not a single Jewish letter to be found, and a Silesian orchestra is playing"...
After the first cup we recited the second "kol ḥamira" (after burning the ḥametz...) and off we went to the Purim ball at "WIZO".
* * *
The ball was supposed to take place in the new hall "Atlantic", but owing to "certain reasons" the permit was not given at the last minute, and the ball took place in the hall of the "Kupcy" [the merchants] on Kowalska [Street].
On the way to "WIZO" a black cat ran past me, which put me and my friend in a far from cheerful mood. Later it turned out that the black cat had been an omen [?] that at the "WIZO" ball too there is among the orchestra
— a Ślązak..
At the ball the same miracle occurred of "they stood crowded yet bowed down with ample room" — the hall unsuitable [?], and yet
— roomy...
And since "when the rebbe dances, all the little Hasidim dance", people danced in the corridor, in the side rooms, as long as they danced. After all, one cannot sit with "folded hands" when the orchestra strikes up a "new" hit — or a "Jewish hopke" that could "move" even a stone...
Half the crowd we found already in the foyer, as before eating the afikoman, worn out, tired and filled up with water. (That is why there really was a shortage of water..)
The "seventh power" had a bit of "influence" at the ball: the husband of the Madam President [prezesowa] consented to speak Yiddish in public, and the Madam President herself wished:
— Next year in Jerusalem...
— If only, sweet father, at the Purim balls over there they would not play "szlagwekes" [?] and one would also hear a Yiddish word...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tisa)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tisa
The Portion
—o—
a) "Tablets written on both their sides" (Ex. 32:15)
1.
The Gemara says (Shabbat 104) that the mem and the samekh among the letters of the Tablets had to hang by a miracle, because the letters were engraved right through, visible on both sides. What did this symbolise?
The Midrash (portion Re'eh) says: the bread and the rod came down together from heaven. Likewise the book and the sword. If you throw away the book, the sword gains dominion, and then, instead of bread, comes — the rod.
Therefore the mem and the samekh had to be readable from both sides: either s-efer (book) or s-ayif (sword); m-akhal (bread) or m-akel (rod). The mem and the samekh can thus be interpreted two ways... Bnei Shmuel.
2.
"The two tablets of the testimony".
[In Aramaic:] "The Ten Commandments — five were on the one tablet, and set against them were 'your heads, your tribes'...; and on the second tablet were set against them the five last ranks, which are: 'your little ones, your wives and your stranger'... ranks."
The first five commandments, on the first tablet, contain the commandments between man and God ("I am", "Thou shalt have no other..."); the other five, on the second tablet — the commandments between man and his fellow ("Thou shalt not murder", "Thou shalt not steal").
And indeed it is divided just so: the "heads", the "elders", the "notables" — they keep only to the first tablet, to the commandments towards God; whereas the commandments concerning people they leave to the hewers of wood and drawers of water: not to steal, not to murder — that is a business for the rabble... Imrei Hen.
—o—
b) "And he cast the tablets out of his hands" (ibid., 19)
"When the Holy One, blessed be He, gave Moses the Tablets, they carried themselves; once he descended and approached the camp and saw the calf, the writing flew off them and they became heavy in Moses' hands." Tanhuma.
The Tablets "carried themselves" — they bore their own weight; but as soon as Moses came with them to the worshippers of the calf, their inwardness went out of them and they grew heavy...
A commandment performed with inwardness is light, for it has a living spirit in it. But one performed without inwardness is heavy and burdensome; and so it goes [?]: when one draws near to the servants of the golden calf, the inwardness vanishes... Yalkut Peninim.
—o—
c) "And they looked after Moses until he was gone into the tent" (33:8)
All the time they kept looking after Moses: they searched out every sin in him and gossiped about all his deeds; but — "until he was gone into the tent": about what he does in the Tent of the Divine Presence, about that they did not want to say anything at all... Evil things were invented, and the good they did not want to see. That is how the people already treats its leaders. Yalkut ha-Drush.
—o—
d) "And behold, it is a stiff-necked people" (32:9)
Every day we say the blessing "Who girds Israel with might". Is that not a blessing in vain? Where is our might?
But what is meant is our stiff-neckedness: letting all kinds of currents sweep over our neck and still not bowing our head. "Israel is the most obstinate of the nations." Or ha-Tsvi.
* * *
"Unless Thy law had been my delight, I should then have perished in mine affliction."
The Gemara says (Beitzah 25) that the main reason the Torah was given to the Jews was to break their insolence. Poverty, too, is a remedy against insolence ("The poor useth entreaties, but the rich answereth roughly"). And to break Jewish insolence there is either Torah or poverty... Shevet mi-Yisrael.
* * *
"In heaven above and the earth beneath".
"In heaven above" — in heavenly matters one must lift up one's head, a holy boldness; "and the earth beneath" — in earthly matters one must bow one's head. But — "they are a perverse generation": they twist the verse; in spiritual matters they bow their head, and in earthly ones they lift it... Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
—o—
e) "And abundant in goodness and truth" (34:6)
Once there came to Rabbi Meirl of Przemyślany a rabbi dressed like a tsaddik, but a great ignoramus. Said Rabbi Meirl to him:
Among the attributes of mercy "and truth" is also counted. One may ask: truth is, after all, strict justice and not mercy!
But when a rabbi like you disguises himself as a tsaddik, God ought to repay you [?] measure for measure, according to strict justice, and be exacting with you as with tsaddikim, to a hair's breadth... It is, however, one of the attributes of mercy that with such as you He deals "and truth" — according to the truth of what you really are... Margenita de-Rabbi Meir.
—o—
f) "When thou goest up to appear" (ibid., 24)
The Gemara (Pesahim 8) expounds on this verse that the pilgrimage to Jerusalem must be "for its own sake", not for the sake of material enjoyment...
Radio Bulletin

[Radio.]
Far from the eye — near to the heart
A rare radio celebration.
145,000 letters from all over the world.
These days it is five years since "Papa Stefan" of Katowice began sending out over the radio waves his letter-box, which has won fame all over the world.
As proof of how great the popularity of this likeable and talented speaker is, one may cite the fact that "Papa Stefan" has already received 145,000 letters from abroad, often from the most distant and remote corners of the world.
Thanks to his letter-box, special clubs of friends of "Papa Stefan" have sprung up in Germany, France, Belgium, America and even in Australia. Thanks to his kind, warm-hearted, humane words, Professor Titieniecki [?] (the real name of "Papa Stefan") has won tens of thousands of friends in all parts of the world, who feel themselves one big family of Katowice radio listeners. Across the borders of countries, peoples, races and classes the voice of a friend of humanity, calling for peace and brotherly relations, has carried over the radio waves.
It appears that his appeal has struck the hearts of millions of people, for wherever "Papa Stefan" now shows himself he is received with enthusiasm. His tour through Austria, Italy, France, Belgium and Holland, where he has just been, simply turned into a triumphal procession. In the city of Lyon, for example, the mayor, former Premier Herriot, gave a festive banquet for him. It turned out that Herriot is one of his most faithful followers and does not miss a single radio letter-box of "Papa Stefan".
For the fifth anniversary of the Katowice letter-box a special programme was broadcast with the participation of several foreign members of the Katowice radio family, who came to Katowice especially for this celebration.
In June of this year the first world congress of the "Katowiceans" will take place. 150 delegates from all corners of the world have already registered, among them several Japanese and Malays [?]. This congress will be the expression of a peaceful demonstration for the brotherly and friendly relations that bind the "Katowiceans".
The slogan of the "Katowiceans", "Far from the eye — near to the heart", is now no longer an empty sound but a fact of first-class importance for the development of a spirit of peace among nations.
A radio set — the latest technical wonder.
The brilliant inventor of radio, the Marchese Marconi, has now completed a radio set that represents the last word in technology.
This set receives all wavelengths, starting from the ultra-short and ending with the long waves.
The set looks like a handsome cabinet in Louis XV style. The cabinet also contains a loudspeaker that gives out the purest tones. In the lowest part of the cabinet there is an armchair that can be pulled out. The height of the set is 6 feet, the width about 4 feet. The wooden parts of the set are made of the most expensive wood.
Such a wonderful set, however, only a few individuals can afford. This "pleasure" costs a trifle — 4 thousand dollars in all. The first set that Marconi completed he presented to the Pope.

Help, the Husband's Coming!

Who betrayed whom?...
With a pounding heart Zina ran up the stairs; a door on the second floor opened without a sound and Filip appeared on the threshold.
Zina was a little flustered and as if frightened by her own daring.
"I'm late, Filip, aren't I?" she asked. "You must surely have thought I wouldn't come... But my husband, as if out of spite, simply would not leave the house... He was so nervous today, so agitated... For a moment I even thought he suspected something..."
"But now you are here with me," Filip said. "My heart is overflowing with love... and that alone is all that matters to me now..."
"Well, good," said Zina with sincere frankness. "For me, Filip, happiness came on the day I met you..."
"How cosy [?] it is here at your place!" she sighed [?]. "Do you know, Filip, what I'm thinking now?... I ought to have come to you long ago... I remember very well the day it became clear to me that I was in love... For a long time I hesitated to say 'yes' to you... But now I am yours... I am happy, Filip, that I came to you today..."
She got up, took a few steps across the room, went to the window and mechanically drew aside the curtain, reflecting that soon she would no longer be here. Suddenly she cried out in terror:
"Filip! Look... there... in the street... my husband!... He is pacing up and down... He looks so angry... Filip, we are lost!"
She stepped back from the window, pale, trembling all over.
"I told you before," she went on in a broken voice, "that today he didn't look at all as usual... He must have suspected something... What shall we do now? What a terrible scandal!? It was foolish of me to come to you, and how ungentlemanly it was of you to lure me here..."
Filip himself was also shaken, yet he did his best to calm the frightened Zina.
"What do we do now?" Zina no longer spoke [?] but groaned with fear. "He must have a revolver on him... He will shoot me."
"Calm down!" Filip muttered helplessly. "Calm down, you know very well I won't let anyone harm you. I'll strangle him on the spot before he touches you."
"But what is he still waiting for? It's terrible, terrible... Perhaps he is waiting for the police? They will come up here, knock on the door... I won't survive the shame..."
Filip paced about the room like a tiger in a cage. The danger was terrible and inescapable... Would it really come to bloodshed? Married men are so wild in their jealousy... And his flat had no more than one exit to the street.
Zina's husband was still walking about, distraught [?], on the other side of the street; one could see from his face that he was burning with jealousy, his eyes flashed with anger.
All at once Filip, standing at the window, let out a cry of surprise, then burst out laughing, and in a wild outburst of joy he began jumping on the spot and clapping his hands... Zina jumped up, frightened to death [?]. Had he lost his mind? She ran to the window. Her husband was still down in the street, but this time no longer alone: a young, pretty woman was standing facing him. He held her hand in both of his, his face was now all smiles, beaming with contentment. From his expression one could tell he was gently scolding the woman for having kept him waiting a little too long. He took her by the arm, and the couple set off with the special cheerful, floating gait of two lovers... Soon they had vanished from Zina's sight.
"Why, it had nothing at all to do with us!" Filip cried merrily. "Your dear husband was simply waiting here for his sweetheart... Comic chance would have it that he arranged to meet her right under my window... How do you like that?... And we got scared like silly children..."
But Zina did not share Filip's joy that the danger had passed; she was utterly shaken with rage, her face was aflame, her eyes burned with green jealousy.
"To deceive me like that!" she cried, apparently forgetting entirely that she herself was just as guilty... "What a low person he is."
The swift change from fear to anger that Filip saw in his sweetheart bewildered him completely. Zina now stood there a stranger; she was no longer a lover. She was no longer a woman deceiving her husband and trembling before his terrible jealousy... She herself was now the jealous wife who had discovered by chance that her husband was deceiving her with another. Her womanly pride was gravely wounded; a great baseness had been committed against her — how he had lit up, the low creature, when his sweetheart arrived!.. how glad he had been to see her!... and how intimately he had taken her arm and gone off with her!... Surely they were by now alone within four walls, in private... At this thought she ran short of breath; she clutched at her heart and sat down on the soft sofa next to Filip.
"To deceive me like that!!" she repeated again and again.
She pressed herself against Filip, nestled [?] into him completely, seeking in his closeness comfort for her grievous insult, and added:
"And all this before my very eyes!... Under our window..."
Y. Perlman.
What Did the Leipzig Fair Look Like?

[Germany — economy; Leipzig Fair.]
From our special correspondent Z. Haber.
For the 1669th time the great fair in Leipzig has now been opened, which today is without any doubt the largest fair in the whole world. — Six thousand three hundred exhibitors from twenty different countries all over the world have brought their goods here to show, covering all kinds of branches from the whole world. Some eighty thousand people are expected to come to Leipzig, in order to see what is now being exhibited and what they can buy for their enterprises.
The present fair was opened at a very difficult time, on the day of the German elections, and one must admit[?] that the Leipzig fair management for some time carried around the idea of postponing the fair to another date; but since a very large part of the buyers from the distant countries were already on their way, and since most of the exhibitors had already made all their preparations, it was not possible to postpone the fair to another day, and the fair had to be opened on election day itself.
Nevertheless, election day frightened no one who had truly been carrying the thought of coming here. The trains ran quite normally and arrived at the appointed minute. The special trains that came to the Leipzig fair from England, Holland, Switzerland, Czechoslovakia and Austria were full of passengers and brought more fair guests from those countries than a year ago; true, such a large part of the fair guests from Poland, Romania, the Baltic states and also from Austria arrived only on Monday and Tuesday, after the elections...
But even on election day it was calm and quiet. In every fair building there was a polling station for those German voters who had been unable to cast their votes at home.
In the streets one saw the usual calm picture as at every fair; apart from fair badges nothing at all was noticeable, and the fair buildings were full of people who for the time being were looking around to see what was new.
Prices have fallen again. It is literally half for nothing; it really hurts one's heart that one does not have those few marks to buy such beautiful and cheap things.
"Never, and in no place in the whole world, has one been able to buy as cheaply as now at the Leipzig fair," says to me the greatest German economic expert, the general director Dr. Köhler, of the Leipzig Fair Office.
At the same time he reminds me that the Leipzig fair has more than once gone through all kinds of crises, and for the 1669th time it is now being opened full of hope that the present crisis, too, will soon come to an end.
In 1914, about three weeks before the fair was opened, the World War broke out, but the fair was opened and good business was done. — In 1920, when the first technical fair was opened on the new site in Leipzig, all the ministers, diplomats and other distinguished guests gathered there had to walk the long way back on foot, because on that very day the Kapp Putsch broke out, and not only[?] the trams but also all the automobiles stopped.
In that same year, while the fair in Leipzig was being opened, the French occupied Frankfurt, and during the second Leipzig fair the English occupied the entire Ruhr region with its mighty industrial centres.
Nevertheless the Leipzig fair overcame all difficulties, and it also reckons that very soon it will overcome the present crisis too, with all its attendant phenomena.
It is also interesting to take a look at who has actually come to exhibit at the Leipzig fair now, because it gives a picture of those countries and those branches that still have something to show in their present hard economic struggle, which they are going through in every country.

A King Who Fled His Throne in the Middle of the Night (5)

[Serialized historical tale — France, King Henri III and the Duke of Guise; installment 5.]
(Historical story)
By El—Be.

After the death of the Duke of Alençon, King Henri III, who was childless like all his brothers, faced the question: who would inherit the throne of the Valois dynasty? And as the only suitable heir to the throne he settled on his brother-in-law, Henri of Navarre.

When the Catholic League heard that Henri of Navarre, the king's brother-in-law, was the candidate for heir, it became extremely indignant. How could it be? Henri of Navarre, the enemy of the Catholics, the damned Huguenot, should become heir to the French throne?

And once again the Catholics resolved to begin a fresh struggle, a war of extermination against the Huguenots, to use all their forces to bar the way to the throne for Henri of Navarre and to open the way for Henri of Guise, the friend of the Catholics.

Philip II of Spain entered into a formal agreement on this with Henri of Guise. The Pope gave his blessing to the holy war against the heretics, against the Protestants; the priests received the appropriate instructions, and a terrible incitement against the Protestants began. Before the benighted masses they displayed frightful pictures of what the Catholics would suffer if a heretic like Henri of Navarre, the king's brother-in-law, came to power in France.

This was already open revolt, and Henri III decided to take steps that would thwart the plans of the Duke of Guise.

Henri sent a written order to Henri of Guise and warned him not to dare to enter Paris. Since the king had no money to send the order by courier, he sent it by post. But the Duke of Guise declared that he had not received the order, and to spite the king he did come to Paris, backed by the Spanish king Philip [printed "Pilim"].

The Duke of Guise insolently entered the palace, without even a guard. He had first presented himself to Catherine de' Medici, and she then led him in to her son, the king.

When Henri saw the Duke of Guise before him, he was filled with rage and cried out to him:

— "But I sent you an order that you should not come."

To this the Duke of Guise [printed "Gin"] replied:

— I have not come here for the purpose of taking your throne from you; I have come to clear myself before you of the slanders that my enemies have invented about me.

Good friends of the king had long advised him to remove the Duke of Guise from his path. One of the friends had even declared himself ready to do it, but Catherine did not allow it, and now too she interceded for the Duke of Guise.

The king, seeing the situation that had arisen around the French throne and not being sure of his army, summoned to Paris hired soldiers from Switzerland and also part of the French Guard, on whom he relied to defend him in time of danger, trusting that he could depend on them.

In Paris civil war broke out. The townspeople of Paris were on the side of the Duke of Guise and rebelled against the king. Barricades were set up in the streets, and chains were stretched across the streets of Paris.

The king fortified himself — or, more correctly, he was besieged — in his palace, and the duke fortified himself in his palace.

Two days passed like this; each side waited for the other to attack. But the mob had no patience to wait and already wanted to storm the king's palace and slaughter the hired Swiss soldiers, the king's protectors.

The duke, with the city mob behind him, could easily have deposed the king; but he did not want that, he did not want to go that far. Coming out of his palace dressed in a white caftan with a little stick in his hand, he calmed the enraged mob as if by magic.

Having thus saved the Swiss soldiers, the duke sent them back to the king with curses and insults. Then the king went out into the street, where he stood for several hours and spoke to the crowd.

Suddenly he saw a great crowd carrying Catherine de' Medici in a sedan chair ["throne-carriage"]. He went up to her, and she began to negotiate with him about a peace. But while the two were talking, the duke [so printed; historically it was the king] stole out of the palace and fled to Blois [printed "Bula"], threatening Paris from there with an attack [printed "shtake", apparently a misprint for "atake"].

in that moustache
lies the chief feature
of the famous
Hitlerite.

He has a weakness
for ruling,
for driving people
with the whip;
he wants to translate
the Mussolini
misfortune
into German.

He often dreams
of Napoleons,
takes on their stance
and pose;
in the black
chorus of crows
he wants to become
Germany's greatest cock.

He wants to play
a shako role,
to become mighty,
great and strong;
he wants to rule
the "ghetto" people
and to sit
on its neck.

Drunk with power
is the hero now,
and intoxicated
with his success;
he wants to exchange
Goethe's poetry
for a Hitlerite
fist.

It galls him
that Chancellor Bismarck
is popular
in Germany;
everyone asks
the waiters:
"A Bismarck herring —
bring it here!"

Let us hope
that his dream
will come true
soon;
and Hitler herrings
will become
the rulers
of the kitchen...
A. L. Wolfson.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Rich Christian Woman Recommends a Cantor for the Będzin Jewish Kehilla

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla, cantorate.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 19 Adar 5693 — piątek 17 marca 1933 [Friday, 17 March 1933].)
Będzin
A rich Christian woman recommends a cantor for the Będzin Jewish kehilla.
These days Mr. A. Trapojer[?] received a letter from Warsaw from Mrs. Ciechanowska, who asks him, as a representative of the kehilla, to make efforts so that the candidate she proposes be accepted as cantor of Będzin.
The content of the letter is as follows[?]:
Honoured Mr. Trapojer!
"I recommend Mr. Osman[?] with the request that he be engaged as cantor in the Będzin synagogue, for which, as I have heard, a cantor with a beautiful voice and an honest man is being sought.
I know Mr. Osman and his wife and can assure you that the Jewish community in Będzin will be satisfied with my recommendation, especially when the candidate is recommended by me, the mother of the Polish consul in Washington, who distinguishes himself by his patronage on behalf of the Jews.
Mr. Osman, whom I recommend, is a religious, honest, solid and hard-working man; he is a good person, a good husband, a good father, a right-thinking Jew, a famous singer, possesses a strong and beautiful voice, and I shall be pleased if Mr. Trapojer will give him his patronage."
Respectfully,
Maria Ciechanowska.
The Household Goods of a Jewish Shopkeeper Sold for 15 Zł.

[Będzin — Taxes, distraint.]
On Tuesday a bailiff (egzekutor) of the tax office took from the family P. on Modrzejowska Street their few household goods: a table, 5 chairs, a clock and a mirror. The items were sold at a public auction (licytacja) at the market halls for 15 zł.
"Because of the Crisis He Cannot Marry Without a Dowry"

[Czeladź — Court, fraud.]
Mr. P. Honigsztajn of Czeladź signed an engagement contract (tenaim) with Miss Birenholc, the daughter of a local tinsmith (blacharz).
After the engagement the groom "got wiser"[?] and demanded a dowry, with the excuse that he needed to take up a position against a deposit (kaucja).
The bride's father gave the groom 380 zł., and preparations for the wedding began. But a few days before the wedding the groom announced that because of… perhaps the wedding would have to be postponed.
This week the groom stood before the court. He was charged with committing a fraud and was sentenced to 2 months' arrest.
The convicted man lodged an appeal, arguing that because of the crisis he could not marry without a dowry.
A Plot Bought for a Cemetery

[Będzin — Kehilla, cemetery.]
On Wednesday the kehilla board bought a plot of 150 pręty (square rods) for a cemetery.
The new plot is located next to the present cemetery.
A Large Sum of Smuggled Goods Confiscated

[Będzin — Police, smuggling.]
The local police received word from Upper Silesia that a car carrying smuggled goods was travelling in the direction of Groytse (Grodziec?).
The police went out to the indicated road, and when the car approached, the police ordered the driver to stop.
The driver, who is deaf, not hearing the call of the police, drove on. The police then fired after him, and one bullet punctured the rubber tyre of the wheel, because of which the car came to a stop.
In the car a large quantity of rubber goods and lighters (zapalniczki) was found, worth several tens of thousands of zł.
Railway Discounts for School Youth

[General — Railways, education.]
According to a certificate from the school authority[?], from 1 April onward 50-per-cent discounts will be issued on the railways in every direction for an unlimited number of journeys.
The schools may issue these certificates the whole year round, not only in the holiday period. For collective excursions the 75-per-cent railway discount will continue to apply, with the difference that instead of the required minimum of 10 travellers, only 8 will now suffice.
General Meeting of "HaShachar" in Będzin

[Będzin — Societies, youth.]
On Saturday the general meeting of the Będzin "HaShachar" took place in its own premises. The meeting was opened by Mr. Rafael Liwer, who gave a review of the activity to date. Mr. Manele was invited to chair.
After the reports of Feivel Skórnicki, Rafael Liwer and Mordechai Herszlikowicz, the following board was elected: Rafael Liwer, Mordechai Herszlikowicz, Feivel Skórnicki, Alter Szojmer, Blima Grünbaum, Zelig Manele and Moshe Fryderyk.
General Meeting of the Jewish Charity Society

[Będzin — Charity, societies.]
This coming Sunday, the 19th of this month, a general meeting of the members of the local charity society will take place in the premises of the "Merchants' Association".
On the agenda are a number of important items, and whoever is concerned about the further existence of this important institution should come to the meeting.
Suicide of a Jewish coal dealer
[Będzin — incidents.] The Jewish coal dealer S. poisoned himself with "hydrochloric acid" [?]. The suicide was taken [?] to hospital.
This Saturday — a ball of the Charitable Society

[Będzin — charity.] The board of the Charitable Society is holding a ball this Saturday night, at the close of the Sabbath, at the "Bryzhi" [?] hall. Given the important purpose, it is to be hoped that the event will be a success.
—o—
For the orphanage in Będzin
[Będzin — charity.] In honour of Purim the following donated: Mrs. Anna Patak [?] (Katowice) 20 zł., 2 kilos of butter, confectionery and 1 bottle of oil; Mrs. Ts. Szajn 15 zł.; Mrs. Dr. Weinzieher 10 zł.; Mrs. Gutsze Gutman 10 zł.; Mrs. S. Weinstock 10 zł. Mr. and Mrs. J. Szajn — a radio with all accessories.
—o—
Last deadline to pay taxes
[Będzin — taxes.] Tuesday was the last deadline for paying into the magistrate's cash office, without interest, the first instalment of the local tax for 1933 and the fourth instalment of the tax on real estate for 1932.
There is still a grace period of 14 days. But during that time the tax office can already send out an "upomnienie" (reminder notice).
Sosnowiec — Amateur performances will be exempted from tax

[Sosnowiec — municipality and taxes.] From the session of the Council of Commissioners in Sosnowiec.
At the last session of the Council of Commissioners in Sosnowiec a series of tax statutes for the year 1933/34 were discussed.
Over the tax statutes on entertainments, performances and the levy on goods brought in by rail a lively discussion developed. According to the latest ordinance of the Ministry of the Interior, all events put on by amateurs will be free of the tax (podatek) in the year 1933/34.
The tax on cinema films has been [?] reduced and will amount to only 35 percent (previously 60); on artistic films 25 percent (previously 30); on educational films, as until now, 10 percent.
The tax system on goods brought in by rail was confirmed at the same level as last year...
The tax on hotels and flats was confirmed with the following change: a flat of up to 3 rooms with a kitchen will be exempt from the dwelling tax.
Bicycle users who prove that they ride to work will be free of the tax.
Dozór member Mr. Saks protests against a decision of the kehilla board

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] A few weeks ago the kehilla board adopted a decision to set up a "Chesed shel Emes" (community burial society) and for that purpose to engage several officials.
Against this decision the board member Mr. Saks has turned with a protest to the starosta (district head).
The protest states: 1) that the proper quorum was not present at the session; 2) the board members were not notified about the session in advance; and 3) that in the new budget no salary has been provided for the new kehilla officials who are to carry out the functions of the "Chesed shel Emes".
Suicide of a mentally ill Jewish merchant — throws himself under the train and is killed on the spot

[Myszków — incidents.] In Myszków the local merchant S. Danziger threw himself under the train and was killed on the spot.
The suicide, a mentally ill man, had already several times wanted to put an end to his life, but each time he was rescued.
— Another victim of the crisis...
Loan-seekers are multiplying, but there is no money...

[Sosnowiec — free-loan fund.] How far the crisis has reached among Jewish merchants and traders is shown by the following fact.
At the last board session of the local Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund, 92 applications were considered from merchants asking for loans of several hundred zł.
Because of the large number, the board was compelled to reduce the loan amounts so that everyone could receive a loan.
Ze'ev Jabotinsky in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; Revisionists.] Next Thursday, 23 March, a major lecture will take place at the "Palace" by the president of the World Union of Revisionist Zionists, Ze'ev Jabotinsky, on the topic "The struggle for the Jewish state".
As could be foreseen, the lecture has aroused strong interest in connection with the forthcoming elections to the 18th Zionist Congress, since, as is known, Jabotinsky is an ardent supporter of an independent Revisionist movement.
The master of the spoken word will set out in his Thursday lecture his position on all the current Zionist problems that stand on the agenda today.
The lecture is the only one in Zagłębie. From Sosnowiec Jabotinsky travels on to Warsaw.
Italian strike at the "Klimontów" coal mine

[Sosnowiec — labour.] In connection with the news that the "Klimontów" coal mine is to be flooded, an Italian (sit-down) strike has broken out at the mine.
The workers declare that they will not leave the mine until the management assures them that the mine will not be flooded.
80,000 zł. for Building Purposes in Sosnowiec

The Sosnowiec magistrate [municipal council] has received notice that, out of the sum the government has earmarked for building purposes, Sosnowiec will receive 80 thousand zł.
The sum will be given on credit, for building small houses of 3 rooms with a kitchen.
An Excursion Train to Wieliczka

Next Sunday an excursion train leaves Katowice for Wieliczka. Departure from Katowice 7 a.m., return — the same day at 10 p.m.
In Kraków the train will stop until 1 p.m., so that one can visit the Folk Museum, the castle on the Wawel, etc. At 1 o'clock the train will leave for Wieliczka, where the excursionists will visit the salt mines. A ticket costs 7 zł.
Tickets can be obtained at the travel bureau "Orbis" in Katowice and also at the Katowice railway station.
—o—
Fell from a Cart and Was Mortally Injured
At Czechowski's factory in Sosnowiec the carter Mendel Ładny fell from the cart onto the pavement. Ładny was mortally injured and was taken in a grave condition to the Jewish hospital.
—o—
Academy in Honour of Marshal Piłsudski's Name Day
On Sunday, the day of Piłsudski's name day, a festive academy [ceremony] will take place at the Jewish gymnasium.
—o—
The Kielce [printed "Selcer"] Voivode in Zagłębie
These days the Kielce voivode stayed in Zagłębie and held several conferences on current matters.

Found Death at Work
At the coal mine of the Sosnowiec Company a worker was seriously injured by a coal tub. On the way to the hospital the worker died.

President Madeyski — Director of the Labour Fund
The president [mayor] of Dąbrowa, Deputy Dr. Madeyski, is to be appointed director of the Labour Fund. The office of president is to be taken over by Director Kaczkowski, chairman of the B.B. and councillor of Dąbrowa.

Craftsmen Who Sell Their Products at the Market Are Exempt from Patents
The tax offices have received an order to apply in practice the decision of the Supreme Tribunal, according to which all craft workshops that are exempt from buying an industrial patent [licence] may also sell their products at the markets and on market days without a patent. Until now they had to hold 4th-category patents.
The order applies to all craft trades.

The chairman of the local kehilla has tendered his resignation. The board rejected the resignation.

The board of the local "Dobroczynność" [charity society] is holding its traditional Purim ball tonight, on Saturday night [motzei Shabbat].

In the note concerning the fact that the rabbi's attention had been drawn to the informing [mesirot] of one Jew against another, an error crept in. It was not the head of the "Opieka Społeczna" [social welfare office] who drew attention to it, but the inspector.

If One Won't Pay 400 zł. for Performing the Wedding Ceremony, One Is Threatened with Arrest

(A letter to the editor).
This week a scandalous incident took place which must not be kept silent from the public.
On Tuesday the wedding of my brother-in-law Abraham Gleitzer of Niwka took place. On the day of the wedding the bride's in-law, Mr. Gleitzer, went to Rabbi Englard to pay the "RaHaSh" fees [rabbi, cantor and beadle] and at the same time to invite him to perform the wedding ceremony and betrothal (chupah ve-kiddushin).
Rabbi Englard, on hearing this, demanded that my brother-in-law pay him no less than 400 zł. Not having the means to pay such a legendary sum, my brother-in-law went to Rabbi Schwarz, who, taking 40 zł., declared that he permits anyone to perform the kiddushin.
And the kiddushin was indeed performed by the guest R' Yitzchak Hirsch Manczyk of Będzin. The next morning Rabbi Englard's son came to Mr. Manczyk and threatened him in his father's name that "if the 400 zł. are not settled immediately, Manczyk will be handed over to the public prosecutor".
With the same threat Rabbi Englard's son came in the evening to the Krymiłów (Kromołów) Hasidic shtibl, which provoked [indignation — word missing in print] among the worshippers.
I thank you, Mr. Editor, for granting space to the following fact, which proves well enough how far lawlessness on the Jewish street has gone.
Respectfully, Eli Dawid Balimowski.
—o—
7-Year-Old Boy Killed by a Car.
On Staszica Street in Sosnowiec, as 7-year-old Stachecki wanted to run across the street, he fell under a bus, which killed the boy on the spot.
From the World of Sport.

"Hakoah" — "Maccabi" 4:3
Once again "Maccabi" won a great victory over its strong rival "Hakoah". This victory proved that the title of Champion of Zagłębie, which the "Hakoah" players had claimed for themselves, does not belong to them.
The "Maccabi" players earned the match fairly and showed themselves to be the better team. The points [goals] for "Maccabi" were won by Nowarski, Brandes, Pukiet, Ekstein. For "Hakoah" the points were won by Rubinlicht, Strochlitz, Urbach. Rubinlicht stood out most with his ambitious play.

"Azef".

This Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a parents' performance with a rich programme of attractions will be held at Public School No. 4 in Będzin. The Hakoah orchestra takes part.
The proceeds go to the feeding campaign for the school's poor children.

On Wednesday the trial began at the Sosnowiec District Court against a gang that manufactured 20-złoty banknotes.
On the motion of the defence counsel that several doctors be summoned as experts, the trial was postponed.

[P. 8, middle column of the ads block; original in Polish]
The L.O.P.P. [Anti-Aircraft and Anti-Gas Defence League] in Będzin.
God guards those who guard themselves; for unpreparedness for danger always brings disaster. To have a clear conscience one must always strictly fulfil one's duties, and not only towards oneself but also towards the State. Therefore, among other things, anti-aircraft and anti-gas defence should lie close to everyone's heart, so as not to be exposed to the consequences of war should it come. Anti-aircraft and anti-gas defence does not propagate war. Now, when on the lips of almost every mortal one sees an ironic grimace, and on his face resignation, one should not be an optimist in this matter. After all, one hears how our neighbours are preparing for defence, what means they already possess, and newly built gas shelters are ceremonially put into use. Abroad there are ever more shops selling anti-gas equipment alone. Our society does not appreciate the importance of the tasks that the L.O.P.P. has, and therefore the future may take its revenge. Above all the population itself, and especially the population living in industrial centres, should flock to the ranks of the L.O.P.P. and try to get trained at the courses which the L.O.P.P. organises. Zagłębie Jews protest against the Hitlerite murders

Open-air meetings — sharp boycott resolutions. Sosnowiec Jews demonstrate. — Down with Hitler! — Long live Poland!
The call of the united committee, which was formed in the kehilla hall on Sunday evening,
In Będzin
to protest against the Hitlerite hooliganism, found a resounding echo among the Jewish population of Będzin. Already at 4 o'clock in the afternoon great masses of Jews began streaming toward Kościuszki Street, to the sports ground of „Hakoach“, where an open-air meeting took place with the participation of about 2000 persons.
All Jewish shops (except a part of those known as „practical merchants“) were closed at 5 o'clock.
The first to speak is the director of Fürstenberg's gymnasium, Dr. Einhorn, who says that the Jewish star in Germany has been clouded over by the Hitler people, who have turned into bandits and barbarians. In tsarist times — says the speaker — the pogroms were made by the benighted mob; today we see that the German people, those who created so rich a culture, commit the same deeds as the inquisitors of old, but — the speaker cries out — Am Yisrael Chai!
The second speaker, Dr. Weinzieher, gives a survey of the sufferings and torments since the time when the Jewish people lost its independence, its land; but what is happening in Germany surpasses human imagination. The people that enriched German culture, that brought forth from itself the greatest men of science, is being tortured and murdered by the Hitlerite barbarian gang. Dr. Weinzieher appeals to boycott German products and to use domestic goods.
A strong Jewish speech is given by Mr. A. Liwer, who describes the great sufferings and troubles of the Jews living in Germany. Mr. Liwer's speech leaves a strong impression; many people wept.
Mr. Wygodzki quotes verses from the Bible and gives a survey of Jewish „terminology“[?] in comparison with the harsh tortures[?] inflicted by the Hitler gang on German Jewry.
After the adoption of an appropriate resolution, a street procession is formed into the synagogue.
The procession, in which several thousand persons took part with the rabbis[?] at its head, marched from Kościuszki via Małachowskiego, Kołłątaja and the Old Market to the synagogue. [—] the banners[?] with anti-Hitler slogans; cries were heard: Down with the Hitlerite government! Long live the Polish government! Long live Marshal Piłsudski!
It was impossible to get into the synagogue, because it had already filled earlier with Jews who were reciting Psalms; also the moreh tzedek Rabbi Fridberg and Doctor S. Y. Riński described to the assembled public the deceitful deeds of the persecutors of the Jews in Germany.
In Sosnowiec
On Monday at midday a national committee was formed, which in special leaflets called on the Jewish population of Sosnowiec to close the shops at 5 in the afternoon and to come to the protest meeting, which took place in the open air in the courtyard of Mr. G. Abramczyk.
The large courtyard, which holds about 3000 persons, was soon overflowing with people. With fiery speeches about the persecutions in Germany there appeared B. Rozman, Rabbi Hager, Y. Klarman, Ch. Unger and Dr. Molodysta[?], who expressed thanks to the Polish government for its intervention regarding the Hitlerites' attacks on the Jews in Germany.
Then appropriate resolutions were adopted, among others that an economic boycott against Hitlerite Germany is declared.
With the singing of „Hatikvah“ the great protest meeting is closed.
In Zawiercie
The great protest meeting took place in the synagogue courtyard. After the opening speech by the well-known communal worker Mr. Bernsztajn, Messrs. Buchner, Cwajgel and Landau speak.
After the reading of the resolutions „Hatikvah“ is sung.
In Myszków
A protest meeting took place in the beit midrash. Speaking about the German persecutions were: Lejbisz Szwimer, Israel Herman (Zawiercie), the rabbi, Bunem Epsztajn, Natan Bams, and sharp protest resolutions were adopted.

The hunger strike in the „Klimontów“ and „Mortimer“ coal mines has ended

The hunger strike of the workers in the „Klimontów“ and „Mortimer“ coal mines, which lasted about 3 weeks, was ended this week.
This happened after the visit of the Kielce voivode Paciorkowski, who visited the mines. The striking workers, on learning of the voivode's visit, climbed out of the underground darkness and came to hear what the voivode wished to announce to them.
The voivode gave a speech before them, in which he announced the government's decision that the two mines may not be flooded and that the unemployed will be able to remain free of charge in their flats in the houses of the mine owners.
The voivode also conveyed the government's decision regarding their demands for relief. After the voivode's explanations the workers announced that they were breaking off the strike, and, accompanied by their families, who had already been waiting for them, they went home.
Gorgonowa comes to Sosnowiec tomorrow

As our readers know, the trial of the well-known Mrs Gorgonowa, who is accused of killing the estate owner Zaremba, has been going on in Kraków for about three weeks. For certain reasons the court is being transferred to Sosnowiec, where there are still many important witnesses.
In this connection the accused will be brought here tomorrow, Saturday, at 12 noon, under a strong police guard from Kraków.
The news has caused a great sensation, and it is to be expected that Madame Gorgonowa will be given a warm „welcome“ (kabbalat panim) in Sosnowiec.

"In the Struggle for a Jewish Kingdom."

[Sosnowiec — Zionism; Jabotinsky's lecture.] A lecture by V. Jabotinsky in Sosnowiec.
On Thursday evening — as we have already reported — a lecture by the Revisionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky took place in Sosnowiec. The lecture, on the subject "The Struggle for a Jewish Kingdom", drew an enormous audience from all strata of the Jewish population of Zagłębie.
Before the lecture began, reports spread that Jabotinsky's opponents had prepared "explosive materials" in order to disrupt the lecture. The mood was tense.
The first signal was given when Mr. Klarman greeted the distinguished guest in Hebrew. Finally the shouts of "Yiddish!" stopped, and the speaker is received with stormy ovations.
Jabotinsky announces right at the beginning that his lecture today will be a fantastic one. Let us imagine — he says — that we are already standing in the year 1938 and drawing up the account of the year 1933, and we want to see what Zionism has gone through during such a "pyatiletka" [five-year plan].
During the 5 years it was understood that the main force building Eretz Israel is private capital; the Keren Hayesod has been transformed into a large credit institution. The Keren Kayemet fund is used for the redemption of water, for solving the difficult water question in Eretz Israel. Through good propaganda every Jewish housewife was persuaded to spend one percent of her expenses on Eretz Israel products. The orange plantations have developed so strongly that from 6 to 7 million oranges are exported from the country. The port of Haifa has developed. In the course of the years the events in the country will repeat themselves, but Jewish self-defence will already be larger and stronger.
In the wider world, too, great changes will come. Around 1938 the crisis will improve. Relations among Jews themselves were settled by an arbitration commission, the restriction on immigration was lifted thanks to the League of Nations, etc.
What I have told you here — Mr. Jabotinsky concluded the first part of his lecture — is no prophecy, no dream; I have merely taken all sides into consideration and, foreseeing the events, I have drawn up the sum total.
During the first part of the lecture small "explosions" occurred, which were quickly liquidated. The second part, however, brought unpleasantness and much bitterness to the listeners. As Jabotinsky began to continue his lecture, the shout was heard from the gallery: "Enough already of your fantasies!" The interjection threw the Betarim off balance, and they wanted to remove the group of members of the League [for Labour Palestine], on whom fell the suspicion that they had come to disrupt. A tremendous tumult broke out in the hall, and amid terrible shouts and uproar the police ordered the audience to leave the hall.
The brawl was renewed in the street. The police intervened and liquidated the incidents.
As is reported, the opposing camp had prepared pigeons, sneezing powders, tear bombs and other "ammunition" in order to break up the lecture.
Later they managed to calm the audience, and Jabotinsky continued his lecture before a smaller audience; it left the proper impression.

Institutions that must be created

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — health and welfare.] (The realisation of the Sosnowiec out-patient clinic [ambulatorium] and the project for a similar institution in Będzin)
Each of us is preoccupied and toiling, and chases bitterly after the hard livelihood to bring home; and chasing about all day long, from morning to night, one forgets for the time being the human duties, the necessary obligations which everyday life demands of us.
True, in such unbearably hard times, when people are simply dying of hunger, one cannot have any complaints against the average person, who is constantly sunk in their hard toil in order to scrape out what their vital needs demand. Those, moreover, who do not earn a living — they are, after all, utterly null and void; they have no courage to show themselves before society, they are lost at every step, and therefore they do not count themselves among those active for society, among those who strive to benefit the community and to ease the lot of the miserable, helpless, suffering people.
As for the rich, the well-to-do, who are nonetheless such a minority — they seldom try to cast a glance into the darkened world, for various reasons: in the first place they do not want to tear themselves away from their businesses, and secondly they are afraid that the misery might affect them unpleasantly, which might perhaps disturb their nerve, and they will reflect: who knows — the little magnates will then think — perhaps it really is only fair to devote a little time also to the oppressed and hungry, in order to help them ease the terrible living conditions in which they find themselves and which in any case become worse from day to day, harder and more unbearable from day to day. Therefore the best way for them is to keep at a distance, to have no dealings with them at all; in this way one will knock the sorrow entirely out of one's head, and it will be forgotten that one must care for a certain oppressed contingent, for a certain category of people who supposedly throw themselves under everyone's feet. When one considers the situation seriously, when one analyses all this, one must come to the conclusions stated here.
And yet, and yet we were not crowned in vain as a people of "merciful sons of the merciful"; we do know, in the hardest of times and under the worst conditions, not to let people fall into the deep abyss. If X and Y have withdrawn from public life, if Reuben and Simeon have left the arena and no longer have the possibility to stand in their former public ranks — then other faces spontaneously appear, who know how to support the miserable fallen one, the helpless one, who has fallen into illness.
We have already dwelt on the question once before; we have already dealt with the matter and welcomed the initiative at its very beginning.
When the Sosnowiec "Linat ha-Holim" took upon itself the mission of establishing — even with the most modest means — an out-patient clinic, we found it necessary to dwell on it and to support it, because we know, after all, that from project to reality is a long, long way. Now, however, that this dream has become reality, it certainly, certainly deserves to be welcomed.
It is with satisfaction that we can report that the Sosnowiec clinic is an accomplished fact and that it is about to be opened in these very days.
This is truly a fine and useful deed in the present hard times. Jewish Sosnowiec thereby acquires a tremendously necessary institution, which will have the possibility of alleviating to some extent the distress of those who need to be cured.
Let the Jewish citizens of Sosnowiec therefore treat the institution with due respect, and let it be supported materially as it should be, so that it can develop and thereby gain the possibility of accomplishing what ought to come within its possession and its competence.
Let Jewish Sosnowiec once and for all take well to heart that, if we have said that from planning to realisation is a long way, it is still longer from founding to existence. True, it is good that an institution is being founded, because then we have before us an object, a work, on which one can labour and with which one can achieve much, very much. But that is still not everything, for when an institution is set up, one must pay great attention to its further existence, to its later prosperity. And in order to realise this properly, one must take care at the very founding not to deceive oneself, if you please, not to set the institution up, if you please, on goose legs, on fantastic foundations.
Let the initiators give an account of this at the very beginning, in order to set the useful establishment on a secure and real foundation.
It would therefore only be fair to draw the attention of the Będzin "Linat ha-Holim" as well, to follow the example for Będzin too, which likewise needs such an institution. Formerly the magistrate [municipality] gave the proper support in this field; it saw to it that the sick should be treated at the community's expense; now all that has been reduced to the utmost, and there is no one to heal those who have no means to pay the doctor for a visit and the pharmacist for the medicines.
In Będzin too there would be people who would support the founding and the existence of such an institution, without which the town cannot manage at the present moment. There would also be doctors who would devote a little time to these helpless sick, who have no other way out than to turn to public aid.
Let the activists of the Będzin "Linat ha-Holim" consider and discuss this proposal at one of their board meetings, and let only a resolution be adopted to found this necessary clinic — afterwards care will have to be taken that there are also means to maintain the institution. It must therefore be borne in mind that at the "Linat ha-Holim" the expenses will be minimal, because the institution can still find modest premises on its own, so that all this will bring in money and the expenses will then be minimal. In the present hard times economising plays a great role.
So let the question first of all be put on the agenda, and then it will certainly be possible to carry it out.
Here comes Passover, the intermediate days of the festival, days when one can afford to reflect a little and to see how things look, where the world stands — let these intermediate days be used for the common good, and let a resolution then be adopted that at the Będzin "Linat ha-Holim" too the necessary clinic will be founded.
R. Lem [?].
Political Letters

[Political letters — commentary; Japan and the League of Nations; Hitlerism.]
To my dear friend, our teacher R. Shlomo, may his light shine.
Don't you feel how the air is trembling? You will perhaps ask: how can it be? One may feel the earth trembling, other tangible things trembling, but how can it be that a person should feel the air trembling? To this I will answer you: there are moments in a person's life when he begins to see not only with his eyes, but truly with all his limbs... he is transformed entirely into a single sense of sight... Such moments can be exalted either by their deep calm or, on the contrary, by their tremendous storminess... When a person secludes himself for a long time somewhere in a wild forest or in a desert, where constant stillness and calm reign, his senses become so sharp that he is able to bring them to the greatest perfection. He sees for miles, he hears the slightest rustle, and the like. And likewise the reverse: in times of strong upheaval of the soul, when sufferings, troubles and terrible experiences befall a person, his senses too become greatly sharpened.
Mankind, too, is sometimes like an individual, and experiences the same as the latter...
Here, for example, we have been living through very difficult moments lately... In the Far East the fire is spreading ever wider and wider... It has already come to the point that Japan has officially announced its withdrawal from the League of Nations.
Actually, this is no surprising news, for such is the way of the diplomats: they hold by justice and by institutions that are supposed to protect justice, so long as the institutions do not interfere with their plans; but as soon as some danger threatens, from whomever it may be, they make a scapegoat of all principles, of the fine words, and do as they please.
True, there are still naive people who still believe in the power of the League of Nations, but one must be too great a simpleton to really have faith in the League of Nations, for until now we have not seen even once that the power of the L. of N. has actually manifested itself... For as soon as it comes to a serious conflict between two states, they both stop believing in the power of the League of Nations...
This reminds me of a saying of the Biłgoraj Rabbi on the verse "until Shiloh come"...
The Biłgoraj Rabbi was once in a company among whom there were several "young people of today," freethinkers, who, to spite the rabbi, began to mock the belief in the Messiah...
R. Shmuel Eli, the Biłgoraj Rabbi, listened calmly, then turned to the company and told them a story:
A fox caught sight of a bird sitting on a tree in the forest. He calls to the bird to come down to him, but the bird will not let itself be persuaded...
"I do understand [?]," it says, "what you need me for. You are surely hungry, poor thing, and my flesh tempts you..."
"God forbid," the fox answers with a pious face, "haven't you heard the great news? The Messiah has already come! 'The wolf shall dwell with the lamb' has already been fulfilled; one creature no longer does any harm to another, and so you have nothing to fear.."
Meanwhile, as they carry on this conversation between them, the sound of trumpets and the barking of dogs is heard in the forest...
"What can that mean?" the fox asks the bird. "You are standing up on the tree, you should see everything better than I..."
"It's nothing," the bird answered, "hunters are going with dogs..."
"Really?" The fox took fright and got ready to take to his heels ("and he fled").
"Why are you running away, why?" the bird asked the fox. "'The wolf shall dwell with the lamb' has already been fulfilled; one creature no longer does any harm to another, so what are you afraid of?"
"Yes, right," the fox answered and started running, "but the trouble is that the dogs, you understand me, do not believe in the coming of the Messiah..."
The modern "Messiah," the League of Nations, whose task is to realize "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb," can achieve nothing, because every time the "dogs" set out on the war-hunt they forget that one must be a believer in... the League of Nations.
And not only in the Far East is the air trembling, but also in our nearby Europe... The "sitra dimina" (as, for example, the Hitlerite gang in Germany and in other countries) have lately clamped themselves onto the body of the world, and each [?] cries "it is all mine"...
And the further it goes, the sharper and more embittered the struggle becomes... It is not a "dispute for the sake of dispute," not theoretical differences of opinion as there always used to be, but a dispute over power... The world has left the middle path; today there is evidently no more room for "let them divide it" and for compromise rulings; this one says it is all mine and that one says it is all mine, and by "says" one does not necessarily mean talking, but really shooting, stabbing, killing, burning, beating to death and the like... And if you wish to rule "let them divide it," both sides will stone you, because each of them will regard you as a traitor...
Such a situation cannot last long... It will have to come to an end, one way or the other... And perhaps in time a new generation will be born that will reawaken faith in humanity and in justice...
Who knows?
[?] your friend "S." [?]
