Law and Order

[Essay — Germany, Hitler and the Jews.] By Ab. Goldberg.

A Jew comes to me and speaks to me in a muffled voice, trembling, his eyes clouded with tears. This Jew is an educated man. He says: I don't know why, I can't explain it, but something frightens me. It seems to me that something terrible hangs over our heads. Any minute it will burst and pour out, like a curse, like the hail in Egypt. It seems to me that the ground is shaking under our feet, and any moment it will slip out from under them altogether, and we will be left hanging in the air, between heaven and earth, hurled [?] in the hollow of a sling, becoming once again the spectre of the world and a misfortune to ourselves.
My friend, this educated man, spoke with so much feeling and so much pain that I did not have the courage to enter into an argument with him. Nor did I find the right words with which to comfort him. By the law, too, one may not comfort a man while his dead lies before him, at the hour of death!
Moreover, I must confess that his mood infected me, his despair seized me, and a shudder ran through my body. And one question hammered in my head: is it really so bad with our people in the world, have all the appointed ends truly passed, and is nothing left but the rope! I made the reckoning of the soul later, by myself; I passed in my mind's eye over all the countries where Jews are found, the dispersion of the exile scattered over the seven seas, and it came out to me that my friend is right — although I felt at the same time that the fear that grips him, and that really has nothing to do with the present, for he himself speaks of what will be, of what is to come — that this fear has to do with his shattered nerves, with a lost balance. It is not logic through and through, but psychology. Feelings that cannot be controlled, that crawl out of the "halabalies" [?] and master a person instead of his mastering them.
It was at the time of the election campaign in Germany; very [printed "ver", a misprint for "zer" — very] disturbing reports reached us here of Hitler's triumphal march in one of the highest countries of culture — Germany, with her Kant and Goethe, with her Brahms and "Tozart" [sic; Mozart]. In such a country there arose a Hitler, a demagogue of the purest water, a man-beast with scant education and unbridled ambitions, a phrase-thresher and clown with a Charlie Chaplin moustache, who speaks in the language of a drunken beast, with his tongue stuck out, like a wild dog torn loose from its chain; and he speaks about Jews in a language that no Haman at any time — that all the Hamans of all times — did not [want] only "to destroy, to slay and to annihilate", but simply: he wants nothing other than to tear the Jewish people out by the root, to put an end to the Jewish race, so that of "the enemies of Zion" [a euphemism for the Jews] no remnant or survivor shall remain. And this ugly figure has become the idol of millions of Germans.
I knew very well that when my friend spoke those bitter words to me, there stood before his eyes Hitler in the form in which the Angel of Death is depicted: a skeleton with eye-holes that spread death, and in its bony hands a scythe that cuts heads as reapers cut ears of grain. But really it is not only Germany. In the other countries, in Germany's neighbourhood, it is no better either. How do things stand with the Jews in Romania and Hungary? It is the old picture that fits the Jewish situation so remarkably: over the heads of millions hangs a sword tied by a hair. Let the hair snap and there is a catastrophe — Jewish blood, God forbid, is spilled. This, it would seem, is the sad truth, and yet it is not the whole truth, but [calls for] calmer reflection. And when one regards the Jewish situation not in isolation from the state of the whole world, and when one has in mind not only today, the present time, but also yesterday, and draws a comparison between today and yesterday, between years gone by — let us say two hundred years ago in that same Germany — and the terror-inspiring present, one must tell oneself that the despair is groundless; on the contrary, that we have every reason to look to the future full of hope. Bad as it is, bitter as the situation is, there is no doubt that we are not going towards the worse but towards the better; that what is now happening in Germany and in the other countries — all the evil forces that have balled together, preparing to fling themselves upon us with their clenched fists, ready in a sadistic assault to strangle us and dance with joy on our body — that these are in fact the last efforts of a dying world, that it is thereby gathering its last strength in order to hold its position, that this is its cry of despair, that this bitter struggle is a sign of its despair, and that although it speaks in a language as if this were a rising age, the sprouting of a new era — in truth we stand at the decline of an outlived world, at the death-throes of a withered world-view.
If you will, we Jews even have a right to rejoice in the victory of the new spirit over the old, for despite all temporary setbacks and failures, the new spirit, founded on humanity, on integrity and justice, triumphs over the old spirit, which leaned on violence, on the sword, and worse still on the bestial instincts and cruel feelings that live in human beings; and this new spirit, which has been fighting for thousands of years against all evil forces, suffers defeats and yet does not give up, and in every era we see how it breaks through and grows stronger and stronger. Its victory is our victory, and its victory we see [printed "ven", a misprint for "zeen" — see] in ourselves — we are the true barometer.
Nobody wishes to belittle the danger of Hitlerism, but all those who talk like this overlook one thing: that unlike in former times, when Jews used to stand outside the law and order, when the two — law and Jews — were regarded as separate categories, today, when one speaks of law and order, this automatically includes the Jews as well. Law and order cannot today live together with the contradiction of lawlessness towards Jews, of the sadly famous "kromie yevreyev" [?] [the Tsarist Russian legal formula "кроме евреев" — "except Jews"].
In former times it was different: for Jews a ghetto was made even within the law. If they were given any right at all, it was not even called by that name; it was called "privileges", for which they had to pay and which depended on the caprice of the ruler or of the ruling people. Jews were forced to plead not for the justice of the law, from which they were excluded, but for the good heart of the governor — that he should think good thoughts about the Jews and not issue any new decrees.
The situation now — even every pessimist must concede — is quite different. Now what Jews must fear is that lawlessness should not overturn the law. But if law and order remain standing, the Jews are protected. The law and the order, whether they love us or hate us, whether they hold a high opinion of us or not an exalted one — they feel that in their own interests they must protect us; otherwise it is no law, it is no order.
A Little Feuilleton

[Humorous feuilleton.] I'm Not at Home!
Listen! A man mustn't be a sucker at all — you have to know how to turn the world around!
Here, as you see me, I'm steeped in debts. I'm pawned, borrowed-up and mortgaged with my head and with the whole lot, only I have them "in Łowicz" [a jocular idiom, apparently: I don't care a fig about them].
Well, you'll say: when the butcher comes, when the tailor tears your veins and the shoemaker makes a fuss [lit. "twists a spodek"] — "davai [give] money!" — so I do my acquaintance a favour and take a little interest-free loan from him.
Only don't be a sucker. You have to know how to turn the world around.
But lately it's become nasty. The creditors don't budge from the house: I get up in the morning — there they are: "Dzień dobry!" [Good morning]; I sit down to lunch: "Smacznego" [Enjoy your meal]; I go to bed: they sit down by the bed and catch a nap too.
In short, things got tight for me! Nasty! So my wife hit upon the idea: "Pana gieta w domu" [sic; for Pana nie ma w domu — the master is not at home] — I'm not, that is, at home.
So I left home and began to do "debt-exile", and it became a sheer relief: I don't see a single creditor before my eyes.
But here's a new trouble: my own wife has started looking for me — to her too I'm a debtor, she says. Passover is coming. She needs a dress, a shoe, matzah, beetroot and other vegetables; you hear words from your own wife worse than from a stranger. So I decided: that's it — I'm not at home. She comes in through one door — I go out through the other.
You mustn't be a sucker at all.
At night I peek in through the window, and when I see she's asleep I slip into the house and push my way to my things [?].
When day breaks — I'm already outside. You have to know how to turn the world around.
And my wife, my own wife, runs around the whole town and looks for me just like a stranger — my own wife!
If you see her, tell her I send her my regards.
Only home I don't come. I'm not at home.
P. M.
A "Victim" of Sport

[Humorous feuilleton — sport.] (Told by a father who has three sons who are "sportsmen")
From time immemorial we led a quiet and solid life in my home. You never heard anybody there let out a loud word, and the whole courtyard of neighbours simply wanted to burst with envy of us. I was an ordinary everyday Jew [lit. "a Jew of the whole year"], dealt in onions and lemons and always strove to make a living; my wife too was not one of the worst, and simply moved worlds to earn a penny [grosz]. She was fit for everything, and there was no case of any trade existing in the world that she did not know well. In summer she dealt in young chickens [kurczaki], in winter in lime-preserved eggs, and the rest of the time she was a broker for servant-girls, or collected money for poor women in childbed. Children we had — truly a blessing to be said over them, and people predicted that out of these lads would one day grow very important [ważne] rabbinical heads. Well, we really led a life — may all Jewish children have the same — such that I never had anything to complain about. It was worth living.
Now, three years ago, God save us, an upheaval came over my whole household [?], and of the old times not even a trace remained. My three sons grew up like oaks and took up sport. Well, whom could it bother that they do sport [?] or make all kinds of "kozhalkes" [koziołki — somersaults]. I thought to myself: doctors say it is a healthy thing — why should precisely my children be sick? So every day they banged each other in the "mugs" [mordy], jumped, danced, worked with their arms and legs and persuaded me that from minute to minute whole kilos of health were added to them. It even embittered me that three such lads, like lions, do nothing but sport and give not a thought to earning a few gulden [złoty].
Well, never mind; as long as they left me in peace I kept quiet and let them enjoy all those "shtukes" [sztuki — tricks]. But my youngsters [junacy] grew bolder and bolder, until they took me on in earnest [lit. "not in jest"]. One came to me that I should buy him a pair of white trousers, because otherwise he cannot fulfil the sporting law of tennis, and his health might, God forbid, be seriously endangered on that account; the second came with an uproar that if I do not buy him a "rover" [rower — bicycle] within twenty-four hours, his whole life will go for naught. The youngest son again pestered me that for his sport he must have a pair of leather gloves, and just so with "bare" hands it is no business for him to hit the other fellow in the "mug".
I didn't even try to say two words and bought my crew all that nonsense ["bli-zin"], and thanked God that I would now have rest from them for a while.
But since then a bitter plague has arisen in my house, so that I simply don't know [?] how to get rid of the sporting troubles and of the shouting and scandals that lately play out at my place in good order. The cyclist has emptied all my rooms, put the whole little bit of furniture and the beds up in the attic, and holds "vyshtshiges" [wyścigi — races] through the rooms and shouts that this is called "training". The second, just imagine, doesn't take off his white drawers for one minute the whole day and runs around with a "rakiet" [rakieta — racket] in his hand, and as if out of spite he hits me on the head with all the balls [piłki]. From the third I have the greatest troubles, and he is simply shortening my days. He has taken into the house the watchman's [stróż] gentile boy, and for a gulden a day lets himself be beaten murderously, and simply makes mincemeat of the gentile. From morning till night he keeps pummelling him ["zbegken", ?] without mercy in the "pyskes" [pyski — mugs], the shouts reach the heart of heaven, and my heart pounds like a robber's. After such a portion, when he has properly mauled him and bloodied him, he lays him down on the ground, strokes him back and forth, applies cold compresses to him and calls this, in his language, "massage". Nothing doing — they are killing me without end, and I have not a minute's rest from them.
A few weeks ago they had a Maccabiah, and once again they harnessed me to the work, and again I had to buy them skis, skates with various straps ["drenger", ?], little wheels and crazy contraptions, on which they flew through all my rooms like demons, danced, jumped, and told me to imagine that this is what the Maccabiah would look like.
I would gladly have put up with all of that, were it not that in our old age they have taken on me and my wife and want to make sportsmen of us through and through ["rukhoys", prob. for "durkhoys"], supposedly so that we should be strong and healthy — and what shall I tell you? Half my health I have surely lost in this time. Every day at 6 in the morning the sons drive us out of our beds and torment us with their gymnastics; my wife they have "clothed the naked" in a green costume, and I go around almost entirely naked in a pair of short red pants, in which I must run and do sport as they order. Suddenly I began to compromise them with my figure. They talk me into believing that I hold myself crooked and am growing a hump, and the main thing — they meddle too much in my private life, since their mother, that is my wife, is too fat for them, and sport must make her into a decent little wife. Me they keep pulling and tearing by the arms and legs, twisting my head right and left, hacking at my shoulders with all their might and shouting blue murder that only by sporting and hardening [hartować] me will they drive away my hump.
Meanwhile I have been lying deathly ill in bed for several weeks, and my "sportovnikes" [sportsmen] don't leave me alone for a minute, and at every opportunity they give me a couple of healthy punches [kułaki] in the bones. I cannot get rid of them by any means, the neighbours make my life a misery, the landlord threatens me with eviction, and my wife has suddenly noticed that she has a hunchback for a husband and wants, in her old age at that, to divorce me.
No, gentlemen, it's no good! If you should ever hear that a Jew with a hump has died, you should know that he fell a victim of sport, with which his 2 sons [sic] chastised him, and instead of making him healthy, they brought him, poor man, quite innocently to a Jewish grave.
Luks.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayikra)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayikra
The Portion
—o—
a) "And He called unto Moses" (1:1)
"'And He called unto Moses' — from here they said: any scholar who has no knowledge, 'a carcass is better than he'." Yalkut.
The small aleph in the word "Vayikra" points to Moses' humility: because he held himself so small, therefore he merited that God should speak with him. Of a haughty man, on the other hand, God says: "I and he cannot dwell under one roof" — we cannot live together.
And about arrogance the Gemara says: "Whoever is haughty, if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him" — and therefore, when a scholar loses his understanding, which happens because of arrogance, a carcass is better than he, because from such a scholar there comes a worse smell than from a carcass... As the folk say of a haughty man: "the arrogance stinks from him". Sifsei Daas.
—o—
b) "If any man of you bring an offering unto the Lord" (ibid., 2)
"'Adam' (a man) — why is it said? Just as Adam, the first man, did not offer anything stolen... so you too shall not offer anything stolen." Rashi.
The question arises: in Sukkah (44) the Gemara derives "to exclude stolen property" precisely from the word "of you" (mikem).
But here Rashi means a different theft: "stealing the mind" of people [deceiving them]. For when Adam brought an offering to God, there were no other people in the world, and his piety was surely not in order to boast of it — such offerings you should bring: without any ulterior motives, without any wish to be praised by others... Arono shel Yosef.
* *
Rabbi Noah of Lachowicze used to say:
God one cannot deceive, and people one must not deceive...
* *
Rabbi Noah of Lachowicze once asked his father, Rabbi Mordechai:
"We know that there are thirty-six hidden tzaddikim; so it must be that the known tzaddikim do not belong to the thirty-six?"
"My child," Reb Mordechai answers him, "woe would be to us if the hidden tzaddikim were the same as the known ones..."
—o—
c) "And when any soul will offer a meal offering unto the Lord" (2:1)
Only in the case of the meal offering is the word "soul" (nefesh) said. For who brings a meal offering? — a poor man; and it is as dear to God as if he had offered his soul — so says Rashi.
It follows, then, that the rich man is more arrogant and more repellent than the poor man not only in his sinning, but even in his repenting, even in his bringing an offering...
Metziat Yitzchak.
—o—
d) "A guilt offering unto the Lord" (5:19)
He who sins by robbery sins against God as well, and the Gemara says in Bava Batra (88) that the sin of robbing an ordinary person is graver than robbing money from the Temple treasury.
And therefore the verse says: "Let us search and try our ways — and turn again to the Lord." First: "let us search our ways" — first one must be in order among ourselves, rob [?] nobody among men, and only then "and turn again to the Lord". Shaar Bat Rabim.
*
Rabbi Nathan Adler, the rabbi of Frankfurt, renounced all his property as ownerless, so that no one, God forbid, should stumble through him into the prohibition of robbery...
—o—
The Haftarah
e) "But thou hast not called upon Me, O Jacob, but thou hast been weary of Me, O Israel" (Isaiah 43)
Like that merchant who gave a porter a suitcase of precious stones to carry, and seeing how the porter was sweating from carrying it, clutched his head: "Oh, oh, a disaster! Nobody sweats from a suitcase of diamonds — they must have stolen the diamonds and put in stones..."
If you, Israel, are so tired of the Torah, if "thou hast been weary of Me, O Israel", you are probably not carrying My diamonds in the Torah; they have probably been exchanged for heavy stones — "thou hast not called upon Me". The Dubno Maggid [printed "Dorner Maggid"].
—o—
f) "One shall say, I am the Lord's... and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the Lord."
Saying "I am the Lord's" — many say. Saying costs no money; those are called in the aspect of "Jacob" (Yaakov), which means deceit ("for he hath supplanted me these two times"). The main thing, however, is "and another shall subscribe with his hand" — how many good deeds a person does. Ahavat Yehonatan.
The significance of touring and knowing the land (Landkentenish).

[Będzin — touring/regional studies; article.] (On the occasion of the Sunday general meeting of the society in Będzin).
The specific conditions in which we live lead to this: that although we take an active part in all fields of culture, economy and politics, as citizens of a modern state, there is nonetheless felt among us an urge towards a communal life of our own, one that embraces our cultural necessities. Hence the strong tendency among us, by which we centralise our social life, is understandable.
In our state of neglect and disorientation, when everything among us is torn apart and splintered, the existence of the Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land (Landkentenish; Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze) deserves special attention: it is apolitical and bears a non-party character, and in its essence it is called upon to concentrate, gather and hold together our cultural forces, and it is on the path of centralisation, up to a worldwide character.
Whereas among our neighbours, who are recruited mostly from landowners and in general from people who, because of their occupation, are bound to the land — and so too their town people, having relatives in the village, often get to spend time in the countryside — the development of a society for knowing the land is not of the very first importance, with us the situation is quite different. First of all because we have colossal internal difficulties and various obstacles that must be uprooted and fought.
In the hard struggle for a piece of bread, the broad Jewish masses forget to care for and tend the dearest thing we possess — our bit of health.
It is therefore clear that there must be a factor that will drag the overworked Jewish masses out of the holes with stifling air and acquaint them with the beauties of nature in the world. Despite the great apathy and resignation that the crisis has called forth in all areas of our cultural life, one must nevertheless not let one's hands drop and put everything down to the crisis. A properly broad propaganda must be carried out among the broad masses, giving them the opportunity, from time to time, by means of cheap tourist events, to refresh their exhausted strength and to enjoy a little fresh air and sunshine.
The ideal of knowing the land is therefore the only one capable of tearing the broad masses out of the terrible melancholy in which they find themselves; it is the only means of refreshing the exhausted strength and nerves of the masses, who are in a state of constant destruction because of the present hard economic living conditions and toil beyond their strength, both physical and mental.
The society for knowing the land gives the broad masses the opportunity, for a minimal payment (and quite often it ought to be free of charge), to enjoy the glorious world and its springs of life. One need only explain to the poor man that water costs no money, so he can always wash and always be clean — and he will surely profit from the instruction; the same applies to the ideal of knowing the land: one need only teach the harried, overworked man of the people and convince him in practice that taking part in a touring excursion brings much enjoyment in every respect and causes no material loss.
The tasks of the Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land are not limited merely to what has been said.
This is proved by the society's intensive cultural activity. There is a whole series of problems that cry out "expound me": in particular, in my opinion, the idea is already ripe of adding to the society's name the ideal of "knowing the world" (Veltkentenish) in general.
Z. Jakubowicz.

A King Who Fled from the Throne in the Middle of the Night (A Historical Tale)

[Historical tale — France, King Henry III (Valois); conclusion.]
By El-Be.

With cynical joy King Henry looked at the dead body of the Duke [Henri, Duke of Guise], and on seeing his mother arrive he ran towards her, embraced her and cried out with joy:
— Madame, now I am king again! After this affair I am no longer afraid of my enemies, who lie in wait [?] to take the crown from me.
— Well „cut“ — said the mother — but reckon with this, my son: the danger has not yet been entirely removed; there is still one more who is a stone in your path.
Henry understood what his mother, that bitter, bloodthirsty woman, was driving at with these words, and whom she meant, and he resolved to kill also the Duke's brother, the Cardinal of Lorraine.
Carrying out this murder came hard to him, not as easily as the murder of the Duke, because to kill a cardinal no volunteer could be found so easily; everyone whom the king urged to carry out the murder hesitated [?] to raise a hand. But in the end it came down to money: for a well-paid fee a volunteer was found, who killed the Cardinal.
The news that the Cardinal of Lorraine had been murdered naturally stirred up the Catholic world. A hellish fire burned among the Catholics; the church bells did not stop ringing and calling for revenge. At a special session of the Sorbonne the verdict was pronounced that, after the murder of the Cardinal, the French people was released from its oath of loyalty to Henry III. Rome too did not keep silent: it excommunicated Henry and cursed him in this world and in the world to come.
In all towns and townlets where there were any Catholic communities at all, orderly processions took place; long columns demonstrated with torches in their hands, went to the churches and prayed that just as the torches would be extinguished, so too would the House of Valois be extinguished — the dynasty from which King Henry descended. Paris revolted openly, and so did many other cities of France.
The result of the processions and of the anti-monarchist agitation was that Henry was in fact a king without a throne. He had no one to take counsel with. His mother, Catherine de' Medici, who had become the one who set the tone and talked him into evil deeds, had died — even after the murder of the Guises. And having no friend, no redeemer, Henry turned to his brother-in-law, Henry of Navarre, to conclude an alliance with him against the aroused Catholics. The alliance between him and his brother-in-law was concluded, and both set energetically to work to suppress the uprising.
The work was successful: within two months they managed to organise an army of forty thousand men, and on the eve of 30 July 1589 they were already standing before the walls of Paris.
In the city a tumult broke out. But the priests did not stop inciting, the Catholics set fires, and the sisters of the murdered Guises rained pitch and brimstone and called on the Catholics that at least one of them be found who would save Catholicism, „the true Christian religion“, and go and kill the apostate king. The sisters' call had its effect, and indeed someone came forward who undertook to murder the king.
This happened on 2 August 1589, when the army under the command of the two Henrys — King Henry III and his brother-in-law Henry of Navarre. One day before the assault on Paris was due to begin, a young monk from the Dominican monastery, a certain Jacques [?] Clément, quietly slipped out of the besieged city of Paris and went straight to the headquarters.
Arriving there, he asked to be admitted at once to the king, because he had to hand over to him an important secret which would make his victory over the enemies easier.
The main guard, hearing this, at once led the young priest in to the king.
— Well, what good do you bring with you? — the king addressed the young monk. But instead of an answer the monk, without hesitation, thrust a knife into his belly.
— The vile monk has killed me — cried the king, and pulling the knife out of the bleeding wound himself, he hurled it into the murderer's face.
The guard at once came running and killed the murderer, the monk, on the spot.
With this ended the rule of the heirs after Catherine de' Medici.
(The End)

Spring Is Coming!

[Humour — the "Spring" page (in place of the "Kokh-Lefl"); a Passover poem.]
Spring
In place of the "Kokh-Lefl" ["The Cooking Ladle" — the regular humour column]
By Ben Amotz

Spring is coming!
Oh, woe is me —
spring
makes itself heard;
I feel a fresh
spring wrinkle
on my wrinkled
brow.

For after spring
there drags along
the festival of freedom,
Passover;
and everything at home
goes "padaram" [?],
darkness
reigns there.

They air out
the bedding,
they wash
the windowpanes with it;
feathers fly
all around
the house, like white
doves.

Little red biters [bedbugs]
run about,
terrified
of doom,
when women's fingers
search
every crack
and crevice.

They sense, poor things,
the danger
and try
to save themselves,
when the housewives
set about
cleaning
the beds.

For spring means
death for them,
devastation
and annihilation;
no one [?] has yet
sung of spring
in a poem.

If spring came
here on its own,
I too would
welcome it —
with shouts of joy
and a jubilee dance
and merry
songs.

Yet, alas, there drags
behind it
the festive
guest,
who costs the Jew
money and toil,
who costs him
the wealth of Korah.

Goose [?] fat
and matzah meal,
and wine
and matzah shmura,
and for the stamp
"kosher for Passover"
they flay
the hide off you.

They flay your skin
for every kilo,
they gouge you
for every bite;
a roast [?] ("gosh-brat")
of the freedom festival
is torn away
for a trifle.

A piece of fish
is worth its weight in gold,
and meat — a lot [small weight unit]
for a rendl [gold coin];
and if you do get a chicken
cheaply,
it is as thin
as a splinter.

That explains
my deep "oy"!
the tear
in my eyes;
I feel
so "exodus-like" —
I am being
drawn out.

Z. L. Wolfson.

Why is it so hard for a girl today to make a match.

[Society — women, marriage and matchmaking.] Some time ago an English woman writer poured out her heart to her readers and told them the truth: although as a writer she is popular, as a woman she is a complete failure.
The writer is already nearly fifty years old, has not yet married, and has never even been loved by anyone.
Is she ugly?
No! In her youth she was known among her friends as a beauty.
Here is what she herself writes about herself: „I had a head of golden-blond hair, a lovely figure, small feet, a white, smooth little face".
But men avoided her, and they avoided her precisely because — she says — she had a masculine head on her shoulders and a sharp tongue, with which she could tell someone something he would not like.
All her life she hated empty phrases[?] and clumsy, foolish people. And both things are all too noticeable in a man who meets a girl for the first time. At the first acquaintance the young man will try to display his gentlemanliness in an exaggerated manner, or else he will display his embarrassment, his excessive modesty.
So she set about „getting at the years"[?] with her barbs, and therefore the young men came to avoid her.
And now the said writer philosophises over whether she did well.
In one place she writes that when she looks at her friends, who are her own age, and sees how they have aged, what troubles they have, what sufferings marriage has brought them, she is then glad that she has remained an old maid.
„Every love ends in marriage and every marriage, without exception, is a disappointment"...
And only after all this does the said writer ask herself: „Perhaps those who go along with the idea[?] are right, that the feelings of love one experiences when one is in love are worth bearing all the sufferings for them later"?
After all, the whole of life is nothing more than a chain into which are forged little rings of joy and disappointment, suffering and happiness, troubles and pleasures.
If lovers have had joy, they sometimes have troubles afterwards too.
If for some the marriage ends in disappointment, they have, on the other hand, the consolation that earlier they had pleasure and contentment.
Another woman writer, an American, tells about herself that she actually began as a lonely, forlorn woman and ended by becoming popular and loved by everyone.
In the first years, when she had finished university, it seemed to her that New York had no man at all who would be worthy of her, and it looked as if it would not bother her at all if she should end up remaining an old maid, a „left-on-the-shelf" woman.
She threw herself into all sports games, used to speak at women's meetings, was free and easy with her friends, behaved towards them like a good fellow and a good pal.
No man could outswim her, outrun her, beat her at tennis, at horse racing, at cards, or even at ping-pong and billiards.
And when a man got into an argument with her, he could not win at all either. She would out-talk him and debate with him so long, until she had shown him that she knew and could do more than he.
Morally she was a good girl; no one could cast any dust on her character. On the contrary, everyone said that she was the best, the most respectable girl in the whole area. It goes without saying that there was not a single young man who could have boasted that he had ever given her a kiss.
When the years ran on and she was left alone, her friends had married and already had children, and she was still regarded as a strictly moral girl, only then did she realise that her conduct would not take her far. She saw the wall that she herself had built and set up between herself and the world of men.
But she caught herself in time and adopted a new tactic: she carved onto her face the constant smile one so often sees on young girls when they come into the company of men. She learned to talk about nothing, about things that interest her little but hold a certain interest for men.
The said writer began to imitate the simple girls and had success with the young men she knew.
And now she gives girls lessons in how to be successful in love.
Now she knows how one must look, how one must talk and how one must behave in the company of men. Young men now swarm around her like bees around honey, and she has already had several proposals of marriage from very respectable men.
„If a young man tells a joke" — she warns her women readers — „laugh with all your heart".
„Girls must learn to look in such a way that it is both pleasant and not brazen; girls must be restrained and not old-fashioned. The smile of the mouth and of the eyes must be such that no young man should make the mistake of thinking the girl brazen, but neither should he make the mistake of thinking the girl too high and mighty.
„A girl must be able to tell a joke and to listen to a joke. If the joke is at her own expense, she must not get angry; on the contrary, it will do her no harm if she herself from time to time makes a joke at her own expense.
Most of today's girls behave wildly and hold wild carousals. The said writer assures us that she has not yet seen a young man who would marry the girl with whom he had been at an overly merry carousal. A man likes to have a good time with a woman at a wild orgy. But he will not marry that woman. A man will not even marry a woman who smokes, who drinks and tells coarse jokes — unless he is already a man truly in love, or a very practical person.
Men also hate to marry those women who are not sparing with kisses. Men have no desire for women who are ready to kiss any man at all; they themselves may well want to have a good time with such a woman, but marry her they will not.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Are Tenants Obliged to Pay for Water?

[Head of the local page; Będzin — housing and water.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 4 / 4 Nisan 5693 — piątek 31 marca 1933 [Friday, 31 March 1933].)
Będzin
Are tenants obliged to pay for water?
Several weeks ago, on the basis of authoritative information from the Magistrat [municipal office], we wrote that in houses which had water in the year 1914 the tenants need not pay for water.
In connection with this report in our paper, the new House-Owners' Association intervened with the Magistrat commissioner, demanding that he officially deny the report.
In reply to this intervention the House-Owners' Association received from the Magistrat a written answer that "according to the decree of the President of the Republic of 14 March 1928 the water question has been clarified on all sides, and exempt from paying for water are only those tenants who live in towns which had a municipal water supply before 1924; whereas in all other towns, where until 1924 there was no municipal water supply, regardless of whether there was private water in 1914 or not, [the tenants] are obliged to pay for the water from the municipal water supply".
So the House-Owners' Association informs us.

On the Guest Performances of Dr. Paul Baratoff with His Ensemble in Zagłębie.

[Będzin — theatre.]
The guest performances which the famous great Jewish actor Dr. Paul Baratoff is giving in Będzin with his ensemble, whose first performance, "David Golder", took place yesterday, have aroused great interest in the widest circles of lovers of better Yiddish theatre.
Dr. Baratoff is no new face in our town. His guest performances here 2 years ago won him great recognition and admirers of his art of acting, which rises far above the average. His masterly stage creations have remained to this day in the memory of the audience.
Now Dr. Baratoff has come to us with a new play, not yet seen here, entitled "David Golder" by Irena Nemirovska [Irène Némirovsky], which is being played on the most important European stages with immense success. The performances of "David Golder" in Warsaw, Łódź and lately in Kraków aroused great favour on the part of the public, as well as on the part of the theatre critics, who dedicated enthusiastic songs of praise to Dr. Baratoff.
Today, Friday, at the 2nd performance in Będzin, the well-known social drama "Hinkemann" by Ernst Toller will be played, in which Baratoff is unsurpassable and which belongs among the best stage achievements of this great artist.
There is no doubt that our theatre public will not miss this gratifying and rare opportunity to see the great master Baratoff.
Meeting of the Będzin Small Traders' Association

The floor is taken by the chairman Mr. Herszlewicz, who sharply attacks the outgoing board, [saying] that the previous board did not live up to its tasks, that things [?] were done which should never have any place in a public institution. He therefore proposes: 1) that the meeting be interrupted and postponed to a second date; 2) to elect a temporary committee, which shall carry out a reorganisation of the association and draw up a suitable list of candidates for a new board, and meanwhile the committee is given the right to administer the affairs of the association until the continuation [?] of the general meeting.
Those present declare their solidarity with the chairman's proposal, and a temporary committee is elected by acclamation, consisting of Messrs. Hersz Herszlewicz, Gerszon Rechnic, Dawid Gutensztajn, Iser Kricler, Józef Rus, Herszel Stopnicki and Szymszon Majman.
With this the meeting is closed.

Sosnowiec — Jewish councillors of the Chamber of Commerce decide to call a conference on boycotting German goods

[Sosnowiec — anti-German boycott; Chamber of Commerce.] On Tuesday evening, after the plenary session of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, a special consultation of the Jewish councillors took place, at which they discussed how to define precisely the boycott action against German products and goods.
After a lengthy discussion it was decided to turn to the central committees of the Jewish economic organisations in Poland asking them to call a conference, at which the exact plan for conducting the boycott action should be worked out.
Murderers found who in 1922 killed a whole family in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — crime; murder.] In April 1922, on Kaliska Street in Sosnowiec, the widow Durłowa [?] and her 2 children, a girl of 11 and a boy of 7, were murdered for the purpose of robbery.
At 1 o'clock at night several masked bandits entered Mrs. Durłowa's flat and, threatening death, demanded the several thousand dollars she had received from America. When Durłowa explained that she had bought a house with the dollars, one of the bandits struck her on the head with a hammer, from which she fell dead on the spot.
The children, seeing that their mother had been killed, began to cry for help. Then the same [?] bandit murdered the two children too with the hammer.
The murderers then searched the whole flat and, having robbed 8000 marks, vanished.
11 years passed and the murderers were not discovered. This week the local police received confidential information that the local resident Bolesław Sakowski is one of the murderers.
Under interrogation Sakowski confessed. The police are already on the trail of the other murderers.

Jewish Reservists Named After Jabotinsky / The Conflict with the Caretakers Settled / Those Who Keep Commercial Books Do Not Pay the Tax for the Unemployment Fund / Cheaper Postal Rate for Abroad and for Sample Mail / The Radomsko Rebbe Has Returned / Workers in a Slaughterhouse Stop Work in Protest Against the Hitler Gang

On Monday a meeting of former Jewish soldiers took place with the aim of founding, on the model of all the other towns, an association of reservists named after Jabotinsky. The task of the association is to carry on cultural work and to stand at the command of the creator of the Jewish Legion, Jabotinsky, in the service of the upbuilding of the Land of Israel.
After a discussion, in which Messrs. Glidman, Perczyk, Szładowski, Nachemia, Altman and Majtlis took part, the following committee was elected: Mr. Erlich (chairman), Perczyk (secretary), Z. Nachemia, Glidman and Altman.
On Sunday morning the general meeting will take place.
—o—
The Conflict with the Caretakers Settled
For several months the conflict between the house owners and the caretakers (stróże) over their pay has been going on.
A large number of house owners in Zagłębie actually want to reduce the number of caretakers, because they themselves are ready to do the caretakers' work.
About the conflict a series of conferences took place, which gave no positive result.
On the proposal of the Sosnowiec labour inspector the matter was handed over to an arbitration commission, which consisted of representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Justice and Social Welfare.
The arbitration commission settled the matter in the following way: the pay for caretakers will amount to 20 to 150 zł a month depending on the number of flats. In houses where there are institutions such as banks, schools, offices etc., the caretakers will receive supplementary pay.
—o—
Those Who Keep Commercial Books Do Not Pay the Tax for the Unemployment Fund
The tax offices have received a circular from the Ministry of Finance stating that the circular of 5 October 1931, according to which [a surcharge] for the unemployment fund is added to every tax, remains binding; an exception is made only for those who keep commercial books and have already deducted in the books from their income the payments for the unemployment fund.
—o—
Cheaper Postal Rate for Abroad and for Sample Mail
From tomorrow, Saturday, 1 April, the rate for abroad will become cheaper by 10 gr., i.e. from tomorrow on a letter abroad will cost 50 gr. The rate for sample mail will also become cheaper.
—o—
The Radomsko Rebbe Has Returned
The Radomsko Rebbe, who spent a whole winter in Berlin for purposes of a cure, came back from Berlin on Tuesday evening, accompanied by his Hasid Mr. Kaszycki.
—o—
Workers in a Slaughterhouse Stop Work in Protest Against the Hitler Gang
On Monday afternoon Mr. Mendelewicz gave a speech to the workers in his slaughterhouse, in which he recounted the brutal deeds of the Hitlerites in Germany.
As a sign of protest the workers interrupted the work for about an hour.
To Whom Do the Boots Belong? / A Tax Curiosity in Zawiercie.

In Zawiercie a bailiff (sequestrator) came to the flat of Mr. Deich to carry out a distraint. A pair of boots was drying on the stove, and the sequestrator wanted to take them. Although Mr. Deich declared that these were his father's boots, a sequestration order was placed on the boots. But when the sequestrator came for the "goods", he found Deich's father wearing the boots...
A report was drawn up against Mr. Deich for tampering with state property.
"Finds" Are Being Planted Outside the Post Office in Będzin.

As we are informed, there are swindlers in Będzin who plant "finds" in front of the post-office building. With the help of these "finds" they manage to steal parcels from naive people, or in the confusion to pull out of their pockets whatever can be pulled out.
The "Merchants' Association" in Będzin ought to react to this.
The OWP Dissolved in Upper Silesia.

On the basis of an order of the Ministry of the Interior, the "OWP" [Obóz Wielkiej Polski, Camp of Great Poland] has been dissolved on the territory of the Silesian Voivodeship. By a special order the OWP branches in Katowice, Königshütte [Królewska Huta, Chorzów] and Nowy Bytom were dissolved.

What Happened on Tuesday Night in Berlin?

Torah scrolls torn up. — Jewish homes demolished. — Jewish passers-by beaten.
As this issue goes to press we are informed by a Berlin Jew, who arrived in Sosnowiec yesterday, about the cruel deeds of the Hitlerites on Tuesday night in Berlin, on Grenadierstrasse.
The Hitlerites entered the prayer houses and synagogues located on that street and tore up the Torah scrolls; then they fell upon Jewish homes, dealt cruel blows to those present, and smashed the furniture and whatever else was to be found. They took about 100 Jews away with them, and it is not known where they are.
The wives of the tortured men, mostly Polish Jews, have turned for help to the Polish consul in Berlin.

On Public Collections of Money

[Law — public collections.] In number 22 of the “Dz. Ustaw” [Dziennik Ustaw, the Polish Journal of Laws] a law has appeared on public collections, which are regulated in detail by the administrative authority. Under the provisions of the law one must obtain, for every collection campaign, a permit from the administrative authority.
The permit is given only when the purpose of the campaign is not against the law and is worthy of being supported from the standpoint of the public interest.
Such permits can be granted only to registered associations, organisations that have the rights of legal persons, or specially created committees.
Only members of the associations or of related institutions, as well as persons invited by name, may take part in the campaigns.
It is not permitted to pay for taking part in a collection campaign.
The law provides for very close control of the campaigns by the administrative authority. Thus, for example, the authority has the right to inspect the cash books and documents, to take part in the meetings, and the like.
The result of every campaign and the manner in which the collected money is used must be reported to the authority and published in the press within 1 month of the end of the campaign.
The authority has the right to withdraw the permit at any time in case of failure to conform to the provisions of the law. In that case the authority may transfer the collected money to any social institution whatever or to humanitarian purposes.
Acting against the provisions of the law is severely punished, with arrest of up to 1 month and a fine of a thousand zł., or one of these penalties.
Both the organisers and the participants in the collection campaign may be punished.
Money collected without permits is confiscated and handed over to other institutions.
The law does not apply to collections in closed private premises, synagogue [or: school — “shul”] collections and the like (art. 13).
The law comes into force on the 30th[?] of this month.
It is clear that the law radically changes the system in use until now: a large number of associations and societies which have until now based their budget on the collection campaigns (“flower days”) will from now on not receive the permits. Those, too, who will benefit from the campaigns will have to fulfil various formalities, such as: keeping books, exact minute books in the language of the country, etc.
The above-mentioned law further provides for the issue of an ordinance by the Minister of the Interior, which will regulate in detail the technique of the collection campaigns.
It is therefore important that the associations and societies which must resort to public help should acquaint themselves with the law in good time and adapt themselves to its provisions, in order to be able to benefit from the campaigns.
Dr. R. R.

[Taxes — Finance Ministry circular.] In a circular of the Ministry of Finance of 23 March 1933, L. D. V. 11560/1/33, it is stated that, in order to remove from the books the tax arrears that are impossible to collect, the Treasury Chambers [Izby Skarbowe] are empowered to remit the tax arrears from before 1 December 1931: 1) in turnover tax up to 10 thousand zł. 2) in income tax up to 5000 zł. 3) in property tax up to 10 thousand zł. 4) in taxes on capital and annuities up to a thousand zł. 5) in land taxes up to 1,500 zł. 6) in taxes on immovable property up to a thousand zł. 7) in local taxes up to 500 zł.
The enumerated [sums] also include the share of the state tax; apart from that, the Treasury Chambers may also remit all surcharges to communal taxes, among others.
The Treasury Chambers are also empowered to remit all fines from before 31 December 1931.
The tax offices [Urzędy Skarbowe] are empowered 1) to remit taxes up to 100 zł., as well as fines, among others; 2) to spread payment in instalments (except advance payments — “zaliczki”) over 30 months up to a sum of 2,000 zł.; 3) to charge 3 per cent interest annually on taxes from before the year 1927 and 6 per cent from before 1930.
Whoever wishes to benefit from the said reliefs must submit an application, which should be reasoned.
The action of remitting the taxes must be completed by the end of the 6th month of this year.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — news column.]
German newspapers burned and Hitler "hanged" in Katowice.
On Sunday large anti-German demonstrations took place in Katowice, organised by the Polish academic youth.
Before noon 5 motor-cars appeared in Katowice with students sitting in them; the cars stopped at all the newspaper kiosks, from which the students took away all the German newspapers, weeklies and monthly journals.
Part of the newspapers the students tore up and part they burned in front of the building of the Voivodeship office and on the Rynek (market square), where a huge crowd of onlookers had gathered, who greeted the deed with applause.
Then a doll was hung on an electric wire on the Rynek, representing a Hitlerite storm-trooper with a swastika on its belly. The assembled public reacted in lively fashion. After the singing of Konopnicka's "Rota" a demonstration procession formed, which passed through[?] 3 Maja Street. In front of the editorial office of the "Kattowitzer Zeitung" shouts were raised, condemning the provocations of that chauvinist press organ.
Soon police arrived, who did not allow any further demonstrations; the editorial premises of all the German newspapers in Katowice were under police guard.
As is being said, Sunday's anti-German demonstration is the beginning of a broad campaign which will be carried out in all the towns and townlets of Polish Upper Silesia.
In connection with this, the German government has ordered the German consul-general in Katowice to hand the Polish authorities a categorical protest because a doll representing Chancellor Hitler was burned on the Rynek in Katowice.

The Mortgage Moratorium Is Being Introduced.

[Law and economy — mortgages.] In reply to the inquiry of many persons we explain that the moratorium law on mortgage debts has been passed and is valid from the 1st of this month.
The law, however, has not yet been published in the "Dz. Ustaw" (Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws), and therefore one cannot yet rely on it. But in the coming days it will be published.
One may take steps in court to obtain a stay of auctions (licytacje) on the strength of the law.
The mortgage moratorium applies to all debts that are entered on the mortgage register, urban and rural alike. It also applies to debts with which one has oneself gone onto the mortgage register.
The moratorium applies to mortgage debts and to mortgage guarantees on account of which the house is put up for auction.
